articles.title: Researchers warned of North Korean hacking tactics years before record $6.3B Binance heist
articles.body:
Crypto giant Binance says North Korean hackers used fake social media profiles and the lure of a potential job offer as part of a months-long scheme aimed at tricking an employee into downloading malicious software onto their laptop.
Researchers have repeatedly warned about long-running social engineering attacks that can go on for months.
This latest attack allowed the hackers to patiently worm their way into Binance’s systems to steal a record $6.3 billion in crypto last week, the company has now confirmed. The hack, disclosed in an updated statement posted on X on Tuesday, prompted the world’s largest crypto exchange to suspend customer withdrawals across its network.
The FBI and blockchain investigators have blamed North Korea for the heist. The country has been long accused of carrying out massive cryptocurrency thefts in recent years to fund its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program.
In its latest statement, Binance said that North Korean hackers, posing as recruiters hiring for a job, contacted a software engineer who works on wallets at the company. Following two interviews with the purported company, the engineer was instructed to download an apparent coding assignment as part of the interview process. When opened, the assignment contained malicious code that compromised the engineer’s work-issued laptop. Binance said its security tools did not detect the malware.
That foothold in Binance’s network allowed the hackers to access an internal tool capable of taking over the work computers of two other engineers on the wallet team. One of those engineers had unwittingly downloaded a tampered app containing password-stealing malware months earlier after searching for the software in search engine results. While Binance replaced that compromised engineer’s laptop, the hackers used the engineer’s stolen credentials to break into the computer of a third engineer, whose job allowed them access to systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in crypto.
Binance said the attack “should not have happened,” and that it had improved its network security following the theft.
The hack underscores an ongoing tactic in the North Korean regime’s repertoire of attacks targeting the crypto industry and high-net worth individuals. Researchers have warned for years that North Korean hackers pose as venture capitalists, investors, and recruiters using dossiers of stolen American identities to trick employees into granting access to their systems.
These attacks are widely known across the crypto industry and have been the subject of repeated warnings from the U.S. government and cybersecurity giants in recent years. Some half of all intrusions at U.S. tech companies last year were attributed to North Koreans posing as remote IT workers and fake recruiters.
By Binance’s own account, the company faced at least 57 suspected attacks from North Korea, which it said reflect the “persistent threat posed by state-sponsored actors targeting the cryptocurrency industry.”
But how the hackers were able to convince the engineer into downloading malware given the highly publicized threat, and bypass security weaknesses in Binance’s own network, will likely be the focus of investigators’ attention.
While the case exposes how North Korean hackers use social engineering, such as offers of employment, to trick employees into granting access to their systems, it’s ultimately the responsibility of the company to ensure its systems cannot run unauthorized or untrusted software that could cause a compromise.
A Binance spokesperson referred to the company’s public statement but declined to answer TechCrunch’s questions on the record about the incident. Those questions included how Binance prevents unauthorized or malicious code from running on its employees’ laptops, if at all, and whether any third parties had performed cybersecurity audits of Binance’s network prior to the hack.
The company said it would bring in cybersecurity experts to review the incident and has put new security measures in place to prevent a repeat incident.
The heist remains the largest theft of crypto in history.
Updated to remove name of Binance spokesperson in thirteenth paragraph.

articles.title: People Against Genocide Smash Military Satellites on Balfour Anniversary
articles.body:
Videos and images are free to use, with no credit needed
In the early hours of Monday 2nd November, on the 109th anniversary of the Balfour Declaration, a 3-person People Against Genocide (PAG) team, once again successfully evaded security at the Tring site of military tech and cyber warfare company Ultra Intelligence & Communications (Ultra I&C), and gained access to the building. Once inside the facility at Icknield Way, Tring, Hertfordshire HP23 4JX, the PAG team began dismantling military equipment including military satellites. The three were arrested after allegedly causing extensive damage inside the weapons facility.
Ultra I&C are a key supplier to UAV Tactical Systems, the Leicester subsidiary of Elbit Systems, Israel’s biggest weapons maker, who produce 85% of the Israeli military’s killer drone fleet, and 80% of their land-based weaponry and equipment. Elbit boast that their deadly products are “battle-tested” on Palestinians, and they have been used against civilian populations across West Asia.
Ultra I&C claim to specialise in “AI mission solutions” and “secure battlefield communications systems”, but job listings for Ultra I&C’s Tring site show that it is a manufacturing facility. This was confirmed by a data breach in 2024, which showed that as well as working with Elbit, Ultra I&C work with the Israeli military directly. On a previous PAG raid of the Tring factory, action-takers also found, and dismantled, satellites bound for the Israeli military, which the Crown Prosecution Service claim were worth £1.3 million.
Today’s action was timed to coincide with the anniversary of the signing of the notorious Balfour Declaration, in which the British government committed itself to the establishment of a “Jewish homeland” in Palestine, leading to the Palestinian Nakba, the destruction of hundreds of Palestinian villages, and the murder and expulsion of thousands of the country’s indigenous population. Today also marks one year since the Palestine Action prisoners began a collective hunger strike, which lasted 73 days.
Because of their involvement in the genocide in Gaza, PAG have targeted Ultra I & C facilities on a number of previous occasions. In addition to the previous action at Tring, they blockaded the Maidenead site in June, using lock-on devices, covering the Cambridge premises in blood-red paint and graffiti, at the end of July, and breaking into the Aberdeen site in August.
People Against Genocide issued the following statement:
“Our action today is timed to coincide with the 1917 signing of the bloody Balfour Declaration, in which the British government betrayed the Palestinian people. Consequently, the Palestinians suffered hundreds of attacks from Zionist terrorists, such as train and market bombings, and village massacres, which led on to the Nakba of 1948, and a further 78 years of ethnic cleansing and murder, culminating in the current genocide in Gaza, the pogroms in the West Bank, and a concerted attempt to exterminate the entire Palestinian population of Occupied Palestine.
“Not only did the British government sign away a country that was not theirs to give, they have continued to assist in the Zionist occupation of Palestine, and in the murder of its native population, right up to the present day. Chief among the other foreign actors actively assisting the genocide is, of course, Britain’s unruly offspring, the US, where Ultra I & C is headquartered. The firm is part of the military Industrial Complex, which makes billions from the slaughter of Palestinians, and uses Gaza as a testing ground. articles.title: I use AI (Oct 2026)
articles.body:
How I use AI (Oct 2026)
Wow, things have changed.
Last October, I took stock of how I was using AI — specifically the cool stuff like LLMs that we call 'AI’. I’m so glad I did. Things are very, very different 12 months later.
Background
I still believe I use AI fairly typically, but I’ve had a notable change in background. Last October, I was an engineer on Microsoft’s Windows AI team. I am now a research engineer at Salesforce AI Research. I spend more time supporting scientists & building rapid prototypes, rather than working with a large team of engineers. I spend about ~$3,000/month in tokens.
In any case, I mostly use AI in the same ways as last year:
- Coding
- Research & search
- Summarization & transcription & (new) voice
- Writing
- Art & music & (new) video
Also new this year, I’ve drafted a personal AI policy; we’ll start there.
As before, this remains purely my opinion & speculation. If you use AI differently, let me know!
My AI policy
This year I began drafting a personal AI policy — as in, a document for how I want to use AI in my life. I am very excited about it. I am also working on an explicit AI policy for this site (still thinkin’; probably based on Hank Green’s policy), but a personal policy is to give me a framework for using these tools day-to-day.
AI leaks into life. Teammates ask Claude to write their Slack messages, grandparents generate creepy memes of their grandchildren, and researchers delegate their thinking to machines. I’ve seen all of these things; even strong creators like Hank Green and BrainPOP get lost.
Humans clearly do not have norms for using these tools, and we’re messing up. I hope that a personal policy will ground me as AI becomes smarter. I hope to adapt that policy over time, and I’m eager to see how it evolves. I’m also open to draft 1 being utterly, hopelessly wrong.
Ultimately, I want to spend my life making cool things with other people. AI can help, AI can hurt. A policy helps me find the difference.
Coding
Writing code is solved.
Last year, I waxed poetic about how GitHub Copilot autocomplete transformed how I write code.
Well, uh, I no longer write much code. Agentic coding has made it obsolete.
My workday now means managing ~5–6 Claude Code (or OpenCode or Codex or Pi) agents. I’ll give Claude a feature to implement, or a bug to reproduce, or any other task I used to do by hand; each agent gets its own copy of the code (a Git worktree, if you’re technical), then just… gets to work. The agents write code, run tests, even create & review PRs.
They are nothing short of magic:
- They let me build fast: agents will prototype any new feature in ~20 minutes. I truly cannot count the number of features, bugfixes, tests, and tools I’ve (AI’ve?) been able to build because of these agents. For example, AI let me test confusing audio code on macOS and iOS in just a few minutes.
- They let me try crazy things: human teams aim to “fail fast”; agents can fail ultra-fast. I’m happy to test crazy new ideas and throw out what doesn’t work well. It was able to wire & test a huge change to Mumble that added better noise cancelling; I use my beta build of it nearly every day.
- They remove drudgery: I’ve had agents diagnose & fix urgent bugs with nothing more than a description and a “please fix!” while I continued working on other things.
- They let me be kinder: since agents write everything, it is simple to propose sweeping changes to my teammates during code review, or even write my own versions — both things unthinkable in the era of hand-written code.
I do not believe engineering is solved: left to run on their own, agents will build poorly-functioning, over-architected, unreadable, self-congratulatory piles of slop. Every friend I’ve asked agrees that agents still need human taste and experience to produce good work. Some of that is minutiae (like that annoying status dot Claude likes to throw onto sites), but most of it is critical. Agents tend to get lost on their own. My most successful work this year was hand-writing a tool, replacing ~4,000 lines of vibe-code with a few hundred. My system has proven more flexible, easier to test, and more generalizable than what it replaced.
It remains to be seen how long that human edge will last, though.
I also now reckon with the fatigue of using these agents. Managing 6 different conversations with 6 different robots about 6 different features is overstimulating & exhausting in a way that coding never was. When I started using agents, I remember rushing to answer their questions like they were human colleagues waiting for help! While I have tempered that anthropomorphic bias, it’s exhausting to juggle so many problems at once. The allure of sending just one more prompt before lunch… then dinner… oy. There is also, as I wrote in Consider the chairmaker, the decline of craft. My friend Peter laments ceding the joy of programming to machines: for many of us, honing the code, finding the right design, seeing the parts mesh together — that was the meditative purpose we found in our jobs. Now, we rarely write anything. We instead delegate it to agent number 7.
But let me return to the joy of working with agents: they are so fast, so open to feedback, and so intelligent. Working with them can be utterly delightful.
For example, while I was building a harness for voice agents, one programming agent decided (correctly) that my simple test harness was insufficient. So it used my Mac’s built-in text-to-speech to directly test the voice agent it was building. Then, newer agents started doing it, too. Either they had documented the technique, or they were each smart enough to independently discover it. Directly testing the product they were building. Absolutely brilliant.
Agents frequently recommend knobs & settings that I’ll reject for being too complex and unnecessary — and, voilà, I’ll need the knob next week. Silly human!
Anyway, because of agentic coding, agentic pull requests are increasingly the way I review agent code. “Make a draft PR,” I write, “I’ll review it soon!” And review it I do — agents still aren’t reliable enough to trust without validating, so I’ll still review their code & test it manually. However, I don’t do the “line-by-line” code reviews I used to do with humans. I focus instead on architecture, on larger patterns in the code. Are there systemic issues with an approach? Should I add new agent guidance to CLAUDE.md? Can I build better test harnesses, so the machines can test their own code?
Agentic code review is surprisingly helpful here: I try to write rules for the code review robots whenever I notice a recurring issue with generated code, so the agents will identify & fix issues by themselves. One rule I enjoyed creating: a "Claude-y comment detector." You think my writing is verbose? Try Claude’s.
On more typical engineering teams, human code review seems increasingly difficult. A friend of mine complained that his teammates simply ask “their” Claudes to review code written by other Claudes. An ouroboros of Claudes! Agents catch bugs & stylistic issues very well, but they are abysmal at designing architecture. Agentic code review is certainly not a replacement for humans yet.
Last year, I was skeptical of inline editing and code mode, both features of GitHub Copilot. They were not very useful then, and they are even less useful with agents. I have removed them from the table.
Research & search
Last year, I was excited about research & search: they were the most frequent reason I used ChatGPT. Now, generative AI is the default way I do those things.
The biggest change has been Google’s AI summary. Google’s first or second result is almost always an AI summary, and it’s usually decent. So my traditional search is now AI-first by default. Is it perfect? Absolutely not. In one day, it gave me incorrect URLs for NPR’s RSS feeds and couldn’t find the origin of “AI’ve”.
But none of the top results clearly gave me NPR’s RSS feeds either, and even Claude couldn’t find “AI’ve”. Meanwhile, searching “HP Reverb G2” gave me the specs I was looking for, “ai intelligence is spiky” pointed me to the correct term (“jagged”), “emoji sigh” gave me the right emoji without sending me to a scummy site, and “rel nofollow markdown” reminded me how to link that site without giving them search engine juice.
Product search is still mediocre. I’ll look at the summary when I search “best hysa”, but I don’t trust Gemini to have good advice on where to put my money. Claude certainly helped me explore budget VR options and understand technical details about grease for KitchenAid mixers, but can I trust its coffee table recommendations? Sleeper sofas? Let’s not even mention how uncomfortable it is to see ads in my ChatGPT chats.
Pub facts—stuff I’d ask my wife at a pub — remain awesome with LLMs. Again, Google’s AI summary means “lego cat on a balcony tiktok guy” will help me find @avadonye’s precarious LEGO builds, and “art vtuber who is a lizard on TikTok who gives short tutorials” will help me find Mallow, the art vtuber who is a lizard on TikTok who gives short tutorials.
I often avoid using LLMs for pub facts, in the same way I generally avoided Google for them before, because I like puzzling with my friends. I like Fermi problems.
But I’m more and more excited about using LLMs as teachers to explore well-known concepts. I breezed over this last year, but that is unfair to LLMs. I believe they are the greatest teachers humanity has ever created.
- I had an LLM walk me step-by-step through fine-tuning Mistral to speak like a pirate (yarrr).
- I used Claude to practice responding to an EMS call I heard on the radio.
- I had Claude use a socractic method skill I found via Dan MacKinlay to help me brainstorm new approaches for semantic endpointing (knowing when a user is done speaking) in voice agents.
- I asked Claude to explain typical approaches to a complex legal document.
- I’ve even had Claude quiz me on a long code review, to ensure I understood what the agent had written. The open-source project Mumble actually added a similar quiz to their AGENTS.md a few weeks ago.
I am actually jealous of the endless care & patience that these machines show. I hope we discover how to share this patience with our kids while ensuring our kids still learn. Veritasium’s Derek Muller discusses this in What Everyone Gets Wrong About AI and Learning: AI is incredible at drilling repetitive practice, at giving immediate feedback, of all the things a private tutor can do… if you ask it to.
“The world is full of heavy objects,” he says, “and yet most people are not ripped.”
That is my greatest fear with AI tutoring today. That these machines must be reminded to teach. Per Muller, learning requires Type 2 thinking — enaging the slow, reasoning mode of your brain. This is very difficult. Your body will surreptitiously & continuously nudge you out of this mode. Tutors exist to force you back into it. But ChatGPT exists to do things for you: it is so fine-tuned for that use that it tends to forget “it’s meant to be a tutor”, even when previously asked. What learning may occur when you have both forgotten your desire to learn?
This differs from my biggest concern last year: accuracy. Responses then often had basic factual errors, but that seems less of an issue today. I think there are 2 basic factors:
- I am more AI-literate. I think more of us have a “sense” of what AI can do well, so we avoid the jagged edges. I don’t, for example, trust ChatGPT’s ability to read sparsely-digitized documents from 1867. So I asked hopefully, then basically ignored its findings.
- AI is smarter. Just like in coding, I think we hit an inflection point this year, where models are simply smart enough to answer more things reliably. MAJOR spoilers for Control if you click, but there’s a reason Google’s AI summary of its ending (using Gemini 3, from November 2025) is simple and correct while Bing’s (using ~GPT 4o, from May 2024) is not, conflating the game with its sequel.
This trend extends to literature searches. Last year, I shared my trepidation about using LLMs for complex literature searches. My skepticism remains: these machines have access to everything ever written, so they can support any premise in good faith. Also, it is well-demonstrated that LLMs have default bias, politically or in other fields, like business strategy. I am worried about their ability to subtly impose worldview, either on their own or at the behest of corporations and governments.
Yet LLMs are now my first choice for literature searches. That’s partially because Google searches have that AI summary on top, so I end up reading it, but also because LLMs have been much more effective than traditional search at finding good, nuanced data for me — despite potential bias. You must remember that Google Scholar search kinda sucks: when I started researching Car touchscreens are cheap, not good, for months I could not find any studies beyond one done by an auto magazine—Vi Bilägare. That was despite having worked at a Georgia Tech lab that researched car user interfaces! Especially as they’ve gotten smarter & I’ve developed intuition, LLMs are good finders. Just see Claude’s investigation into human perceptions of latency for me:
Ultimately, though, human experts are still more reliable than agents. That’s how I moved forward with “Car touchscreens”—I asked someone from that GT lab. I’ve also been buying more books, even slightly-obsolete ones like Card, Morgan, & Newell’s The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (everyone, including LLMs, cite it) or old editions of Wicken’s Engineering Psychology and Human Performance (via a nuclear consultant I met at a wedding). They ground my research, simply by offering a legible worldview.
And that’s why I’ve been disappointed in AI as collaborator for novel research. AI has harmed some research I’ve been doing.
My team at Salesforce has been working on voice stuff, and I’ve been trying to improve turn detection — understanding when a user is done speaking. That’s a hard problem, and it’s been a great opportunity to read fundamental research on how human conversation works (finally!). AI was great at finding that research and good datasets (though my teammates gave me context the AI never did). And it was great when I asked it to use the Socratic method to help me design my own turn detection model — until, on a whim, I asked: “are there better architectures?” Why yes, yes there were. AI had led me astray.
That’s not the only time AI waylaid me. LLMs could not figure out how to annotate that model’s training data correctly. I spent days going back and forth with them, trying to decide how to separate turns from interruptions. It is embarrassing how simple the problem became after one good discussion with a human teammate. LLMs are not yet good companions when brainstorming complicated things.
It is weird to write this when OpenAI just solved a Millenium Problem, proved a weaker version of another, solved hundreds more, and releases more solutions every day. But those results cost “millions of dollars”: you need to burn tokens, having agents review agents review agents… just to produce something coherent. In my case, I find I enter this “AI fog” where it takes more effort to review the agent’s response than to come up with my own answers.
It is obvious that AI researchers are coming. Just… not today, not with me.
Summarization & transcription & voice
LLMs (and local models!) remain uninterestingly good at summarization & transcription.
I’ve been using OpenWhispr and Handy to dictate to my computer, especially to talk to my agents. The best models on the planet run on your computer locally, for free. My biggest complaint is that the apps have bugs (hotkeys work inconsistently, etc.). It’s hard to describe a more boring type of success.
My meetings have automatic notes. My friend built a local pipeline to transcribe & search his childhood home videos. Vikram Oberoi built a site (in 2024!) that automatically transcribes NYC city hall meetings. You can do all of these things on your Mac.
However, I have yet to reliably use voice beyond dictation.
There’s a reason my team at Salesforce is researching it: voice is the original modality. It should be a seamless way of talking to these human-like robots. But I have never felt compelled to talk to my robots; it’s never been frictionless or private-feeling or useful enough. Does old-school Siri count?
Writing
Last year: “ew.” This year: “ew.”
I still do not use AI to write from scratch, nor as an outlining aid, for things I make.
I’ve narrowed this rule a bit from last year. Last year, I argued that LLMs always lacked context and so were poor communicators. With agentic coding, that’s changed. So I’ve had agents document experiments I designed but had no hand in executing, or write READMEs for code they generated end-to-end.
But even that limited exception irks me. I do not like when I stumble upon AI-generated spew, so why should I subject others to it? To that end, I’ve started prompting my agents to identify themselves whenever they write prose, and I often end up rewriting their documents myself (or at least adding an executive summary). That has helped, but I’m not certain it is enough.
In general, I’m surprised how bad AI remains at writing. AI writing is demanding to read: usually plodding, repetitive, and vapid — but then randomly terse and vague, like it doesn’t understand its own words. Agents will so often cite & quote & summarize every paper ever published, then synthesize it all into a mound of nonsense. That is the AI fog I hit: do I misunderstand all these new papers, or did the LLM just serve up some pseudo-profound bullshit? It is bewildering to me that these models can solve generational math problems on one hand, yet utterly fail to describe turn-taking behavior in humans on the other. That is, I guess, their jagged intelligence. They do not reason like we do. They cannot be fine-tuned to speak like we do. So they solve problems we cannot, and share them in reports we struggle to understand.
In any case, it should not be surprising that I do not use AI for writing or outlining in my communication; neither at work nor on this blog. My employer pays me for my ideas, which only I can voice. And I write on this blog for fun. Writing is an art and a skill I enjoy pursuing.
Why would I delegate my voice to a machine that writes tedious dreck?
It’s still great for finding words. Google AI talked me out of writing “hawking off” (which is not an expression) instead of “ceding” later on. But I’m tempering my regard for it as an editor. Despite my positive & worried assessment last year, when I spoke to several friends who asked agents to edit their job applications, their feedback was universally tepid. Agents were sycophantic, reluctant to be critical. And anyone who worked around this (by saying, for example, "my friend wrote this") found that agents offered misplaced, trite advice that lacked nuance. The agents seemed to regress to the mean: helping those with the worst writing and hindering those with the best. The agents were… fine.
As one friend put it:
[AI writing] is as good as it was 3 years ago. Which, when you consider how much everything else has changed since then…
I avoided using AI editors altogether this year, out of fear that they would erase my voice. But I’m increasingly certain they would just blandify it. AI tells remain the same as always (“You’re absolutely right!”), and these machines seem incapable of improvement without substantial guidance. Perhaps it’s survivorship bias, but these very smart machines produce very mediocre writing.
Art & music & video
Finally, art. I still don’t have a good use for image generation.
Last year, I used AI to generate a few odds and ends, but I stopped this year, mostly out of a vague sense of discomfort. I felt like I was ceding opportunities for creativity to the mediocrity machine.
I’ve enjoyed a lot of the low-effort memes I’ve seen; We need more data centers is one of my favorite jokes all year. And AI helped design some useful presentations I attended. But I’m not sure how AI art fits into life on Earth. Last year I thought I saw AI art at a gift shop. Well, now I’ve seen AI Sketchers ads, AI event posters, AI restaurant menus, AI logos for stores and e-sports teams, AI canvases at HomeSense, and AI t-shirts at Walmart. It’s everywhere, and it’s explicitly replacing human art. Gross.
AI music generation is perplexing in the opposite way. Last year, I worried that I would grow equally tired of it. But no! I’m really enjoying some AI music — and so is the rest of the world. The viral San Juan song inspired covers from humans and lip sync videos from “Mila Kunis, Charlie Puth and Jennifer Love Hewitt”. AI has also inspired new genres: I’ve been humming AI is normal technology? (95k views), LGTM (Looks Good to Me) (1.6M), and The Simulation’s Ending (169k) for weeks. As one commenter wrote on OMG! We’ve found other agents (120k):
I think AI art & music are beautiful when they are used as lenses for human creativity, rather than replacements for it. I guessed something similar last year, and I think last year’s music proved me right. As soon as commercialism replaced creativity, I was out. I soured on Eiden XII when they started sharing new “but it hits different” covers weekly, and I got bored of steel coils-style edutainment after hearing the first clone. There’s something cynical and manipulative about a synthetic woman belting “talk me out of dying” when some dude (presumably) makes money every time I play it.
Similarly, I haven’t listened to any of the new Doompop that’s hit my feed. It’s cool when you generate a few songs; less cool when you post every day. It feels like vultures picking ad revenue from the corpse of a good idea.
That is evident in the world of video generation. I largely escaped last year (although my mom got some weird whale-cleaning videos), but now I’m seeing a bunch. I see AI ads all the time — most memorably with horrid horse-people in Sixt ads. I got baited into a video of a fake Edna Mode lookalike & some slop WW2 history videos, and my wife got tricked by AI summaries of Adventure Time marketed as sleep aids. All of them hoping to get views, to get ad revenue, to get — as Corridor Digital puts it—“a little bit skimmed off of that YouTube trough.” It is sobering to open an AI history video in Incognito and gaze at the misleading slop recommended next to it:
It is horrid to see these machines that can mass-produce art being used to mass-produce art. And I know that seems silly, but there’s a world where we use these tools to elevate artists, just like coding agents elevate me.
I am lucky I do not make my living from art. Art remains valuable to me. Even if AI can write a song faster than I can, I still doodle, I still play piano.
Drawin' it yourself is more fun, anyway.
Conclusion
So here we are, 12 months later.
12 months since my first abortive attempts to have agents write code. 10 months since Claude Code first made me say, “wow,” when it built me an insurance comparison tool in one shot. And now machines write 90%+ of my code.
It is easy to forget how new this is. 15 months ago, AI did well at a prestigious high school math competition. 2 months ago, AI solved Navier-Stokes.
Last year, I wrote: “I’m confident we’re just starting to see what AI can achieve.” That remains true. We are just now beginning to see what these mechanized coders and mathematicians can build. My friends have built each other tools to communicate. I was able to finally clean up and share a tool I’d started in 2020. Agents helped me finish up an open-source change I’d wanted to make for years, start making an app, test massive changes to old software, and quickly understand new operating systems.
That is just the start.
It is a brave new world. Where these machines also ship corporate slop and leave mathematicians in shock. But I think of how my uncle uses these tools to build his own software; how my friends make software that helps us stay in touch; how these things have helped me learn so, so much. Tools can be used to help people.
That is how I hope to use AI.
Thanks to Peter Kreiseder and Atherai Maran for consulting. Claude helped make the status icon look more Claude-y.
Want next year's article? (and others in between)
No spam. Just an email for new posts.
Appendix: my subscriptions
In case you’re wondering, I’m subscribed to:
- Claude Pro ($17/mo)
- GitHub Copilot Pro ($10/mo)
I cancelled OpenAI about a month ago, which is crazy. OpenAI was my first AI subscription! But most of my personal usage is Claude Code, and I ended up using Claude for random questions instead of ChatGPT. And last year we thought OpenAI was so far ahead!
I use GitHub Copilot Pro solely for autocomplete.

articles.title: How I use AI (Oct 2026)
articles.body:
How I use AI (Oct 2026)
Wow, things have changed.
Last October, I took stock of how I was using AI — specifically the cool stuff like LLMs that we call 'AI’. I’m so glad I did. Things are very, very different 12 months later.
Background
I still believe I use AI fairly typically, but I’ve had a notable change in background. Last October, I was an engineer on Microsoft’s Windows AI team. I am now a research engineer at Salesforce AI Research. I spend more time supporting scientists & building rapid prototypes, rather than working with a large team of engineers. I spend about ~$3,000/month in tokens.
In any case, I mostly use AI in the same ways as last year:
- Coding
- Research & search
- Summarization & transcription & (new) voice
- Writing
- Art & music & (new) video
Also new this year, I’ve drafted a personal AI policy; we’ll start there.
As before, this remains purely my opinion & speculation. If you use AI differently, let me know!
My AI policy
This year I began drafting a personal AI policy — as in, a document for how I want to use AI in my life. I am very excited about it. I am also working on an explicit AI policy for this site (still thinkin’; probably based on Hank Green’s policy), but a personal policy is to give me a framework for using these tools day-to-day.
AI leaks into life. Teammates ask Claude to write their Slack messages, grandparents generate creepy memes of their grandchildren, and researchers delegate their thinking to machines. I’ve seen all of these things; even strong creators like Hank Green and BrainPOP get lost.
Humans clearly do not have norms for using these tools, and we’re messing up. I hope that a personal policy will ground me as AI becomes smarter. I hope to adapt that policy over time, and I’m eager to see how it evolves. I’m also open to draft 1 being utterly, hopelessly wrong.
Ultimately, I want to spend my life making cool things with other people. AI can help, AI can hurt. A policy helps me find the difference.
Coding
Writing code is solved.
Last year, I waxed poetic about how GitHub Copilot autocomplete transformed how I write code.
Well, uh, I no longer write much code. Agentic coding has made it obsolete.
My workday now means managing ~5–6 Claude Code (or OpenCode or Codex or Pi) agents. I’ll give Claude a feature to implement, or a bug to reproduce, or any other task I used to do by hand; each agent gets its own copy of the code (a Git worktree, if you’re technical), then just… gets to work. The agents write code, run tests, even create & review PRs.
They are nothing short of magic:
- They let me build fast: agents will prototype any new feature in ~20 minutes. I truly cannot count the number of features, bugfixes, tests, and tools I’ve (AI’ve?) been able to build because of these agents. For example, AI let me test confusing audio code on macOS and iOS in just a few minutes.
- They let me try crazy things: human teams aim to “fail fast”; agents can fail ultra-fast. I’m happy to test crazy new ideas and throw out what doesn’t work well. It was able to wire & test a huge change to Mumble that added better noise cancelling; I use my beta build of it nearly every day.
- They remove drudgery: I’ve had agents diagnose & fix urgent bugs with nothing more than a description and a “please fix!” while I continued working on other things.
- They let me be kinder: since agents write everything, it is simple to propose sweeping changes to my teammates during code review, or even write my own versions — both things unthinkable in the era of hand-written code.
I do not believe engineering is solved: left to run on their own, agents will build poorly-functioning, over-architected, unreadable, self-congratulatory piles of slop. Every friend I’ve asked agrees that agents still need human taste and experience to produce good work. Some of that is minutiae (like that annoying status dot Claude likes to throw onto sites), but most of it is critical. Agents tend to get lost on their own. My most successful work this year was hand-writing a tool, replacing ~4,000 lines of vibe-code with a few hundred. My system has proven more flexible, easier to test, and more generalizable than what it replaced.
It remains to be seen how long that human edge will last, though.
I also now reckon with the fatigue of using these agents. Managing 6 different conversations with 6 different robots about 6 different features is overstimulating & exhausting in a way that coding never was. When I started using agents, I remember rushing to answer their questions like they were human colleagues waiting for help! While I have tempered that anthropomorphic bias, it’s exhausting to juggle so many problems at once. The allure of sending just one more prompt before lunch… then dinner… oy. There is also, as I wrote in Consider the chairmaker, the decline of craft. My friend Peter laments ceding the joy of programming to machines: for many of us, honing the code, finding the right design, seeing the parts mesh together — that was the meditative purpose we found in our jobs. Now, we rarely write anything. We instead delegate it to agent number 7.
But let me return to the joy of working with agents: they are so fast, so open to feedback, and so intelligent. Working with them can be utterly delightful.
For example, while I was building a harness for voice agents, one programming agent decided (correctly) that my simple test harness was insufficient. So it used my Mac’s built-in text-to-speech to directly test the voice agent it was building. Then, newer agents started doing it, too. Either they had documented the technique, or they were each smart enough to independently discover it. Directly testing the product they were building. Absolutely brilliant.
Agents frequently recommend knobs & settings that I’ll reject for being too complex and unnecessary — and, voilà, I’ll need the knob next week. Silly human!
Anyway, because of agentic coding, agentic pull requests are increasingly the way I review agent code. “Make a draft PR,” I write, “I’ll review it soon!” And review it I do — agents still aren’t reliable enough to trust without validating, so I’ll still review their code & test it manually. However, I don’t do the “line-by-line” code reviews I used to do with humans. I focus instead on architecture, on larger patterns in the code. Are there systemic issues with an approach? Should I add new agent guidance to CLAUDE.md? Can I build better test harnesses, so the machines can test their own code?
Agentic code review is surprisingly helpful here: I try to write rules for the code review robots whenever I notice a recurring issue with generated code, so the agents will identify & fix issues by themselves. One rule I enjoyed creating: a "Claude-y comment detector." You think my writing is verbose? Try Claude’s.
On more typical engineering teams, human code review seems increasingly difficult. A friend of mine complained that his teammates simply ask “their” Claudes to review code written by other Claudes. An ouroboros of Claudes! Agents catch bugs & stylistic issues very well, but they are abysmal at designing architecture. Agentic code review is certainly not a replacement for humans yet.
Last year, I was skeptical of inline editing and code mode, both features of GitHub Copilot. They were not very useful then, and they are even less useful with agents. I have removed them from the table.
Research & search
Last year, I was excited about research & search: they were the most frequent reason I used ChatGPT. Now, generative AI is the default way I do those things.
The biggest change has been Google’s AI summary. Google’s first or second result is almost always an AI summary, and it’s usually decent. So my traditional search is now AI-first by default. Is it perfect? Absolutely not. In one day, it gave me incorrect URLs for NPR’s RSS feeds and couldn’t find the origin of “AI’ve”.
But none of the top results clearly gave me NPR’s RSS feeds either, and even Claude couldn’t find “AI’ve”. Meanwhile, searching “HP Reverb G2” gave me the specs I was looking for, “ai intelligence is spiky” pointed me to the correct term (“jagged”), “emoji sigh” gave me the right emoji without sending me to a scummy site, and “rel nofollow markdown” reminded me how to link that site without giving them search engine juice.
Product search is still mediocre. I’ll look at the summary when I search “best hysa”, but I don’t trust Gemini to have good advice on where to put my money. Claude certainly helped me explore budget VR options and understand technical details about grease for KitchenAid mixers, but can I trust its coffee table recommendations? Sleeper sofas? Let’s not even mention how uncomfortable it is to see ads in my ChatGPT chats.
Pub facts—stuff I’d ask my wife at a pub — remain awesome with LLMs. Again, Google’s AI summary means “lego cat on a balcony tiktok guy” will help me find @avadonye’s precarious LEGO builds, and “art vtuber who is a lizard on TikTok who gives short tutorials” will help me find Mallow, the art vtuber who is a lizard on TikTok who gives short tutorials.
I often avoid using LLMs for pub facts, in the same way I generally avoided Google for them before, because I like puzzling with my friends. I like Fermi problems.
But I’m more and more excited about using LLMs as teachers to explore well-known concepts. I breezed over this last year, but that is unfair to LLMs. I believe they are the greatest teachers humanity has ever created.
- I had an LLM walk me step-by-step through fine-tuning Mistral to speak like a pirate (yarrr).
- I used Claude to practice responding to an EMS call I heard on the radio.
- I had Claude use a socractic method skill I found via Dan MacKinlay to help me brainstorm new approaches for semantic endpointing (knowing when a user is done speaking) in voice agents.
- I asked Claude to explain typical approaches to a complex legal document.
- I’ve even had Claude quiz me on a long code review, to ensure I understood what the agent had written. The open-source project Mumble actually added a similar quiz to their AGENTS.md a few weeks ago.
I am actually jealous of the endless care & patience that these machines show. I hope we discover how to share this patience with our kids while ensuring our kids still learn. Veritasium’s Derek Muller discusses this in What Everyone Gets Wrong About AI and Learning: AI is incredible at drilling repetitive practice, at giving immediate feedback, of all the things a private tutor can do… if you ask it to.
“The world is full of heavy objects,” he says, “and yet most people are not ripped.”
That is my greatest fear with AI tutoring today. That these machines must be reminded to teach. Per Muller, learning requires Type 2 thinking — enaging the slow, reasoning mode of your brain. This is very difficult. Your body will surreptitiously & continuously nudge you out of this mode. Tutors exist to force you back into it. But ChatGPT exists to do things for you: it is so fine-tuned for that use that it tends to forget “it’s meant to be a tutor”, even when previously asked. What learning may occur when you have both forgotten your desire to learn?
This differs from my biggest concern last year: accuracy. Responses then often had basic factual errors, but that seems less of an issue today. I think there are 2 basic factors:
- I am more AI-literate. I think more of us have a “sense” of what AI can do well, so we avoid the jagged edges. I don’t, for example, trust ChatGPT’s ability to read sparsely-digitized documents from 1867. So I asked hopefully, then basically ignored its findings.
- AI is smarter. Just like in coding, I think we hit an inflection point this year, where models are simply smart enough to answer more things reliably. MAJOR spoilers for Control if you click, but there’s a reason Google’s AI summary of its ending (using Gemini 3, from November 2025) is simple and correct while Bing’s (using ~GPT 4o, from May 2024) is not, conflating the game with its sequel.
This trend extends to literature searches. Last year, I shared my trepidation about using LLMs for complex literature searches. My skepticism remains: these machines have access to everything ever written, so they can support any premise in good faith. Also, it is well-demonstrated that LLMs have default bias, politically or in other fields, like business strategy. I am worried about their ability to subtly impose worldview, either on their own or at the behest of corporations and governments.
Yet LLMs are now my first choice for literature searches. That’s partially because Google searches have that AI summary on top, so I end up reading it, but also because LLMs have been much more effective than traditional search at finding good, nuanced data for me — despite potential bias. You must remember that Google Scholar search kinda sucks: when I started researching Car touchscreens are cheap, not good, for months I could not find any studies beyond one done by an auto magazine—Vi Bilägare. That was despite having worked at a Georgia Tech lab that researched car user interfaces! Especially as they’ve gotten smarter & I’ve developed intuition, LLMs are good finders. Just see Claude’s investigation into human perceptions of latency for me:
Ultimately, though, human experts are still more reliable than agents. That’s how I moved forward with “Car touchscreens”—I asked someone from that GT lab. I’ve also been buying more books, even slightly-obsolete ones like Card, Morgan, & Newell’s The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (everyone, including LLMs, cite it) or old editions of Wicken’s Engineering Psychology and Human Performance (via a nuclear consultant I met at a wedding). They ground my research, simply by offering a legible worldview.
And that’s why I’ve been disappointed in AI as collaborator for novel research. AI has harmed some research I’ve been doing.
My team at Salesforce has been working on voice stuff, and I’ve been trying to improve turn detection — understanding when a user is done speaking. That’s a hard problem, and it’s been a great opportunity to read fundamental research on how human conversation works (finally!). AI was great at finding that research and good datasets (though my teammates gave me context the AI never did). And it was great when I asked it to use the Socratic method to help me design my own turn detection model — until, on a whim, I asked: “are there better architectures?” Why yes, yes there were. AI had led me astray.
That’s not the only time AI waylaid me. LLMs could not figure out how to annotate that model’s training data correctly. I spent days going back and forth with them, trying to decide how to separate turns from interruptions. It is embarrassing how simple the problem became after one good discussion with a human teammate. LLMs are not yet good companions when brainstorming complicated things.
It is weird to write this when OpenAI just solved a Millenium Problem, proved a weaker version of another, solved hundreds more, and releases more solutions every day. But those results cost “millions of dollars”: you need to burn tokens, having agents review agents review agents… just to produce something coherent. In my case, I find I enter this “AI fog” where it takes more effort to review the agent’s response than to come up with my own answers.
It is obvious that AI researchers are coming. Just… not today, not with me.
Summarization & transcription & voice
LLMs (and local models!) remain uninterestingly good at summarization & transcription.
I’ve been using OpenWhispr and Handy to dictate to my computer, especially to talk to my agents. The best models on the planet run on your computer locally, for free. My biggest complaint is that the apps have bugs (hotkeys work inconsistently, etc.). It’s hard to describe a more boring type of success.
My meetings have automatic notes. My friend built a local pipeline to transcribe & search his childhood home videos. Vikram Oberoi built a site (in 2024!) that automatically transcribes NYC city hall meetings. You can do all of these things on your Mac.
However, I have yet to reliably use voice beyond dictation.
There’s a reason my team at Salesforce is researching it: voice is the original modality. It should be a seamless way of talking to these human-like robots. But I have never felt compelled to talk to my robots; it’s never been frictionless or private-feeling or useful enough. Does old-school Siri count?
Writing
Last year: “ew.” This year: “ew.”
I still do not use AI to write from scratch, nor as an outlining aid, for things I make.
I’ve narrowed this rule a bit from last year. Last year, I argued that LLMs always lacked context and so were poor communicators. With agentic coding, that’s changed. So I’ve had agents document experiments I designed but had no hand in executing, or write READMEs for code they generated end-to-end.
But even that limited exception irks me. I do not like when I stumble upon AI-generated spew, so why should I subject others to it? To that end, I’ve started prompting my agents to identify themselves whenever they write prose, and I often end up rewriting their documents myself (or at least adding an executive summary). That has helped, but I’m not certain it is enough.
In general, I’m surprised how bad AI remains at writing. AI writing is demanding to read: usually plodding, repetitive, and vapid — but then randomly terse and vague, like it doesn’t understand its own words. Agents will so often cite & quote & summarize every paper ever published, then synthesize it all into a mound of nonsense. That is the AI fog I hit: do I misunderstand all these new papers, or did the LLM just serve up some pseudo-profound bullshit? It is bewildering to me that these models can solve generational math problems on one hand, yet utterly fail to describe turn-taking behavior in humans on the other. That is, I guess, their jagged intelligence. They do not reason like we do. They cannot be fine-tuned to speak like we do. So they solve problems we cannot, and share them in reports we struggle to understand.
In any case, it should not be surprising that I do not use AI for writing or outlining in my communication; neither at work nor on this blog. My employer pays me for my ideas, which only I can voice. And I write on this blog for fun. Writing is an art and a skill I enjoy pursuing.
Why would I delegate my voice to a machine that writes tedious dreck?
It’s still great for finding words. Google AI talked me out of writing “hawking off” (which is not an expression) instead of “ceding” later on. But I’m tempering my regard for it as an editor. Despite my positive & worried assessment last year, when I spoke to several friends who asked agents to edit their job applications, their feedback was universally tepid. Agents were sycophantic, reluctant to be critical. And anyone who worked around this (by saying, for example, "my friend wrote this") found that agents offered misplaced, trite advice that lacked nuance. The agents seemed to regress to the mean: helping those with the worst writing and hindering those with the best. The agents were… fine.
As one friend put it:
[AI writing] is as good as it was 3 years ago. Which, when you consider how much everything else has changed since then…
I avoided using AI editors altogether this year, out of fear that they would erase my voice. But I’m increasingly certain they would just blandify it. AI tells remain the same as always (“You’re absolutely right!”), and these machines seem incapable of improvement without substantial guidance. Perhaps it’s survivorship bias, but these very smart machines produce very mediocre writing.
Art & music & video
Finally, art. I still don’t have a good use for image generation.
Last year, I used AI to generate a few odds and ends, but I stopped this year, mostly out of a vague sense of discomfort. I felt like I was ceding opportunities for creativity to the mediocrity machine.
I’ve enjoyed a lot of the low-effort memes I’ve seen; We need more data centers is one of my favorite jokes all year. And AI helped design some useful presentations I attended. But I’m not sure how AI art fits into life on Earth. Last year I thought I saw AI art at a gift shop. Well, now I’ve seen AI Sketchers ads, AI event posters, AI restaurant menus, AI logos for stores and e-sports teams, AI canvases at HomeSense, and AI t-shirts at Walmart. It’s everywhere, and it’s explicitly replacing human art. Gross.
AI music generation is perplexing in the opposite way. Last year, I worried that I would grow equally tired of it. But no! I’m really enjoying some AI music — and so is the rest of the world. The viral San Juan song inspired covers from humans and lip sync videos from “Mila Kunis, Charlie Puth and Jennifer Love Hewitt”. AI has also inspired new genres: I’ve been humming AI is normal technology? (95k views), LGTM (Looks Good to Me) (1.6M), and The Simulation’s Ending (169k) for weeks. As one commenter wrote on OMG! We’ve found other agents (120k):
I think AI art & music are beautiful when they are used as lenses for human creativity, rather than replacements for it. I guessed something similar last year, and I think last year’s music proved me right. As soon as commercialism replaced creativity, I was out. I soured on Eiden XII when they started sharing new “but it hits different” covers weekly, and I got bored of steel coils-style edutainment after hearing the first clone. There’s something cynical and manipulative about a synthetic woman belting “talk me out of dying” when some dude (presumably) makes money every time I play it.
Similarly, I haven’t listened to any of the new Doompop that’s hit my feed. It’s cool when you generate a few songs; less cool when you post every day. It feels like vultures picking ad revenue from the corpse of a good idea.
That is evident in the world of video generation. I largely escaped last year (although my mom got some weird whale-cleaning videos), but now I’m seeing a bunch. I see AI ads all the time — most memorably with horrid horse-people in Sixt ads. I got baited into a video of a fake Edna Mode lookalike & some slop WW2 history videos, and my wife got tricked by AI summaries of Adventure Time marketed as sleep aids. All of them hoping to get views, to get ad revenue, to get — as Corridor Digital puts it—“a little bit skimmed off of that YouTube trough.” It is sobering to open an AI history video in Incognito and gaze at the misleading slop recommended next to it:
It is horrid to see these machines that can mass-produce art being used to mass-produce art. And I know that seems silly, but there’s a world where we use these tools to elevate artists, just like coding agents elevate me.
I am lucky I do not make my living from art. Art remains valuable to me. Even if AI can write a song faster than I can, I still doodle, I still play piano.
Drawin' it yourself is more fun, anyway.
Conclusion
So here we are, 12 months later.
12 months since my first abortive attempts to have agents write code. 10 months since Claude Code first made me say, “wow,” when it built me an insurance comparison tool in one shot. And now machines write 90%+ of my code.
It is easy to forget how new this is. 15 months ago, AI did well at a prestigious high school math competition. 2 months ago, AI solved Navier-Stokes.
Last year, I wrote: “I’m confident we’re just starting to see what AI can achieve.” That remains true. We are just now beginning to see what these mechanized coders and mathematicians can build. My friends have built each other tools to communicate. I was able to finally clean up and share a tool I’d started in 2020. Agents helped me finish up an open-source change I’d wanted to make for years, start making an app, test massive changes to old software, and quickly understand new operating systems.
That is just the start.
It is a brave new world. Where these machines also ship corporate slop and leave mathematicians in shock. But I think of how my uncle uses these tools to build his own software; how my friends make software that helps us stay in touch; how these things have helped me learn so, so much. Tools can be used to help people.
That is how I hope to use AI.
Thanks to Peter Kreiseder and Atherai Maran for consulting. Claude helped make the status icon look more Claude-y.
Want next year's article? (and others in between)
No spam. Just an email for new posts.
Appendix: my subscriptions
In case you’re wondering, I’m subscribed to:
- Claude Pro ($17/mo)
- GitHub Copilot Pro ($10/mo)
I cancelled OpenAI about a month ago, which is crazy. OpenAI was my first AI subscription! But most of my personal usage is Claude Code, and I ended up using Claude for random questions instead of ChatGPT. And last year we thought OpenAI was so far ahead!
I use GitHub Copilot Pro solely for autocomplete.

articles.title: Snapchat Is Harming Children at an Industrial Scale (2025)
articles.body:
Introduction
On October 1, 2024, investigative journalist Jeff Horwitz reported a startling statistic from an internal Snap Inc. email quoted in a court case against Snap Inc., the company which owns Snapchat. The email noted that the company receives around 10,000 reports of sextortion each month—and that figure is likely “only a fraction of the total abuse occurring on the platform.”
This statistic prompted us to investigate what else Snap Inc. knows or believes about the impact of its product on users, particularly teens (We estimate that roughly 13 million American 13-17 year-olds use Snapchat). Over the past several months, we have examined multiple court cases filed against Snap Inc., many involving severe or fatal harm that was (allegedly) facilitated by Snapchat’s features. From 2022 through 2025, as part of the Multidistrict Litigation (MDL) and Judicial Council Coordinated Proceedings (JCCP) against social media defendants, more than 6001 such lawsuits specifically named Snap Inc. as a defendant. In addition, state attorneys general from Nevada and New Mexico have brought significant cases against the company—two cases which we will draw heavily from in this post.
Following the format of our previous post about the “industrial scale harms” attributed to TikTok, this piece presents dozens of quotations from internal reports, studies, memos, conversations, and public statements in which Snap executives, employees, and consultants acknowledge and discuss the harms that Snapchat causes to many minors who use their platform. We group these findings into five key clusters of harms:
- Addictive, Compulsive, and Problematic Use
- Drugs and Guns
- Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM), Sextortion, and In-person Sexual Predation and Assault
- Cyberbullying
- Knowledge of Harm and Underage Use, and Lack of Action
Similar to TikTok, we show that company insiders were aware of multiple widespread and serious harms, and in many cases did not act promptly or make substantial changes. As Snap’s director of security engineering said regarding Android users who are selling drugs or child sexual abuse material on Snap:
“That’s fine it’s been broken for ten years we can tolerate tonight.”2
With regard to sextortion on the platform, one employee had complained in a private channel:
“God I’m so pissed that were over-run by this sextortion shit right now. We’ve twiddled our thumbs and wrung our hands all f…ing year.”3
The briefs allege that the company is also aware of rampant underage use, and of the ineffectiveness of their age gating process. Snap executives have admitted that Snapchat’s age verification system
“Is effectively useless in stopping underage users from signing up to the Snapchat app.”4
Although the evidence below is all publicly available, no one has compiled and combined direct quotations from company insiders and internal reports across multiple alleged harms. We think this compilation gives vital information to parents, who might want some insight into the business practices of a company that hosts their children’s social lives, owns much of their attention, and influences their social development.
At the start of each section, we highlight a real-life example—drawn from relevant court documents—illustrating the specific harm in question. Each child’s story offers a human perspective on the broader statistics and quotations that reveal the far-reaching harms discussed within the company.
1. Our Conversations with Snap, Inc.
While working on this post we had four conversations with Snap’s leaders and employees during which we asked them about some of the harms that appear in the various briefs. In three of those meetings, we asked specifically about the claim, taken from an internal Snap email that was quoted in the New Mexico brief, that Snap gets 10,000 reports of sextortion each month. We did not get any rebuttals or explanations of that claim.
Snap’s Trust and Safety team made a point that we think is valid and important for readers to keep in mind: the briefs we are drawing from present the allegations of one side in litigation, and there is often another side. Some of the quotations may have been misinterpreted or taken out of context. Snap’s Trust and Safety team pointed us to a motion Snap made to have the New Mexico case dismissed. We read that brief and found that it contested only a few of the many claims made in the New Mexico brief. Two of these claims had been in our list of quotations, so we cut one from the post below, and we added a comment to the other.
Snap’s Trust and Safety team also shared various measures they take to mitigate harm to children and teenagers. The Trust and Safety team said that child safety is their top priority and they told us that they proactively remove significant amounts of harmful content. In Snap’s motion to dismiss they state that Snap has “doubled the size of its Trust and Safety team and tripled the size of its Law Enforcement Operations team since 2020” which has “improved Snap’s ability to act quickly when Snapchat users report harassment or improper sexual content on the platform.”
We have no doubt that Snap does remove large quantities of harmful content from its platform, or that they are trying to remove even more. However, it is difficult to assess whether Snap is solving 5% or 75% or 99% of the problem since its metrics focus on the number of pieces of content removed rather than the percentage of Snapchat users who experience harm on the platform. Even if Snap were to remove a billion pieces of drug or sex related content each year, many teen users may still encounter such content every day. And any teen who wants to buy drugs may still find it easy to find dealers, as has happened in many tragic cases of fentanyl poisoning, including very recent cases. Many may still report seeing sexual content, as there are many ways for users to be sexually explicit without violating policies.
From a parent's perspective: if you were choosing which summer camp to send your teen to, would it be reassuring to learn that a camp used to remove 100 sharks a month from its coastal swimming area, but now they remove 500 a month? Probably not reassuring at all. As a parent, you’d much prefer a camp that put its resources into prevention—such as by putting an effective shark barrier around the swimming area—rather than one that focused on catching sharks more quickly after campers report seeing their fins.
We also had the opportunity to discuss many of our observations about Snapchat’s features with both their leadership and their trust and safety teams. We appreciated their willingness to engage with us. We suggested to them some design changes that we believe would make the platform less addictive and less harmful:
- Remove the Quick Add feature5 for minors, which is one of the main ways that adult predators and drug dealers get access to teens.
- Remove the streaks feature,6 which causes many teens to send photos to each other compulsively, needlessly increasing their time on the app.
- Remove beauty filters for minors
- Remove engagement-based algorithms, at the very least, for underage users.
- Stop deleting posts on Snap’s own servers. The fact that Snap does not store the content of conversations (beyond a limited period) is helpful for drug dealers, sextortionists, and others with criminal intent, but it does not improve the user experience of most children to know that even if something goes terribly wrong, their conversations cannot be discovered by law enforcement officers.
- Do a lot more to remove underage users. Snap is widely used in middle schools. (A 2021 survey by Common Sense Media reported that 13% of 8 to 12 year olds said they had “ever used” Snapchat. We therefore estimate that in 2021 in the U.S., about 2.7 million children ages 8 to 12 had used Snapchat.)
One broader request we made was to collaborate on publicly accessible user experience research that could help quantify and reduce the harms we describe below. It would be important to know precisely what percentage of kids receive unwanted advances on their platform, or know how to access drugs - which are very different questions from the ones that they generally answer publicly. Such assessments have been called for by company whistleblowers and public health experts.
We remain hopeful that Snap will act on some of these requests. Nonetheless, we decided to move forward with this post because whatever safety improvements have been made in recent years, and whatever improvements Snap says it will make in the future, we believe it remains essential for the public to understand the dangers associated with Snapchat, as expressed by Snap’s own employees and consultants, who are quoted in numerous court documents that have emerged in recent years.
While the company has clearly made efforts to address some of these concerns, transparency about their past actions and insider beliefs about the platform's impact are critical for those of us trying to understand: how did we get here? What on earth happened in the early 2010s such that there is now an international youth mental health crisis, increasing evidence of attentional fragmentation and declining functional intelligence, and countless cases of severe harm—from fentanyl-laced drugs bought on Snapchat to suicide after sextortion that began on their platform.
The quotations we give below indicate that the harms that occur on Snapchat (as with TikTok and Instagram) are so vast that even a highly dedicated trust and safety team that removes hundreds of millions of pieces of harmful content cannot prevent millions of children from being exposed to serious harms on their platform. This is why design changes are so urgently needed. Better content moderation is not enough.
Here’s a simple way to determine whether an online platform is safe for kids: Does it connect children to anonymous unverified adult strangers? If so, then a great variety of harms are likely to ensue, and parents should be wary of letting their children use that platform until the company makes very substantial design changes.
2. What We Have From Snap
We draw primarily from Attorney General Raul Torrez of New Mexico who released a 165 page narrowly redacted complaint against Snap Inc. on October 2, 2024. We also draw on internal evidence from The State of Nevada’s Complaint by Attorney General Ford and Co., as well as the civil action second amended complaint, Neville et al. v. Snap.
We have created an annotated version of each of the three briefs (New Mexico, Nevada, and Neville et al.)7 so that you can see each selection we chose in the context of the rest of the brief.
There are also a variety of smaller individual and class action lawsuits which address how specific features of Snapchat caused specific harms on individual minor users. Though we do not rely on these for internal quotes from the companies, they offer testimonies of families who have been harmed by the platform.8
In the rest of this post, we organize the evidence of harm that is currently available to us, taken directly from employees and leaders within Snap Inc. and from reports that they commissioned.

Sexting has become a “regular behavior” amongst Generation Z, and we know it happens on Snapchat. In many (though by no means all) cases, sending what seems like run-of-the-mill sexual content can lead to disproportionate consequences and severe harms.
    - We believe that one of the upstream issues for many (but not all) of these harms involves young people being friended by individuals that they don’t know in real life and furthermore being able to recognize demands for sexual content, the performance of sexual acts and other suspicious activity that can lead to sexting/sextortion cases. Reporting violating content or concerning contact with/behavior by strangers is a key action that teens/Snapchatters can take when confronted with these situations.
    - As a platform that has significant reach and engagement with the Gen-Z community, we recognize our responsibility to ensure teens are educated and informed about the potential consequences of some of the behaviors that currently feel very normalized.
    - We are keen to avoid a finger-wagging tone and want the key messages to be shared in an informative and non-judgemental way. We can’t tell our audience NOT to send nudes; this approach is likely futile, “tone deaf” and unrealistic. That said, we also can’t say, ‘If you DO do it: (1) don’t have your face in the photo, (2) don’t have tattoos, piercings or other defining physical characteristics in view, etc.’ Bottom line: We cannot be seen as aiding and abetting the production of (at a minimum) child sexually exploitative material. We need to run through a very thoughtful messaging & visual storytelling exercise/session on how to best balance education without striking fear into Snapchatters. (emphasis added) [[The original quote bolds “without striking fear into Snapchatters”]]
- NM P. 70, PARA 167 
  - Additionally Snap’s internal documents also contain a “Sextortion handbook” which shows how to use Snap Maps to target a school where they can, “tap on the screen to view any snap stories that might have been shared by students who share snap stories with the ‘snap maps’ options enabled.” [[This is referencing a “sextortion handbook” that was developed by sexual predators for sextorting minors using Snapchat.]]
- NM P. 50-51, PARA 107. 
  - Snap continued to discuss–internally–evidence of ongoing child sexual exploitation on its platform. An internal email dated June 7, 2021, noted “Flagging this piece looking at the % of child sexual assaults that were facilitated by technology. Between 2007-2013 FB was the highest, then dating apps until 2017, after which Snapchat is recorded as the most used platform.” The attached article, “Jump in sexual assaults of children groomed online,” called out the prevalence of child sexual abuse on Snapchat stating, “They found a big upswing since 2015 in perpetrators using social media platforms, especially Snapchat and dating sites, to communicate with children aged between 12 and 17 before meeting and assaulting them.” The article continued, “In the early years of the study, between 2007 and 2013, three-quarters of offenders had used Facebook to communicate with child victims, but between 2014-2016 dating apps, many that children should be too young to access, started to feature. Between 2017 and 2020, Snapchat had been the platform employed by nearly half of offenders.” [[You can find this article here.]]
- NM P. 62, PARA 142 
  - In May 2021, Snap employees discussed this ongoing problem in an internal email titled “Responsible growth initiative,” stating, “We need to come up with new approaches that ringfence our most vulnerable users (minors) and make it hard for predatory users to find them via quick add, search, etc. We believe we can achieve this without meaningfully degrading the product experience for these users if we pursue new strategies in inventory generation/constraints and other techniques to more effectively silo minors from people outside their networks. This is probably the most important long-term thing we need to work on…” One employee continued, “I wish we had more metrics to frame these clearly. What does success look like if we make progress here - obviously large-scale friending spam numbers goes down but what about low-grade “creep” attacks. How does proactively playing D here help us unlock more growth?” As this email indicates, the choice to address features that introduced minors to predators was harnessed to, and would only be pursued to service of, Snapchat's growth.
- NM P. 65-67, PARA 149-155 
  - PARA 149: Thus, a February 2022 PowerPoint prepared by Snap's consultant reported that “many young people reported being added by bots on Snapchat. This seemed to be particularly pervasive issue through 'Quick Add' feature as people described being added and receiving unsolicited messages from unknown senders.”
  - PARA 150: It was clear to Snap that allowing minors to be recommended to users with two friends in common failed to provide meaningful protection to children. A May 2023 internal email described results from a quality assurance test session to “pressure test the friending, chat, and registration experience for minors.” The findings included: 
    - “Minors may receive a ton of random Quick Add suggestions: In tests where someone registered as a minor with their “Contact Book” sync off, they received random Quick Add suggestions once they added 1 – 2 friends. Alternatively, if you add multiple 18+ accounts, a lot of your Quick Add suggestions are adults... Minors can communicate with adults they are not friends with through group chats: There are a number of ways minors (or anyone) can be added to group chats without being friends with people who could abuse them. [[redacted text]] These are difficult features to solve for, but we may want to consider exploring additional safeguards for minors as they pertain to group messages and invite links (e.g. callouts that they are joining a group with people they may not know/aren't friends with; warning when clicking invite links; etc).”
  - PARA 151: Thus, Snap recognized that restricting Quick Add to friends of friends still exposed minors to introductions to adult strangers. If one or more minors in a network fall victim to an adult groomer, that pedophile can contact everyone in that network.
  - PARA 152: Snap acknowledged internally that “Bad actors” would groom 2-3 friends on other platforms, such as gaming platforms, in order to jumpstart the algorithm to suggest additional minor friends.
  - PARA 153: Consistent with Snap's own findings, the 2023 Federal Human Trafficking Report noted that Snapchat was one of the “Top Platforms used in the recruitment of Victims 2019-2023.”
  - PARA 154: On January 31, 2024, Snap published the written Congressional testimony of Evan Spiegel on its Safety Blog, quoting his statement that: “Snapchat's default “Contact Me” settings are set to friends and phone contacts only for all accounts, and can't be expanded.” 
    - [Quote by Spiegel] “We want Snapchat to be safe for everyone, and we offer extra protections for minors to help prevent unwanted contact and provide an age-appropriate experience. Snapchat's default “Contact Me” settings are set to friends and phone contacts only for all accounts, and can't be expanded. If a minor receives a friend request from someone they don't share a mutual friend with, we provide a warning before they start communicating to make sure it is someone they know. As a result, approximately 90% of friend requests received by minors on Snapchat are from someone with at least one mutual friend in common. Our goal is to make it as difficult as possible for people to be contacted by someone they don't already know.”
- However, an internal survey conducted by Snap's Product Research team in August of 2022 indicated that Snap users of all age brackets can toggle their “Contact Me” settings to “Everyone.” In addition, the survey showed that a large number of users who had “Everyone” enabled to contact them were under the impression that “Everyone” only applied to “Just Friends that I Added” (24.8%), a percentage that was highest for users in the youngest age brackets (13-17 and 18-24).
- PARA 155: Additionally, Snap's search term tool allows unknown adults to identify minor accounts. In January 2019, in an internal discussion regarding how to respond to a press inquiry in the United Kingdom, a Snap T&S employee admitted, “I wasn't aware that you were able to use search terms to bring up accounts. Using 'underage' just now there are accounts like 'These Girls R Underage' or 'Underage Nudes' and 'Nude Underage Girls'. I thought that you needed to know an account name in order to be able to search for accounts.” This design defect provides another means for adult predators to find and solicit minors on Snap's platform.
3.3 In-Person Sexual Predation and Assault
* * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * *.
Real life example: The following facts are alleged from New Mexico v. Snap, P. 33 PARA 83: An 11-year-old girl was introduced to an anonymous user, under the Snapchat account “‘sugar_daddy4u29” “through Snapchat’s Quick Add feature”. This user (who was a 27-year-old male) “offered her money and she agreed to meet him in person, where, feeling pressure to do something, she performed oral sex on him. The girl continued to communicate with Marquez on Snapchat and arranged to meet him again on several occasions, where he again sexually assaulted her.”
Real life example: The following facts are alleged in the public complaint Nevada v. Snap P. 49, PARA 143: “In another instance, a 25-year-old used Snap Map to hunt down and sexually assault a 16-year-old in Florida. Per a local news report, the man: [U]sed Snapchat to reach out to the girl, then, unbeknownst to the teen, track[ed] her down in real-time using the Snapchat feature called Snap Map. ‘Our victim posted a life story, and then he used Snap Map to track her down because of the meta tags that's [sic] in the photo,’ [a law enforcement official] said. Detectives said the Snap Map allowed the suspect to see the data the teen posted and know just where she posted it from. [‘]If you don’t hide your location where you make that [sic], take that photo or that posting from, they can use data that's hidden in the photo to track you down,’ [the same official] said.”
* * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * *.
New Mexico (NM)
- NM P. 68-69, PARA 158-164
