According to The Guardian, the campaign they’re funding is spending over $1 million per day trying to defeat Proposition 40, which would enact a one-time 5 percent tax on California’s billionaires. Google co-founder Sergey Brin is reportedly the biggest donor, contributing at least $102 million, alongside other tech executives: The donors to the no campaign are a who’s who of Silicon Valley, including the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, crypto magnate Chris Larsen and several prominent venture capitalists.
- Elon Musk has donated over $276 million to Republican midterm efforts Elon Musk has handed out at least $276 million to Republican groups since July, The New York Times reports, making him both the party’s top known donor and the biggest established midterm donor. $158 million of that money — one of the largest political donations in American history — has been funneled into the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC that aims to secure and maintain a Republican Senate majority. Among others, it’s fighting to retain the party’s Senate seat in Texas, which serves as a major hub for Musk’s business empire. He’s also donated over $76 million to America PAC, a super PAC Musk founded in 2024 that canvasses for hard-to-reach Republican voters. Smaller amounts have also been given to other conservative groups, including: Read Article >
- The midterms are going to be a data security nightmare One messy database is threatening to disenfranchise thousands or even millions of registered voters, while leaving even more at risk of intimidation or data breaches, in the name of solving a problem that barely exists. As the 2026 midterm elections approach, election and privacy experts are sounding alarms about the Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) Program, which President Donald Trump’s administration has expanded to ostensibly catch noncitizens voting. Experts say that amounts to a dangerous, error-prone effort to centralize voter data. “The federal government doesn’t have the authority to do any of that and doesn’t have the expertise either,” says Eileen O’Connor, senior counsel at the Brennan Center. “Inserting themselves into the day-to-day functioning of state elections is unprecedented and disturbing.” Read Article >
- Democrats preview how they’d go after the Ticketmaster settlement if they regain power A handful of Democrats called an unofficial hearing on Capitol Hill Monday to slam the Department of Justice’s “trivial” and “pathetic” settlement with Live Nation-Ticketmaster, previewing how they might go after Trump administration antitrust deals if they win back congressional power in November. While the DOJ settlement with Live Nation, which came one week into trial and with a promise of up to $280 million, received copious pushback, Democrats don’t at the moment have the power in either chamber to set committee agendas. That meant that Monday’s so-called shadow hearing looked different than most official proceedings. Instead of sitting at the elevated seats behind the dais, the lawmakers sat at tables below, eye level with witnesses including California Attorney General Rob Bonta, one of the AGs continuing the fight against Live Nation-Ticketmaster, ousted Trump administration antitrust official Roger Alford, and several entertainment industry players, including a member of the band The Hold Steady. Several artists asked to appear at the forum declined out of fear for their livelihoods, according to House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Jamie Raskin (D-MD), who co-hosted the forum with Senate Homeland Security permanent subcommittee on investigations Ranking Member Richard Blumenthal (D-CT). Read Article >
- AI backlash is coming for elections Ask Americans how they feel about AI and most say they have concerns. Communities have mounted resistance to data center projects, stalling them across the US. On social media, anger at AI companies and executives is unrestrained — sometimes to the point of condoning violence. But look at the issues that most campaigns are focused on, and AI is far less prevalent, experts say. Read Article >

articles.title: Binance says hackers used fake job interviews and an internal AI tool to pull off the $6.3 billion heist
articles.body:
The largest crypto theft to date was pulled off by combining some well-known hacking techniques over the course of a few months, according to Binance. A postmortem from the company says the process started in June with one developer downloading a tampered installer apparently spread by a malicious Google ad, exposing details about the engineers and how they work. Then, in September, another engineer was targeted by someone pretending to be interested in hiring them; that person set up a series of calls and multiple rounds of interviews, shared social media pages to build trust, and eventually prompted them to download a fake interview assignment that was actually malware.
Binance says hackers used fake job interviews and an internal AI tool to pull off the $6.3 billion heist
A North Korean hacking unit reportedly started its break-in with a search engine ad that served up a malware download.
Binance claims that its security teams did detect the first installation of malware in June, and replaced the worker’s device, but that its security tools didn’t detect the second attack that deleted the pyenv executable and replaced it with a malicious version that gave them backdoor access:
The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server. The 0-day malware was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time. The attacker also took steps to conceal the malicious activity and remove traces of the compromise, making detection and subsequent investigation more challenging.
By October 20th, the story goes, the attackers, whom the FBI has identified as a North Korean unit dubbed “TraderTraitor,” used Binance’s own internal AI tool to gain control over wallets for the first engineer compromised in June, as well as a third employee, before logging into the third employee’s computer on October 29th and launching their attack.
The postmortem also goes into why Binance wasn’t able to stop the transactions that occurred nearly two hours after the first unauthorized transfers, saying that “Because the hot wallet used Multi-Party Computation (MPC), there was no single private key that could be used to immediately revoke the malicious EIP-7702 authorizations.” Binance says that it has prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases, and CEO Richard Teng writes that no user is bearing the loss, with about $2.85 billion in stolen assets frozen or intercepted: “At this moment, 98% of impacted tokens had been replenished; we’re completing the remaining 2%. Withdrawals have broadly resumed.”
What’s less clear is why this particular attack worked — the danger of job interviews that ask people to download and execute code on machines with access to employer material has been warned about for years, and there’s little detail on the “internal AI tool” that was used by the attackers and why it was able to help them in the first place.

articles.title: Nvidia – open-source auto-ontology
articles.body:
An open context layer that helps agents give fewer wrong answers on enterprise data.
Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability is what gates agentic analytics: a revenue figure delivered faster is worth nothing if it's wrong. Before an agent queries, it needs to know where the data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar.
Auto-Ontology is a service you run next to your databases to give agents that context. It compiles their metadata into an ontology: business terms mapped to columns, reviewed SQL for measures, and the relationships between tables. Agents query through the ontology, and people review it in a web UI. It complements the semantic models you already own.
With Auto-Ontology, developers can:
- Discover. Generate an ontology from database metadata, import existing semantic models, and explore the result as a semantic graph.
- Ground. Give agents one definition per business concept, mapped across tables and databases.
- Certify. Review, edit, and certify definitions in the UI or through the API.
- Validate. Check whether a question is answerable before querying, and return the SQL and the agent's steps with each answer.
- Expose. Serve context to any agent harness through MCP, agent skills, and a REST API.
The usual shortcut is to paste the schema into the agent's context window. Auto-Ontology gives the agent tools over the ontology:
The companion repository, auto-ontology-eval, measures ontology performance on benchmarks and evals.
For BIRD, BEAVER, FDABench-Lite, and Wide World Importers, each eval item pairs a question with gold SQL, and a run asks every question of the same model twice:
- Control. The model gets the database schema in its prompt.
- Treatment. Auto-Ontology's question-answering agent, the one behind Chat, works from the compiled ontology.
A deterministic verifier scores the SQL from each arm by execution match, using each benchmark's official rule where it has one. The report gives the accuracy difference and lists the questions the ontology fixed and the ones it broke. BIRD-Interact, a multi-turn benchmark where the agent asks clarifying questions, runs on its own harness.
To run the comparison on BIRD, follow the auto-ontology-eval setup, then run:
uv run python main.py --database-name bird
This runs Auto-Ontology with Docker Compose against Wide World Importers,
Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2,
uv, and an NVIDIA API key (nvapi-...) from
build.nvidia.com.
- Clone the repository and create .env:
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology cp .env.example .env Then set these values in .env:
DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY=nvapi-... AUTH_SECRET=<a long random string, e.g. from openssl rand -base64 32> APP_URL=http://localhost:3000 POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<a new password> CONNECTION_STRINGS=postgresql://postgres:<the same password>@postgres:5432/wideworldimporters AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password> PGADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password> Compose publishes Postgres, pgAdmin, and the web app on the host, so replace
each default password before you start it. .env.example also sets an API
key per model role: replace each nvapi-your-api-key-here with your key, or
delete those lines so they fall back to DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY.
- Start Postgres and load the sample database. The seed script lives in auto-ontology-eval; pass it the Postgres password you set: docker compose up -d --wait postgres git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology-eval.git ../auto-ontology-eval (cd ../auto-ontology-eval && uv sync && cp .env.example .env && \ POSTGRES_PASSWORD='<the same password>' \ uv run python scripts/seed/seed_wwi.py --database-name wideworldimporters --drop)
- Build and start the rest of the stack: docker compose up -d --build
- Open http://localhost:3000 and sign in with AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_EMAIL and AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD from .env. Go to Settings → Semantic
Compilation and turn it on. Ingestion runs at startup; compilation starts
immediately and reports Semantic compilation is ready when it finishes.
- Ask a question in Chat: What was revenue for the USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in June 2015? articles.title: Nvidia – open-source auto-ontology

An open context layer that helps agents give fewer wrong answers on enterprise data.
Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability is what gates agentic analytics: a revenue figure delivered faster is worth nothing if it's wrong. Before an agent queries, it needs to know where the data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar.
Auto-Ontology is a service you run next to your databases to give agents that context. It compiles their metadata into an ontology: business terms mapped to columns, reviewed SQL for measures, and the relationships between tables. Agents query through the ontology, and people review it in a web UI. It complements the semantic models you already own.
With Auto-Ontology, developers can:
- Discover. Generate an ontology from database metadata, import existing semantic models, and explore the result as a semantic graph.
- Ground. Give agents one definition per business concept, mapped across tables and databases.
- Certify. Review, edit, and certify definitions in the UI or through the API.
- Validate. Check whether a question is answerable before querying, and return the SQL and the agent's steps with each answer.
- Expose. Serve context to any agent harness through MCP, agent skills, and a REST API.
The usual shortcut is to paste the schema into the agent's context window. Auto-Ontology gives the agent tools over the ontology:
The companion repository, auto-ontology-eval, measures ontology performance on benchmarks and evals.
For BIRD, BEAVER, FDABench-Lite, and Wide World Importers, each eval item pairs a question with gold SQL, and a run asks every question of the same model twice:
- Control. The model gets the database schema in its prompt.
- Treatment. Auto-Ontology's question-answering agent, the one behind Chat, works from the compiled ontology.
A deterministic verifier scores the SQL from each arm by execution match, using each benchmark's official rule where it has one. The report gives the accuracy difference and lists the questions the ontology fixed and the ones it broke. articles.title: Open-Source 5G Ran Platforms: A Dual Perspective on Performance and Capabilities
articles.body:
Computer Science > Networking and Internet Architecture
  [Submitted on 26 Aug 2026]
Title:Open-Source 5G RAN Platforms: A Dual Perspective on Performance and Capabilities
View PDF
            Abstract:Open-source implementations of the fifth generation (5G) Radio Access Network (RAN), such as OpenAirInterface (OAI) and srsRAN, have become increasingly relevant for industry and academic research, rapid prototyping, and low-cost private 5G deployments. The state of the art presents different evaluation scenarios for both platforms; however, these are often limited to individual testbed evaluations, end-to-end studies, or partial comparisons between them. In particular, there is a lack of evaluations considering different Software-Defined Radios (SDRs), RAN configurations, user applications, and numbers of real UEs. To address this gap, this paper presents a comparative evaluation of OAI and srsRAN. The study includes a qualitative assessment of supported features and deployment flexibility, followed by a quantitative performance analysis covering radio resource control setup procedures, compliance with theoretical data rates, and real application workloads with diverse quality of service requirements. Specifically, we consider Video on Demand (VoD) for data rate evaluation, Live Streaming (LS) and Cloud Gaming (CG) as latency-sensitive applications. These workloads provide a comprehensive view of each platform capability.

articles.title: EU Court Advisor Warns Google AI Chatbot May Breach Copyright Rules
articles.body:
EU Court Advisor Warns Google AI Chatbot May Breach Copyright Rules 14
			
		 	
				An adviser to the EU's highest court says Google's Gemini may violate publishers' copyright when it reproduces recognizable portions of their articles or circumvents paywalls and other technical protections to generate answers. Reuters reports:  The case before the Luxembourg-based Court of Justice of the European Union pitted Hungarian website operator Like Company against US-based Google's artificial intelligence chatbot Gemini. A ruling against Google, which could force the tech giant to pay fees for the use of such content, could throw a lifeline to online media such as Like Company. They have seen traffic dwindle as news summaries written by AI chatbots like Gemini increasingly replace traditional search engines' results, which include hyperlinks to the media websites.
"When an LLM (large language model)-driven chatbot retrieves a publication from a press publisher's website, reuses that publication to generate an answer, and provides that answer to the user, the press publisher's right may be infringed in certain circumstances," Advocate General Maciej Szpunar said. Gemini's answers fall under the publishers' right of reproduction when chatbots access publications by unlawfully "circumventing paywalls or other technical barriers, or when they reuse "the form of expression of that publication in a recognizable manner," he said.
Copyright rules do not protect the "mere facts" reported by press publications, but "only the specific form of expression," he added. On the other hand, he said, the use of material protected by copyright to train LLMs -- AI systems that use vast amounts of text to generate human-like responses and summarize information -- is "freely permitted under the text and data mining exception." Szpunar said there was no evidence that Google had used the Hungarian publisher's articles to train Gemini. The court, which follows the majority of its advisers' non-binding opinions, will rule in the coming months.  "Google's powerful gatekeeping role in search makes this particularly important. Publishers depend on Google to reach readers, while Google increasingly delivers AI-generated answers directly to users," said Angela Mills Wade, the council's executive director.
"Publishers should not have to choose between search visibility and protecting their rights. Nor should Google's control over access to audiences become leverage to secure publishers' content for AI services," she said.

articles.title: CrowdStrike to shell out nearly $500M for 2 AI security startups as the market for securing agents takes off
articles.body:
Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike is buying two AI security companies that expand its products to more broadly monitor, test, and cover AI models and agents, as companies across industries start rolling out AI agents and models wholesale.
CrowdStrike said it will buy Fiddler AI, which makes observability software for monitoring AI agents inside enterprises, and Dreadnode, which helps companies automate security testing specifically aimed at detecting flaws in AI models, apps, and agents before they are set live.
The company is paying around $400 million for Fiddler AI, and about $95 million for Dreadnode, according to The Wall Street Journal.
The deals are happening at a time of significant upheaval in the cybersecurity space, especially as companies’ policies and processes lag behind AI adoption within their walls. Teams and individual employees alike are experimenting with AI tools, automating workflows, vibe-coding custom apps, and deploying armies of AI agents to do their bidding, which is understandably causing headaches for security teams.
CrowdStrike, whose products are used widely across enterprises and governments, is clearly trying to leverage its already significant heft and presence to capture a share of this quickly burgeoning market. It’s not alone, of course, as we’ve already seen several startups and cybersecurity vendors raising dozens of millions in funding to solve issues for companies, though most of these approaches are essentially based on the conviction that existing security software isn’t enough to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, or usage.
The company has itself been building detection and response controls, dubbed Falcon Guardian, to help companies see and understand what agents are doing on their devices, and these acquisitions seem to further flesh out its offerings.
Fiddler AI is going to be part of CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform as Falcon Observe, where it’ll ostensibly help the company’s clients evaluate agents before they’re deployed, understand their actions, and monitor what they do, and feed that information as telemetry into the broader platform. Dreadnode, meanwhile, will be integrated into the Falcon Guardian product, to which the startup’s software will feed its testing results as security policy recommendations.
Founded in 2018, Fiddler AI has raised a total of about $99 million to date, according to PitchBook. Dreadnode, founded in 2023, has raised $14 million so far.

articles.title: Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing
articles.body:
Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is rolling out into beta testing on Tuesday, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.
The news was first announced via an emailed press release sent out by Apple’s communications team in India early on Tuesday. The update rolled out in the U.S. and other markets later in the day.
The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist.
However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps.
Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them.
With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the stand-alone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation.
Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things.
When you double-press the digital crown, an audible chime appears and an animation displays on the watch. This is meant to signal to people through the combination of the gesture, sound, and visual display that you’ve recorded something that was said.
These snippets will be deleted automatically after 30 seconds if you don’t save them.
The other option, Siri Recaps, takes this ambient listening technology even further by allowing Apple Watch owners to take high-level notes of their conversations.
Importantly, Apple says it’s not identifying speakers, saving the raw audio, or providing word-for-word transcriptions. Instead, the feature summarizes a conversation with a short sentence and some bullet points that identify key points. For instance, depending on the topic, the bullet points might include things like important dates or deadlines, pricing or payment plan information, and other factual information.
Apple suggested the feature could be used in scenarios like work meetings, parent-teacher conferences, personal training sessions, or other places where you may need to remember what tasks you have to complete or things that were said. Essentially, it’s supposed to mimic a user’s ability to jot down their own notes — without adding emotion or tone.
This could be helpful particularly at times when you aren’t able to write up your own notes, either because your hands are full or you’re trying to concentrate on whatever’s being said at the time. The recaps won’t record conversations when you’re listening to music with your headphones or using their noise cancellation features.
At the end of the day, you’re prompted to review your saved Siri Recaps when the feature is enabled, and then choose which, if any, you want to save. These notes can be saved to your Notes app or even exported to your Journal app, if they’re more personal in nature. If you do nothing, the recaps will delete themselves within seven days.
This reminder to review the Siri Recaps you’ve recorded also appears when you first unlock your Apple Watch in the morning.
Users can opt to enable the Siri Recaps manually, or they can configure a schedule, such as only having the recapping take place while at work, or making sure that they never run at night. Even if they’re running on a schedule, you can still turn off the recapping feature at any time from the Control Center.
Apple notes that Siri Recaps has been designed to omit sensitive information like government-assigned identifiers, financial and authentication data, certain personal identifiers, and any language that would promote self-harm.
The Audio Intelligence features for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 rely on a combination of Apple’s hardware, software, and services. This includes the S11 chip, built-in microphone, and the Apple Intelligence models that run on the iPhone, as well as Apple’s Private Cloud Compute.
The always-on processor includes a secure enclave — a hardware-protected memory space that can’t be accessed by the rest of the operating system — where a dedicated audio buffer processes the raw audio. This allows the audio to be processed without it actually being accessible to anyone, including Apple. The audio is only accessible to the paired iPhone through a secure pairing mechanism between it and the watch.
To work, lightweight AI models on the S11 chip on the Apple Watch detect if there’s a conversation happening that the wearer is a part of, which is then transferred to the secure enclave on the iPhone. On-device processing on the iPhone turns the audio into condensed text, meaning the text of the conversation with the filler words removed. This condensed text is then encrypted and sent to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute (PCC) to create the recap of the conversation that is sent back to the phone. (The recap and any summarizations used to create it are deleted from PCC immediately afterwards.)
The recaps you can then access on your iPhone are only accessible to you, not to Apple. And they’re encrypted when they’re synced between your multiple Apple devices.
Similarly, Apple Watch transfers audio to the iPhone for processing to create the 15-second snippets for Live Rewind.
Apple says none of these features should impact the battery life of your watch or phone. The features will later roll out to the public beta for broader testing before becoming publicly available to all.
Post updated after publication to indicate the current status of the software’s rollout.

articles.title: Apple opens the door to a nightmare world of always-listening tech
articles.body:
Watch what you say: Apple opens the door to a nightmare world of always-listening tech
Apple this week announced plans to roll out "always-listening" features for newer Apple Watches. One of the features, Live Rewind, lets you "go back in time" and replay the most recent 15 seconds of ambient audio as a text transcript. The other feature, Siri Recap, listens throughout the day and summarizes your conversations as high-level notes into a written report on your iPhone.
Apple claims these features are helpful to "jog" your memory. The massive trade-off is that your Apple Watch is always listening to you and anyone else within earshot while the feature is enabled.
Here's the relevant section from Apple's live event:
Given these features we're bound to be controversial, it's clear that Apple put thought into the security and privacy guardrails before shipping these features (which may still change). The tech giant says on its support page that the always-listening tech doesn't record or store audio, and that the recaps are end-to-end encrypted so that any summarized data is inaccessible to anyone else, not even Apple. And, its security documentation [PDF] detailing how the features work is worth reading as well.
What is more concerning to me, to underscore on a point I made in a Bluesky post, is that Apple is opening the door to a world where other companies, device makers, and app developers try to recreate or rival Apple's technology and do a far shoddier job, all the while creating a worse surveillance monster and introducing new security and privacy risks along the way.
So far there have been a few companies and startups that made always-listening devices, like pendants, often including AI. Apple by comparison is one of the largest technology companies in the world and its global reach means millions of people will get these features and switch them on. Apple's market dominance, coupled with its decision to make always-listening tech, sets a precedent that signals it's OK for other companies to follow suit and normalize this intrusive tech. It also implies that there is money to be made in developing this technology, making it a space ripe for disruption (or exploitation) by profiteers.
Bloomberg ($) reports lawyers are already finding that Apple's always-listening tech is at odds with the law in several U.S. states. Some states require all parties' consent before being recorded, setting up the feature for potential legal battles down the line. This comes amid the rise of smart camera-enabled "pervert glasses" like those made by Meta and Snap, which have supercharged abuse and harassment against people by recording them without consent.

Privacy for me, but not for thee?
While Apple has emphasized security and privacy features for its own users, it hasn't explained how people opt out of its customers' recordings.
I chatted this week with Em, a digital privacy and security technologist, activist, and author of the Control Alt Delete blog, and whose work you have no doubt seen while she wrote for Privacy Guides. Em told me that these new Apple features follow a "recent trend of gadgets that are constantly collecting information from surroundings, including from people who aren't wearing or buying these gadgets themselves," like smart glasses and speakers.
Em said that while anyone can make notes of every conversation they have, this kind of technology "normalizes it happening at all time and in every context."
"Even if Apple seems to have put some thought into protecting the privacy and consent of the people using the Apple Watch, this technology doesn't do much to protect the privacy and consent of everyone interacting with people using it," Em told me.
I also asked Thorin Klosowski, a senior security and privacy activist at Electronic Frontier Foundation, for his thoughts and he said similarly that Apple's approach is largely about protecting its customers' data but does little for anyone else.
"Increasingly we’re seeing tech companies frame privacy this way — as personal responsibility — but it has never been just about that, it’s a collective effort that relies as much on personal choice as it does social contracts," said Klosowski. He added that we should all be free to converse without fear of tech documenting everything that's being said. "Especially when combined with all the other similar devices we’re seeing, whether that’s pendants or glasses or rings, there is absolutely a risk of normalization here."
EFF's privacy litigation director Adam Schwartz added that since there's no practical means for people to consent or decline recording, "we suggest people should think twice before using this technology, out of respect to the conversational privacy of others."
For its part, Apple says on its support page that users should "consider those around you where conversations may be private or sensitive." The broader message Apple seems to be sending is: Prepare for a world where everyday devices are always listening in.

articles.title: Only 0.5% of 383,000 CVEs are ever exploited in real-world attacks
articles.body:
The vulnerability landscape continues to expand. From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation.
Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond.
Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack.
Classifying the vulnerability landscape
To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform.
Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve.
- Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction.
- Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content.
- Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold.
- Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges.
- Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls.
- Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen.
- Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets.
- Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification of data or system state.
- Denial of service: Disruption of system or service availability.
- Cross-site scripting (XSS): Script execution within a victim’s browser context.
- Arbitrary file access: Unauthorized access to or placement of files.
- Spoofing or redirect: Spoofing, redirection, or other forms of UI deception.
We also classified vulnerabilities by the platforms they affect, including Windows, Linux/Unix, mobile, network appliances, IoT/OT, virtualization hosts, and developer packages. A CVE can span multiple platforms. Developer packages are treated as a separate category because they are often cross-platform and represent a significant share of the overall vulnerability population.
Most CVEs in the analysis affect application code, including servers, web applications, browsers, productivity software, libraries, and firmware tooling, while a smaller share affects OS and system code such as kernels, drivers, and firmware.
This analysis covers CVEs published through September 2026 using Microsoft’s catalog of tracked vulnerabilities. Each CVE is counted once in the impact analysis and across each relevant platform in the platform analysis.
Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild
The subset of vulnerabilities exploited in the wild is much smaller than the overall CVE population, and looks very different from it. Fewer than 1 in 200 published CVEs are ever used in a real attack, and those that do get used are overwhelmingly concentrated in the takeover classes that maximize threat actor impact and exposure.
The difference becomes clear when we look at impact. Exploitation is heavily concentrated in vulnerabilities that give attackers greater control over a system. Server-side RCE rises from 20% of published CVEs to 37% of exploited CVEs, local privilege escalation from 11% to 18%, and client-side RCE from 4% to 13%. By comparison, XSS falls from 15% to 4% and denial of service from 16% to 7%. OS vulnerabilities show a similar shift, increasing from 23% of the overall CVE population to 41% of exploited vulnerabilities.
These patterns are consistent with threat actors favoring vulnerabilities that can provide meaningful access and control. Remote code execution and privilege escalation can create footholds that support subsequent stages of an attack, while vulnerabilities that primarily cause a crash or limited script execution may offer less utility for broader compromise.
Importantly, a vulnerability’s stated classification does not always reflect what an attacker can reliably achieve in practice. For example, some vulnerabilities described as enabling RCE may ultimately result only in denial of service under real-world conditions. Understanding the demonstrated impact and exploitability of a vulnerability is therefore critical to effective prioritization.
Where defenders should focus
Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast
Patching is slow, and far slower on critical systems than others. Across platforms, servers are the critical assets and the slowest to patch. Microsoft Security Exposure Management data from 2026 shows that the median vulnerability is patched in about two weeks on Windows workstations but in more than a month on Windows Servers. It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on MacOS, and beyond a year on network appliances. That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest.
Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure. According to VulnCheck, 29% of the exploits in 2025 were launched within 1 day of CVE publication. According to CISA, the mean time from CVE publication to CISA KEV catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. 2026 data up to September already have that number dropping to 20 days, with a median of only 3 days since publication. Industry research suggests that advances in AI are a significant factor in the time reduction required to develop exploits, further increasing pressure on defenders to respond quickly.
Impact, exposure and where to focus
Two things determine a vulnerability’s value to a threat actor: impact and exposure. Impact is what successful exploitation provides, such as remote code execution or privilege escalation. Exposure is an asset’s position in the environment and the opportunities it creates for further compromise. An asset’s exposure is shaped by the identities, privileges, and connections available from it.
Servers often use service accounts, application identities, or cloud-managed identities with permissions beyond their operational needs. Compromising such a system can provide access to additional resources, sensitive data, administrative privileges, or trusted network paths. Together, impact and exposure determine the blast radius: a vulnerability that enables full control of a highly exposed system can enable widespread on-premises or cloud compromise.
Threat actors do not exploit at random: they go after the vulnerabilities that give the highest impact and exposure: full control of a system and the privileged identities and critical assets it has access to. As defenders, focusing on these vulnerabilities first can deliver the highest return on remediation investment.
Takeover vulnerabilities like remote code execution, authentication bypass and local privilege escalation lead here. They drive the broadest exposure and the largest blast radius, account for 78% of real-world exploited vulnerabilities, and stopping their exploitation interrupts attacks at the earliest stage, before compromise can propagate across the environment.
Next in line
A second slice deserves attention where context makes it severe: denial of service against availability-critical assets is recoverable in general, but can be mission-ending in parts of your environment where uptime is everything; disclosure of credentials or secrets can be minor as an insulated incident, but it feeds the same privileged-identity path mentioned above.
How Microsoft Security helps defenders act
Threat actors do not begin with a vulnerability list. They begin by looking for a reachable way in. Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management approaches the environment from that same outside-in perspective, continuously discovering internet-facing infrastructure, including previously unknown or unmonitored assets, shadow IT, and third-party dependencies. This gives defenders an opportunity to remove unnecessary exposure before a reachable vulnerability becomes an entry point.
Once the reachable assets are known, the next question is which weaknesses deserve immediate attention. Defenders need a way to prioritize exposure beyond CVSS alone. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management addresses this challenge through Exposure Score and prioritized security recommendations.
Prioritization incorporates threat and exploitability signals, breach likelihood, internet exposure, and asset criticality, helping teams focus remediation on vulnerabilities that create the greatest actual exposure.
An initial foothold is only part of the risk. Attack Path Analysis connects assets and threat actor techniques into end-to-end routes from an entry point to a critical asset. Microsoft Security Exposure Management Attack Path Analysis provides a cross-workload view spanning endpoints, cloud, and hybrid environments, using vulnerability context from MDVM, endpoint data from Defender for Endpoint, and cloud asset data from Defender for Cloud. Within cloud environments, Defender CSPM Attack Path Analysis adds detailed context about internet exposure, vulnerabilities, network connections, identities, and permissions across Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud.
Together, these experiences show how an exposed workload could become a path through a privileged identity to sensitive data or another critical resource, helping defenders identify where to break the path before the initial compromise expands.
Patching remains essential, but it is not the only defensive action available. Microsoft Security helps defenders discover the doors threat actors can see, prioritize the weaknesses they are most likely to exploit, understand where a compromise could lead, and identify opportunities to break attack paths before compromise spreads to critical assets.

articles.title: Fujifilm To Boost Tape Production 5x As AI Fuels Archiving Demand
articles.body:
Fujifilm To Boost Tape Production 5x As AI Fuels Archiving Demand (arstechnica.com) 30
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: In an announcement released Thursday, Fujifilm said it will invest roughly 10 billion yen (about $63 million) to increase its production capacity fivefold for an unlikely beneficiary of the AI era: magnetic tape. Fujifilm attributes the surge in archiving demand to the spread of generative AI, which the company remarked is producing "exponential growth" in data needs worldwide. The 5x increase in production capacity will be measured against fiscal year 2025 production levels.
The investment in Fujifilm's Kanagawa Factory, Odawara site will make it "the largest investment Fujifilm has made to date in dedicated LTO tape facilities." The project will run from fiscal years 2026 through 2028 to fund manufacturing expansion and additional personnel, primarily to produce the latest-generation "FUJIFILM LTO Ultrium10" tape. [...]
According to Fujifilm, "major cloud service and data center operators" have been expanding their use of magnetic tape because it can store large data volumes at relatively low cost. Tape backups can be easily disconnected and stored in a drawer, a vault, or a separate facility. Fujifilm highlights the ability to air-gap tape cartridges as a last defense for user data: "Given the sophistication of cyberattacks, magnetic tape is attracting increasing attention as a means of protecting data from threats such as ransomware."

articles.title: Rivian spinoff Also wants to reinvent the wheel — but first, it has to ship
articles.body:
When Rivian quietly spun off its micromobility brand, Also, a lot of observers wondered if the luxury EV maker had bitten off more than it can chew. Chris Yu insists that’s not the case.
Rivian spinoff Also wants to reinvent the wheel — but first, it has to ship
Also President Chris Yu opens up about surviving the AI server component crunch, rewriting UL battery standards, and why the company’s modular e-bike is just the first step.
Rivian spinoff Also wants to reinvent the wheel — but first, it has to ship
Also President Chris Yu opens up about surviving the AI server component crunch, rewriting UL battery standards, and why the company’s modular e-bike is just the first step.
Yu, a Stanford aeronautics PhD and former CTO at Specialized, runs the startup as an independent business that counts Rivian as a minority shareholder. Under his lead, Also rolled out the TM-B — a quirky, modular e-bike with a raft of unique features, including a swappable top frame, USB-C chargeable battery, a built-in screen, a series hybrid pedal-by-wire system, and proprietary “Dream Ride” software. There’s also the TM-Q, an electric four-wheeler aimed at commercial deliveries.
But it hasn’t been completely smooth sailing. After dealing with supply chain headaches, confusing regulations, and some communication stumbles, Also is finally shipping its early Launch Edition bikes to customers while also getting ready to roll out the standard and performance versions. Meanwhile, customers have been letting the company have it on Reddit over the delayed deliveries, and the few people who have received their bikes have already experienced some minor software problems.
The Verge met up with Yu to chat about scaling production, surviving parts shortages, dealing with the mess of US e-bike laws, and why the company is betting big on autonomous delivery.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
What is the current status of the bike and production ramp?
On the bike, the main thing is the production ramp. It’s one thing to create a product as a traditional OE where you work with several Tier 1 suppliers, get them to deliver on time, and assemble it. With us, we’ve built and designed everything down to individual components and ICs. Over the last year, every imaginable supply chain learning has come across.
We’ve been in the trenches competing with AI server demands for components like ICs, compute, memory, and raw PCBA [printed circuit board assembly] materials. Our inverter board is designed entirely in-house for high performance, and the thermals require a sophisticated board material. It turns out AI server farms have similar thermal requirements, triggering a global shortage, so we had to requalify and resource. But all that is behind us, and we are really starting to flow to customers and ramp up. A huge draw to come to Also was shipping a product that people will enjoy and use on the road every day, and reaching that milestone now has been huge for the team.
How many bikes have you delivered so far? Are you still in the Founder’s Edition phase?
That’s right. We’re quickly ramping up. We have a substantial number out there now, and you can see a lot of volume and traffic online of people taking their first rides. Deliveries are quickly increasing along the classic manufacturing ramp where you start steadily and then add volume.
In hindsight, was targeting a spring launch too optimistic?
At the time, based on everything we knew, spring was very much on plan. But as with Rivian on the automotive side or us earlier this year, a lot of unknown unknowns happened. Certainly I didn’t foresee the intense urgency around AI server hardware, nor the fact that those supply chains are so shared with light electric vehicles.
“Certainly I didn’t foresee the intense urgency around AI server hardware.”
— Chris Yu, president of Also
Was there direct overlap between Also’s supply chain and Rivian’s?
I look at it as a three-way Venn diagram between us — vertically integrated small EVs — and Rivian — full-size automotive EVs — and broader AI hardware like robotics and servers. There is a healthy overlap right in the middle, alongside direct overlap between us and Rivian. Where we overlap with Rivian there is a clear benefit, but it wasn’t easy for Rivian either.
[Rivian CEO] RJ [Scaringe] and I talk all the time. Half the time we’re discussing how to handle a specific part or supply chain constraint. You either fight for the part and lean on suppliers, find an alternative supplier with the identical component, or — as both we and Rivian have had to do — completely redesign and requalify the system around a replacement part.
Can you get specific on what components had to be redesigned or requalified?
It sounds relatively boring on paper, but it’s critical. One example was IC components like high-performance capacitors. Swapping them requires the work of going through full validation testing to make sure the alternative hits our durability and lifespan standards, because those components dictate the reliability of PCBAs.
Another was raw PCBA board material. Only certain base materials meet our flammability, thermal cycle, and structural rigidity requirements. When supplies ran short, we had to qualify third and fourth alternatives. There is no parallelization of verification testing — components must spend weeks inside thermal chambers and on shock and vibration rigs to prove they can handle real-world conditions.
In a letter to customers, [head of product] Saul Leiken mentioned there were regulatory hurdles around power output as well. What happened with UL certification?
It wasn’t so much an impediment as proof of how nascent the regulatory space is relative to what we’re building. Our battery combines several uncommon attributes: exceptionally high power density, an automotive-style software-defined battery management system with two-way flow for regenerative braking, USB-C 3.1 charging at up to 240 watts, and a removable pack.
Those things combined don’t exist in standard e-bike battery guidelines. Certification bodies like UL write standards assuming a typical e-bike pack without USB data connections or such high bidirectional power throughput. When we presented our architecture, we identified undefined areas in the certification rules. Rather than treating it as a gray area and self-certifying, we partnered directly with UL to develop a clarification standard tailored to this type of battery architecture. We went back and forth, completed unit testing on both sides, agreed on the protocol, and we are now fully UL certified.
Do you anticipate any thermal runaway problems, given how battery fires have plagued the e-bike sector?
With any lithium-ion battery, you can never say never — whether you’re Tesla, Rivian, or an e-bike maker. Even from top-tier cell manufacturers like LG, Samsung, or Panasonic, there is an inherent cell fallout rate. Across thousands of vehicles and millions of cells, math dictates a non-zero number. That part is inescapable basic physics.
Where we are super confident is our pack architecture. We took an exceptionally robust and conservative approach from both a mechanical and software protection standpoint, incorporating passive and active propagation defenses learned from generations of automotive EV battery design. The cell architecture, array welding, and management systems all benefit directly from that engineering.
When do you anticipate starting deliveries of the Standard and Performance trims?
Super soon. We have started opening reservation conversions, and anticipation for the Performance trim has been huge. We are focused on fulfilling orders for the supporters who lined up first and waited the longest, and the Performance line will follow right around the corner.
Early reservation holders on Reddit voiced frustration about communication gaps during the delays. What did you learn from that?
I forget sometimes how much of a blessing it is for customers to care that much. It’s easy to make a product where nobody cares and there are zero Reddit comments. The responsibility is on us to be transparent. Our team’s default mentality was heads-down execution: chase suppliers, run engineering, and pass tests. We didn’t come up for air to keep everyone posted.
That was a mistake on our part — not providing regular, transparent updates for the cohort that backed us early. We’ve changed that over the last couple of months, establishing regular communication with our preorder holders about what’s happening in production and what’s coming next.
“That was a mistake on our part — not providing regular, transparent updates for the cohort that backed us early.”
Did the delays trigger many order cancellations?
Very few. Most people backed the project sight unseen, and since then almost everyone has attended a test event to try it out, which led them to double down. The overwhelming sentiment has just been: “I want it. When is it coming?”
Between pedal-by-wire, swappable frames, and custom software, did you overcomplicate the bike when an off-the-shelf design could have shipped much faster?
I don’t look at it that way at all. If we were to revisit the design, I would do the exact same thing. The largest untapped opportunity isn’t cyclists who already tolerate the current bike experience. It’s the massive demographic of people intrigued by leaving the car behind who haven’t opted in yet. Their hesitations are consistent: fear of theft, avoiding maintenance every two months, wanting seamless navigation and audio, and needing to carry a child without having to buy three different bikes.
Solving those pain points requires a baseline of technology. Just like in automotive EVs, once you use software to personalize the ride and eliminate friction, people opt in. The majority of people attending our test rides haven’t ridden a bicycle in 10 or 15 years. Our goal wasn’t to go overboard; it was determining the minimum amount of innovation needed to create an experience as frictionless as stepping into a Tesla Model Y or Rivian R2.
With cities and states cracking down on overpowered bikes and mopeds, how does Also fit into the shifting regulatory landscape?
We are well-positioned by design to navigate a patchwork regulatory system. Current backlash is driven by bad actors selling products labeled as e-bikes that are actually mini-motorcycles, or bikes where clipping a wire uncaps speeds to 45 mph without vehicle safety standards.
The primary issue is a lack of regulatory resolution between genuine Class 1, 2, and 3 e-bikes and unregulated vehicles, leading to blunt blanket bans like we’ve seen in New Jersey. Our philosophy is that the opportunity within legitimate Class 1, 2, and 3 categories is massive, and we remain definitively within that framework.
We engineered the bike with immediate low-end torque so accelerating to 20 or 28 mph is responsive and fun without needing dangerous motorcycle speeds. Furthermore, because the bike is software-defined, the identical hardware can be configured to local rules — whether that’s 20 mph, 28 mph, or European 25 km/h limits. We are also introducing over-the-air parental controls so families can set conservative speed limits for younger riders, which is the exact opposite of the cut-the-wire approach.
Were you concerned about delicate electronics or firmware falling out of calibration during shipping?
Physical package handling was an early challenge. FedEx did not handle the initial deliveries well, so we paused and switched carriers, which resolved the issue.
On firmware and calibration, it is a solved problem. Nobody picks up an electric car wondering if the drive-by-wire calibration got jostled in transit. Mechanically, the bike has very few moving parts. The drivetrain is fully sealed and pedal-by-wire, so traditional failure points like exposed derailleurs and shifters simply don’t exist. The down-tube computer, display unit, and hand controls are robust, solid-state systems rather than fragile instruments.
“FedEx did not handle the initial deliveries well, so we paused and switched carriers, which resolved the issue.”
What is the out-of-the-box assembly process like for non-cyclists?
Very minimal. I pushed the team to make it feel as turnkey as unboxing an Apple Watch. You release a few clips, slide off the outer carton, and find three core elements: the main frame, the top frame, and the cockpit. The cockpit handlebar contains all integrated controls and wiring with a blind internal connector.
Assembly entails mounting the front wheel, powering on the bike from shipping mode, connecting the mobile app, snapping on the modular top frame, and securing the stem base plate with two bolts. Threading the pedals is the final step, which is guided by short 20-second video walkthroughs in the app alongside a provided shock pump to set suspension pressure based on rider weight.
How will service and repairs work for riders who don’t live near an Also brand hub?
Many issues can be resolved over the air. When physical service is required, our onboard diagnostics pinpoint the exact issue immediately through data logs rather than requiring guesswork at a shop. If hardware replacement is necessary, we can dispatch parts proactively.
Our repair network combines our own facilities with authorized local bike shops. We currently have roughly 150 vetted partners, expanding beyond 200 soon. We provide these shops with complete technical documentation, dedicated software tools, and direct parts inventory. Because every component board is digitally serialized to the bike for anti-theft security, authorized partners use our proprietary software to link new parts directly to the frame.
Micromobility saw several high-profile company collapses after the pandemic boom. How does Also protect itself from those pitfalls?
We didn’t start Also solely to be an e-bike company. The bike is our flagship and our handshake with the world, but our broader mission is building purpose-built small vehicles. The vast majority of urban trips are short, low-payload journeys — moving a single passenger or delivering takeout. Designing an urban transportation network from scratch would never rely exclusively on multi-ton cars.
The bike serves as the architectural foundation for a broader vehicle roadmap that is software-defined, vertically integrated, and autonomy-first. Following the bike launch, we are heavily focused on autonomous delivery. Earlier this year, DoorDash joined as a strategic partner to develop and deploy autonomous delivery platforms. A light vehicle platform that carries payload across town at 28 mph offers significant cost-per-mile efficiencies, and our autonomous platform shares direct architectural commonality with that system.
Will that DoorDash collaboration result in a low-speed sidewalk robot?
Sidewalk robots represent a completely different product class — closer to an industrial automated robot than an L4 autonomous road vehicle. By nature, sidewalk robots travel at 1 to 2 mph. While that works within localized, high-density environments like university campuses, purpose-built light electric vehicles operate at vehicle speeds across entire metro areas.
I’m sure you’re aware there is some excitement going on around low-speed vehicles like golf carts.
One hundred percent. And it does feel like this kind of fits into that. There’s been a ton of interest there. And that’s one of the more common questions I get is like when can we get one of these. But I think what you just said is actually – that’s the point that I want to focus on, which is – It’s less about the specific form factor of like a TM-Q or otherwise. It’s more the notion that there’s this huge gap and a huge demand for people to say, hey, the average household has something like two point something vehicles. And nearly everyone agrees that you don’t need two Escalades. You need like one big capable vehicle. And we’ve seen that a lot of people have started picking up things like golf carts and LSVs. And I would argue that it’s in spite of the deficiencies in the category.
Because if you just think big picture, the problem that we’re trying to solve collectively is how do I have something that costs much, much less than an average-priced $50,000 car today? But at the same time, why does that have to be a crappy experience? I want that to be a premium experience and potentially be able to be L4 autonomous as well. And so for us, that’s a huge opportunity. So let’s take the notion of small purpose-built for getting around and doing the everyday trips that everyone does, but have it feel like a magical experience that potentially could be fully autonomous as well. That is a super interesting opportunity.

articles.title: I Dumped Apple's Fucking Word List
articles.body:
~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db
Lexicon.framework
Content note: this article prints the words uncensored, slurs included, because the whole point is to see what Apple flags. The one exception is the n-word: it is in the list in English and several other languages, and I'm not writing it out.
Nick posted this, I asked where it lives, and he answered. A database that tracks my profanity is not something I can leave alone, so I opened mine.
$ sqlite3 -readonly ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db .schema CREATE TABLE properties (ROWID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, key, value, UNIQUE (key)); CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "vword_usage" ( ROWID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, app TEXT, -- app identifier recipient TEXT, -- recipient identifier vword TEXT, -- vulgar word word_reading TEXT, -- the reading form of a word (relevant for Japanese) usage_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0, last_use_timestamp REAL DEFAULT 0, -- last use timestamp (seconds since the reference date) journaled ); CREATE UNIQUE INDEX app_recipient_vword_word_reading_idx ON vword_usage(app, recipient, vword, word_reading);
So the keyboard can know that you say fuck in Messages to one particular friend, but not in Mail to your boss. The unique index is on (app, recipient, word, reading), so that is the granularity.
Mine has zero rows. The properties table holds version = 2 and nothing else. The file was last written in April 2024.
At WWDC in June 2023, Craig Federighi announced the iOS 17 autocorrect rewrite with this line: "In those moments where you just want to type a ducking word, well, the keyboard will learn it, too." (TechCrunch, NPR)
This database is how it learns. The symbol names in the macOS shared library cache spell out the flow:
TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::set_current_app_id(CFString) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::set_current_recipient_ids(vector<string>) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::increment_usage_count(word, reading, recipients) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::decrement_usage_count(...) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::can_autocorrect(word, app, recipients) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::can_autocorrect_somewhere(word, reading) KB::FilterNonVulgarIfTopCandidateVulgar::filter_candidates(...) KB::Candidate::every_vulgar_word_is_allowlisted(VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper*, ...)
Plus log strings like Passing recipient IDs to the vulgar word usage database wrapper; number of IDs: %lu.
In plain terms:
A _KSUserWordsSynchroniser sharedAcrossLanguagesVulgarWordUsageValue symbol suggests it syncs between devices like your other learned words.
I tried to fill it. Using agent-desktop, I opened a new TextEdit document and typed well fuck this shit, damn it., first as a text insert, then as individual key presses. Nothing changed: no row, no log line, and the file's modification date stayed in 2024.
I don't know why, and I couldn't work it out. Maybe the Mac never records anything here, or maybe it only does so in some apps or settings. If you've got rows in yours, tell me what you did.
That would be a short article. But the database only counts words that are already known to be vulgar. So who decides that?
Searching the dyld shared cache for "vulgar" turned up a C API with an LX prefix (LXVulgarWordUsageDatabaseCreate, LXVulgarWordUsageDatabaseCanAutocorrect, …) and, more usefully, two functions on dictionary entries:
_LXEntryGetCategoryFlags _LXEntryGetMetaFlags
LX is Lexicon.framework, a private framework that reads the per-language dictionaries under /System/Library/LinguisticData/. Every word in those dictionaries is an LXEntry with two 32-bit flag fields. If the vulgarity rating is anywhere, it's in those bits.
I looked. NSSpellChecker, UITextChecker, NaturalLanguage and UILexicon don't expose vulgarity. SensitiveContentAnalysis covers images and video, not text. The only places "profanity" shows up on developer.apple.com are App Store age ratings and review guidelines.
So: private functions. Lexicon has no headers, but the C functions are exported, and their signatures are easy to guess because they follow CoreFoundation conventions. This program opens the dictionary for a locale, walks every entry, and prints both flag fields:
// lx.c — dump every word in a system lexicon with its flags. // clang -O1 -o lx lx.c -F/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks -framework Lexicon -framework CoreFoundation #include <CoreFoundation/CoreFoundation.h> #include <stdbool.h> #include <stdio.h> typedef const void *LXLexiconRef, *LXCursorRef, *LXEntryRef; extern CFStringRef kLXLexiconLocaleKey; LXLexiconRef LXLexiconCreate(CFDictionaryRef options, CFErrorRef *error); LXCursorRef LXLexiconCreateRootCursor(LXLexiconRef); void LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively(LXCursorRef, void (^)(LXEntryRef, bool *stop)); CFStringRef LXEntryCopyString(LXEntryRef); uint32_t LXEntryGetCategoryFlags(LXEntryRef); uint32_t LXEntryGetMetaFlags(LXEntryRef); int main(int argc, char **argv) { CFStringRef locale = CFStringCreateWithCString(NULL, argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "en_US", kCFStringEncodingUTF8); const void *keys[] = {kLXLexiconLocaleKey}, *values[] = {locale}; CFDictionaryRef options = CFDictionaryCreate(NULL, keys, values, 1, &kCFTypeDictionaryKeyCallBacks, &kCFTypeDictionaryValueCallBacks); LXLexiconRef lexicon = LXLexiconCreate(options, NULL); if (!lexicon) return 1; LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively(LXLexiconCreateRootCursor(lexicon), ^(LXEntryRef entry, bool *stop) { char word[512] = ""; CFStringRef s = LXEntryCopyString(entry); if (s) { CFStringGetCString(s, word, sizeof word, kCFStringEncodingUTF8); CFRelease(s); } printf("%08x\t%08x\t%s\n", LXEntryGetCategoryFlags(entry), LXEntryGetMetaFlags(entry), word); }); }
$ ./lx en_US | wc -l 199019 $ ./lx en_US | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "fuck" || $3 == "table" || $3 == "Trump"' 00000000 00800002 fuck 00000000 00000000 table 00002000 02000081 Trump
The same thing in Swift, loading the functions at runtime with dlopen and dlsym so you don't need to link against a private framework. It prints only words that carry one of the three tiers:
// lexflags.swift — swiftc -O lexflags.swift -o lexflags && ./lexflags en_US import Foundation let lexicon = dlopen("/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/Lexicon.framework/Lexicon", RTLD_NOW)! func sym<T>(_ name: String, as _: T.Type) -> T { unsafeBitCast(dlsym(lexicon, name)!, to: T.self) } typealias LXRef = UnsafeRawPointer let create = sym("LXLexiconCreate", as: (@convention(c) (CFDictionary, UnsafeMutablePointer<Unmanaged<CFError>?>?) -> LXRef?).self) let rootCursor = sym("LXLexiconCreateRootCursor", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> LXRef?).self) let enumerate = sym("LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef, @convention(block) (LXRef, UnsafeMutablePointer<Bool>) -> Void) -> Void).self) let copyString = sym("LXEntryCopyString", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> Unmanaged<CFString>?).self) let metaFlags = sym("LXEntryGetMetaFlags", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> UInt32).self) let category = sym("LXEntryGetCategoryFlags", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> UInt32).self) let localeKey = dlsym(lexicon, "kLXLexiconLocaleKey")!.load(as: CFString.self) let locale = CommandLine.arguments.dropFirst().first ?? "en_US" guard let lex = create([localeKey: locale] as CFDictionary, nil), let root = rootCursor(lex) else { fatalError("could not open lexicon for \(locale)") } let tiers: [(UInt32, String)] = [(0x0080_0000, "vulgar"), (0x0100_0000, "offensive"), (0x0200_0000, "sensitive")] enumerate(root) { entry, _ in let meta = metaFlags(entry) guard let tier = tiers.first(where: { meta & $0.0 != 0 })?.1, let word = copyString(entry)?.takeRetainedValue() else { return } print(tier, String(format: "%05x", category(entry)), word, separator: "\t") }
Both are read-only. They open the same dictionary the keyboard uses and print it.
Apple doesn't document these flags, so every meaning below is inferred: I grouped words by bit and read samples until each group's theme was obvious. The system code helps with one of them. An enum case called offensiveVulgarSensitive sits right next to the vulgar-word code, and three adjacent meta bits match it.
0x00800000
0x01000000
0x02000000
In en_US a word has at most one tier: they never overlap. Out of 199,019 entries, 4,271 have one.
Roughly: vulgar is swearing and sex slang, offensive is slurs aimed at groups of people, and sensitive is everything a keyboard shouldn't offer you unprompted: mild swears, insults, drugs, weapons, extremism, disease and bodily functions.
The other field is a topic bitmask, and a word can have several topics:
0x00100
0x00200
0x00400
0x00800
0x01000
0x02000
0x04000
0x08000
0x10000
0x20000
0x40000
The topic flags and the tiers are independent. 2,052 English words have a topic but no tier: gay, fat, God, Allah and sex are all tagged "sensitive context" but are not vulgar, offensive or sensitive. My guess is the topic is a hint ("be careful how you rank this") and the tier is the rule.
The lower meta bits are dull: proper nouns, abbreviations, camel-case brand names like iMac and tvOS. Nothing to see there.
This is where it gets fun. Some flags are obviously right, and some made me laugh.
blocklist.dat
The sensitive tier has 109 capitalized words. Here is all of it:
Al-Qaeda, Al-Qaida, Aryan, Aryans, Auschwitz, Bacchus, Beelzebub, Birkenau, Brave(s), Buchenwald, Chief(s), Chippendale(s), Christ-y, Christer(s), Crip(s), Dachau, Eichmann, Frenchier, Gentile(s), Gestapo(s), Goebbels, Goering, Hamas, Hezbollah, Himmler, Hitler, Hitlerian, Hitlerism, Hitlerite(s), Hitlerjugend, Hooters, Isis, Islamophobe(s), Islamophobic, Jehovah(s), Jewfro(s), Jezebel(s), Kalashnikov(s), Kristallnacht, Kuomintang, Londonderry, Luftwaffe, Mao, Mauthausen, Mickie(s), Mollie(s), Mongol(s), Mossad, Nazi(s), Nazism, Osama, Pornhub, Quaalude(s), Reich, Reichsmark, Reichstag, Sachsenhausen, Satan, Satanism, Shoah, Sinophobe(s), Sinophobic, Sodom, Stasi, Taliban, Treblinka, Trump, Trumps, Unabomber, Uzi(s)
(Plurals and possessives folded for brevity.)
Every other real person on that list is dead, and nearly all of them are Nazi officials, dictators or terrorists. Then there's Trump:
category meta word 00002000 02000081 Trump sensitive tier + politics topic 00002000 02000081 Trumps 00002000 02000081 Trump's 00000000 00000000 trump (the card-game word: clean) 00000000 00000000 trumped
For comparison:
en_GB matches en_US. Other languages differ: the German dictionary has Trump clean (and puts Hitler in the offensive tier), and Swedish is the one that flags Putin as sensitive.
What the flag does matters here. As far as I can tell, a sensitive word is one the keyboard shouldn't suggest on its own. You can still type it and it won't be corrected away. Think "keep this out of the QuickType bar unless the user is clearly heading there", which is a lot milder than a ban.
There is a plausible reason Apple would want that for one specific name. In February 2025, iPhone dictation briefly showed "Trump" when people said "racist". It went viral, and Apple called it a "phonetic overlap" in the speech model and shipped a fix within a day (9to5Mac). The dictionary files on my Mac are from July 2025. A rule that keeps the name out of unprompted suggestions would stop that kind of thing from happening again through the keyboard. I can't prove that's why it's there, and I don't have an older dictionary to compare against. But it fits.
Because I'm Norwegian and had to check:
Every party gets the politics topic and none gets a tier. The only Norwegians in the sensitive tier are a mass murderer and a Nazi collaborator.
The same three tiers exist in every European dictionary I tried, Cyrillic included. The counts are entries, not lemmas, so heavily inflected languages like Polish and Russian look much worse than they are: every case and conjugation of a swear word is a separate entry.
The bits don't seem to mean the same thing everywhere. Arabic and Hebrew return hundreds of thousands of "sensitive" entries, so those dictionaries probably reuse the bits for something else, and I left them out. Korean, Catalan and Hungarian return nothing, and Japanese crashes my dumper.
Samples from Norwegian, since that's what I type in when I'm not typing English:
The tier words are mostly what you'd expect, but the edges are different in each language, and that is where the human-edited parts show. Norwegian calls idiot offensive and English calls it sensitive. German thinks Hitler is a slur.
There is a second, separate filter. Every English language model has a blocklist.bundle, and there's a qp_blocklist.bundle for QuickPath, the swipe keyboard:
/System/Library/LinguisticData/RequiredAssets_en.bundle/AssetData/en.lm/ ├── blocklist.bundle/{blocklist.dat, blocklistidmap.dat} └── qp_blocklist.bundle/{blocklist.dat, blocklistidmap.dat}
blocklistidmap.dat is a 20-byte header followed by (lexicon token ID, class ID) pairs of 32-bit integers. Mapping the token IDs back through the dictionary gives 2,544 words in 930 classes. Most classes are inflection groups:
931 fuck | fucked | fucking | fucks 1181 molest | molestation | molested | molester | molesting 1514 died | dies | dying 1611 Holocaust | holocaust | holocausts 1614 denied | denies | deny | denying 923 Semite | Semites | Semitic 1487 ghetto | ghettoes | ghettos 1720 animals | brown | cats
blocklist.dat is a packed trie over those class IDs, so it blocks sequences: "deny" followed by "Holocaust", and whatever 1720 pairs with. A class that puts brown next to animals and cats suggests the list targets specific phrasings rather than single words, though which phrasings I can't tell without decoding the trie. The runtime check is LMLanguageModelTokenSequenceIsBlocklisted in LanguageModeling.framework. I got far enough to learn that its fourth and fifth arguments include an output pointer, but my probe still crashes intermittently, so I haven't read the actual phrases yet. That's for a follow-up.
# Your own learned-swears database (probably empty on a Mac) sqlite3 -readonly ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db 'select * from vword_usage' # Build the Swift version from above and filter by tier swiftc -O lexflags.swift -o lexflags ./lexflags en_US | awk -F'\t' '$1 == "vulgar" {print $3}' | sort -u | less ./lexflags nb_NO | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "faen" || $3 == "helvete" || $3 == "idiot"'
If you'd rather not build anything, the gist has every tiered word for 15 locales as TSV, plus the code and a script that regenerates them. It's a snapshot of macOS 15.6 and won't be kept up to date.
If you find something funnier than Oedipus, I want to hear about it.
