articles.title: Charles Tandy, the mastermind behind Radio Shack
articles.body:
Charles David Tandy was the chairman of the board, president, and chief executive officer of the Tandy Corporation. He was born May 15, 1918 and died November 4, 1978. Tandy was involved in the creation or expansion of three retail chains: Tandy Leather, Radio Shack, and Pier 1 Imports.
Early life
Tandy was the second of three children born to Carmen (née McLain) and David Lewis Tandy in Brownsville, Texas, on May 15, 1918. Charles’ youngest brother, Bill, went on to run his own chain of leather craft stores in the early 1950s before merging with Tandy Corporation.
At the age of 10, Charles and a classmate started selling scraps of leather from his father’s store to classmates for spare change, teaching them how to make belts out of them. With another classmate whose father owned a boot company, they started making heavier belts from scraps of boot leather that they sold to department stores.
In 1935 Tandy graduated from Central High School in Fort Worth, Texas.
Charles Tandy’s education and early career
Tandy’s father co-owned the Hinckley-Tandy Leather Company with his friend Norton Hinckley.
After flunking out of Rice Instutute in his freshman year, he graduated from Texas Christian Academy in 1940. While in college, he sold women’s shoes. He attended Harvard Business School but did not graduate. In the spring of 1941, the Navy offered commissions to Harvard Business School students. Tandy applied and was accepted, serving 6 years.
While in the Navy he set a record for selling war bonds. In 1945, he married Gwen Johnston, a wealthy widow 14 years his senior.
While he was in the Navy, he observed patients recovering in Navy hospitals doing leathercraft for therapy and recreation. He wrote a letter to his father suggesting this might be a way to expand Hinckley-Tandy’s business after World War II ended. This led to them setting up a mail order business, Tandycraft, after he left the Navy.
Tandy developed his small family leather business into an international corporation. He first turned it into a leather craft company when shoe rationing in World War II almost killed the business, and later expanded into selling leather and tools to make such products as wallets. Hinckley and Tandy split in 1950, with Hinckley taking the part of the business that sold shoe findings, and Tandy taking the leathercraft business.
Taking Tandy Corporation Public
In 1954, David Tandy suffered a heart attack, exposing a weakness in the corporate structure. Since Tandy was a private company, his death would have forced a liquidation of the company in order to pay the inheritance taxes. They sought a way to take the company public to protect it. The company wasn’t really large enough to conduct a traditional IPO, so instead, they sought to merge with a company that was already listed on the New York Stock Exchange. After shopping around for prospects, Charles Tandy engineered a leveraged buyout of the Tandy Leather Company by the American Hide and Leather Company, based in Boston, in 1955.
The Tandys and their leadership didn’t agree with the direction American Hide and Leather took the company after the merger. A power struggle ensued, resulting in the Tandys, their extended family, and Tandy managers buying as much stock in the company as they could, often using borrowed money. In 1959, they forced a proxy battle to take over the company. As a result, Tandy partisans received five of the nine seats on the board. They quickly divested three unprofitable subsidiaries American Hide and Leather had purchased after merging with Tandy, moved the corporate headquarters to New York to facilitate the divestitures, then moved operations to Fort Worth. In 1960, they changed the name to Tandy Corporation, taking the ticker symbol TAN.
Pier 1 Imports
By 1962, Charles Tandy had concluded he had ambitions bigger than the leather craft business could satisfy.
One of the businesses they looked into was Cost Plus Imports, which sold imported furniture and other goods out of a converted warehouse at near-wholesale prices. A failed public offering left the company in a cash crunch. Charles and Gwen were already planning a vacation to San Francisco in August 1962, so they visited the store as part of the trip. They found a 15,000 square foot store, several times larger than a Tandy store, selling $7-$8 million worth of merchandise per year when a Tandy store might sell $200,000. Tandy called one of his lieutenants, Luther Henderson, to come visit the store.
Tandy bought into the business, acquiring with it the right to operate stores under the Cost Plus name under Henderson’s leadership. But the partnership only lasted three years. Tandy found the business model worked well for one giant store in San Francisco, but needed substantial adjustment to work as a chain throughout the country. In 1965, they parted ways, with the Tandy-backed operation taking the name Pier 1 Imports.
But Henderson and Tandy found the way Tandy operated its leathercraft stores didn’t fit the furniture business, with its longer lead times. In 1966, Tandy sold Pier 1 to Henderson for $1.8 million.
Henderson and Tandy remained friendly, with Tandy even taking a seat on Pier 1’s board. Tandy chided Henderson, asking why they didn’t run the company that way when it was part of Tandy Corporation. The 1992 book Tandy’s Money Machine quoted Henderson as saying Tandy was a good mentor but he didn’t take the time to understand the differences between Pier 1’s and Tandy Leather’s business models. Given more room, Henderson thought the partnership could have worked.
Radio Shack
Charles Tandy saw the electronics business as a natural expansion for Tandy Corporation, another hobby with a similar business model. He approached Lafayette Electronics and Allied Electronics to no avail. So in 1961, he opened an electronics store called Electronics Crafts, soon opening a second and a third.
Meanwhile, in Boston, the same bank that had helped Tandy match up with American Hide and Leather had another creditor who was having trouble meeting its obligations, an electronics store called Radio Shack. The bank had told Tandy about Radio Shack before, when he was talking with Lafayette and Allied. Tandy wasn’t able to work with Milton Deutschmann, the head of Radio Shack, but with the company $7 million in debt and losing $200,000 a month, the bank forced Deutschmann to come to the table. Deutschmann agreed to an audit, and agreed to sell for a $300,000 advance that would give Tandy the right to acquire 62 percent ownership of Radio Shack at book value. Price Waterhouse conducted an audit and concluded its book value was zero, giving Tandy control of Radio Shack for $300,000.
How Charles Tandy turned around Radio Shack
Tandy’s turnaround plan was to close the large stores and open a large number of smaller stores in rented locations so he could close struggling stores with minimal risk, close the catalog business, and go to cash-only sales, eliminating credit.
By 1966, Radio Shack was profitable. And a decade later, it was a nationwide chain with over 3,500 company owned stores and another 3,500 franchises.
This quote dates itself, but business writer Milton Moskowitz called Radio Shack “the most spectacular retail expansion under one name since the explosion of the A&P grocery chain in the early part of the century.” The subsequent disappearance of both of those chains shows how fragile business is. Maybe Charles Tandy is an Ozymandias, but at least for now there are still a fair number of people living who remember his empire.
As for A&P, I had no idea it liquidated in 2015 because I live west of the Mississippi River. I remember them pulling out of Missouri in the 1970s and slowly fading away. If you live east of the Mississippi, you’re more likely to remember it as something more than the grocery store your grandmother or great grandmother shopped at.
Charles Tandy as a manager
Charles Tandy worked hard and drove his people hard. Although his business was hobbies, he had no hobbies himself. He was notorious for coming into the office late, but then he stayed more than 12 hours and often worked weekends.
He was frequently a harsh critic. By some accounts he would find the person in the room who could best handle a chewing out, then chew that person out in front of everyone.
“There are some delicate souls in the world who wilt at the first harsh words. Then ther are others that you need to use a baseball bat to discuss things with. So I’d have to say that Charles had a dial setting for everybody,” Tandy corporate secretary Bill Michero said.
Ted and Elaine Yamagata, his primary importers from Japan, said he was very demanding. “He would sometimes tear us apart, but he always put us together and we always left very encouraged,” Elaine Yamagata said.
Bill Brown, his banker in Boston, called the act of getting up in the middle of a meeting when things aren’t going your way, walking toward the door, and announcing you were going back to wherever you came from, “pulling a Charles Tandy.”
Charles Tandy’s last years
Tandy made other acquisitions after Radio Shack, including an attempt at running department stores. None of them were as successful as Radio Shack, and in most cases Tandy divested the acquisitions within a few years. His last major project was revitalizing downtown Fort Worth, culminating in the construction of the eight-block Tandy Center.
Tandy died of a heart attack in his sleep on 4 November 1978 at the age of 60, and was buried at Greenwood Memorial Park in Fort Worth, Texas.
David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

articles.title: Study estimates 75% of NFL players who died over 15-year span had CTE
articles.body:
An estimated 75% of professional football players who died over a 15-year span had signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, a study published Wednesday found.
It’s the highest estimate to date. Most recently, a study published in August by the same group estimated that one-quarter of NFL players who died in a five-year span had CTE. The new study, published in JAMA Network Open, put the figure at three times higher.
Not all people with signs of CTE in the brain go on to experience cognitive decline or dementia, and some people may never experience symptoms at all. A smaller proportion of the former players in the analysis were estimated to have dementia, about 27%, the study found.
The results were surprising, said study leader Yorghos Tripodis, the director of statistics and data management at the Boston University Alzheimer’s Disease and CTE Center. Boston University houses the UNITE Brain Bank, which studies the effects of repetitive head trauma in donated brains, including the brains of athletes, military personnel and others.
“I had to double-check the numbers,” Tripodis said. Still, he said, the number is a best guess. “Right now we don’t know how to diagnose CTE when people are alive, so we are trying to estimate.”
In an emailed statement, an NFL spokesperson said, in part, that the league “continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts.”
Repeated blows and bias
When a person’s head jolts during an impact, the brain — which is suspended in fluid inside the skull — can slam into the skull or twist, said Dr. Julian Bailes, chair of the neurosurgery department at Endeavor Health in the Chicago area. Each blow is an opportunity for proteins called tau to build up in the brain.
“If that happens over and over again, that damage accrues,” said Bailes, who wasn’t involved with the new research.
The disease can affect parts of the brain involved with regulating behavior and emotions, which can lead to memory loss, depression, violent mood swings and other symptoms. Those symptoms can also be linked to other illnesses.
Although CTE can cause symptoms similar to those of other neurodegenerative diseases, such as dementia and Parkinson’s disease, the signature it leaves on the brain is unique, Bailes said.
One huge hurdle in studying the prevalence of CTE is that the microscopic changes don’t show up on brain scans. That means the condition can be diagnosed only during an autopsy.
Past research has been criticized for bias, since people with cognitive decline and their families are much likelier to either donate their brains to brain banks after they die or ask for autopsies — a previous study by Boston University researchers found that 99% of the brains donated to research by former NFL players had signs of CTE.
In the new study, Tripodis and his team tried to remove as much of that bias as possible to determine a more accurate estimate of CTE rates in former NFL players. They combined data from the UNITE Brain Bank with national death records of other former NFL players who died from 2008 to 2023.
In total, the researchers looked at data from 396 donated brains, plus information from 1,966 other deceased former NFL players. They factored in the ages of death along with estimated rates of mild cognitive impairment and dementia in former NFL players older than 50.
About 93% of the donated brains had signs of CTE, which shows up as structural damage in the brain. The research team calculated that the families of players with symptoms of cognitive decline were about five times likelier to donate brains than the families of players without symptoms and then performed a statistical analysis to correct for that bias.

From there, they estimated that among the roughly 2,360 former players who died during the 15-year time frame, about 1,760, or nearly 75%, had CTE. In comparison, only about 1% of brains donated to banks in the U.S., Austria and Brazil have signs of the disease, the researchers said.
But plenty of people with signs of CTE never develop symptoms, Tripodis said.
The researchers estimated that 27% of the 2,360 players studied had dementia.
The dementia “can be from all causes,” Tripodis said. “But it is very likely that in this specific population that CTE is causing dementia.”
Reducing impacts
Until doctors figure out a way to diagnose CTE while people are still alive, any studies quantifying how many people have the condition will be estimates, said Dr. Jim Kelly, a professor emeritus of neurology at the University of Colorado Anschutz.
“These are all estimates. They had no autopsies on five times as many players who died as they did have autopsies for,” said Kelly, who wasn’t involved in the research.
Some of the autopsies may also have revealed just one or a couple of lesions associated with CTE, “and it seems unlikely that that would lead to anything in terms of a behavior change or dementia,” he said.
Those are difficult studies to do, Bailes agreed. They seek to determine “how many people out there have a condition when not all of them are symptomatic,” he said, adding that the findings are a call for more research into diagnosing CTE in people who are still living.
“If you can’t tell if someone has a certain disease until they’re dead, you really can’t help them,” he said.
In the meantime, prevention is key, Tripodis said: “If you reduce the number of brain injuries, brain impacts, you substantially decrease the risk.”
The NFL has already implemented measures to try to reduce the number of high-impact hits players face. They include redesigned helmets — such as the Guardian Cap — and the dynamic kickoff rule, which leads to lower collision speeds.

In an emailed statement, an NFL spokesperson said, in part, that the league “continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts.”
Repeated blows and bias
When a person’s head jolts during an impact, the brain — which is suspended in fluid inside the skull — can slam into the skull or twist, said Dr. Julian Bailes, chair of the neurosurgery department at Endeavor Health in the Chicago area. Each blow is an opportunity for proteins called tau to build up in the brain.
“If that happens over and over again, that damage accrues,” said Bailes, who wasn’t involved with the new research.
The disease can affect parts of the brain involved with regulating behavior and emotions, which can lead to memory loss, depression, violent mood swings and other symptoms. Those symptoms can also be linked to other illnesses.
Although CTE can cause symptoms similar to those of other neurodegenerative diseases, such as dementia and Parkinson’s disease, the signature it leaves on the brain is unique, Bailes said.
One huge hurdle in studying the prevalence of CTE is that the microscopic changes don’t show up on brain scans. That means the condition can be diagnosed only during an autopsy.
Past research has been criticized for bias, since people with cognitive decline and their families are much likelier to either donate their brains to brain banks after they die or ask for autopsies — a previous study by Boston University researchers found that 99% of the brains donated to research by former NFL players had signs of CTE.
In the new study, Tripodis and his team tried to remove as much of that bias as possible to determine a more accurate estimate of CTE rates in former NFL players. They combined data from the UNITE Brain Bank with national death records of other former NFL players who died from 2008 to 2023.
In total, the researchers looked at data from 396 donated brains, plus information from 1,966 other deceased former NFL players. They factored in the ages of death along with estimated rates of mild cognitive impairment and dementia in former NFL players older than 50.
About 93% of the donated brains had signs of CTE, which shows up as structural damage in the brain. The research team calculated that the families of players with symptoms of cognitive decline were about five times likelier to donate brains than the families of players without symptoms and then performed a statistical analysis to correct for that bias.

FOR SUBSCRIBERSThe midterms are over, and Trump is over the midterms
FOR SUBSCRIBERSDOJ is deploying a record number of monitors on Election Day
FOR SUBSCRIBERSHow NBC News has prepared to cover election night
FOR SUBSCRIBERSWelcome to the gas price election
FOR SUBSCRIBERSThe fight for young men comes to Michigan
FOR SUBSCRIBERSThe battlegrounds our journalists are reporting from

From there, they estimated that among the roughly 2,360 former players who died during the 15-year time frame, about 1,760, or nearly 75%, had CTE. In comparison, only about 1% of brains donated to banks in the U.S., Austria and Brazil have signs of the disease, the researchers said.
But plenty of people with signs of CTE never develop symptoms, Tripodis said.
The researchers estimated that 27% of the 2,360 players studied had dementia.
The dementia “can be from all causes,” Tripodis said. “But it is very likely that in this specific population that CTE is causing dementia.”
Reducing impacts
Until doctors figure out a way to diagnose CTE while people are still alive, any studies quantifying how many people have the condition will be estimates, said Dr. Jim Kelly, a professor emeritus of neurology at the University of Colorado Anschutz.
“These are all estimates. They had no autopsies on five times as many players who died as they did have autopsies for,” said Kelly, who wasn’t involved in the research.
Some of the autopsies may also have revealed just one or a couple of lesions associated with CTE, “and it seems unlikely that that would lead to anything in terms of a behavior change or dementia,” he said.
Those are difficult studies to do, Bailes agreed. They seek to determine “how many people out there have a condition when not all of them are symptomatic,” he said, adding that the findings are a call for more research into diagnosing CTE in people who are still living.
“If you can’t tell if someone has a certain disease until they’re dead, you really can’t help them,” he said.
In the meantime, prevention is key, Tripodis said: “If you reduce the number of brain injuries, brain impacts, you substantially decrease the risk.”
The NFL has already implemented measures to try to reduce the number of high-impact hits players face. They include redesigned helmets — such as the Guardian Cap — and the dynamic kickoff rule, which leads to lower collision speeds.

articles.title: Apple is all in on AI — its own and everyone else’s
articles.body:
Apple’s latest earnings show how it’s continuing to capitalize on the AI boom without busting its budget on the infrastructure spending consuming its competitors.
Apple is all in on AI — its own and everyone else’s
AI was mentioned 45 times on the quarterly earnings call.
Overall, Apple posted its best-ever fiscal year for revenue and earnings per share. iPhone and Mac sales continued to grow strongly in the fourth quarter. iPhone revenue rose 17.5% from a year earlier to a September quarter record of $57.6 billion while Mac revenue climbed 24% to $10.8 billion, its highest level in four years. Shares nevertheless fell in premarket trading Tuesday after Apple warned that rising memory costs would squeeze its profit margins in the holiday quarter.
Apple hasn’t disclosed how much of its revenue growth reflects AI demand or higher prices, but its executives clearly see the technology as a way to drive further sales.
During the earnings call, CFO Kevan Parekh cited a “wide range of ways that AI can contribute to revenue growth over time.”
“On the product side, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities,” he said. “And we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.”
Apple can sell its giant user base the devices they use for AI, even if the AI itself comes from someone else. It can collect fees on subscriptions to AI apps. And it can charge customers who want more access to its own AI features.
“We see tremendous opportunity in AI,” John Ternus said on his first earnings call as CEO.
AI and Apple Intelligence were mentioned a record 45 times on the earnings call, according to financial research platform AlphaSense — even more than on the call following Apple’s unveiling of the technology and plans for a revamped Siri in June 2024.
Mentions of AI or “Apple Intelligence” on earnings calls
On the call, Apple continued to position itself as the interface through which consumers use AI — including competitors’ technology. With more than 2.5 billion active devices, it already has an enormous audience for whatever AI services emerge.
Apple, unlike its Big Tech peers, isn’t pouring comparable sums into infrastructure. Its approach combines on-device processing, its own servers, and outside AI technology. Siri AI uses models developed with Google’s Gemini technology while Apple reportedly plans to let users choose among outside AI providers for features such as writing tools and image generation.
Apple spent $2.2 billion on capital expenditures last quarter, compared with Amazon’s $77.3 billion and Alphabet’s $51.4 billion. Those totals cover companywide CapEx, not just AI, and exclude some AI expenses. Apple’s operating expenses rose 21% to $19.2 billion as it increased R&D spending, including on AI. Siri AI’s cloud costs will appear in services cost of sales. Those costs could grow with usage: Parekh said it’s too early to predict how many requests will require servers rather than on-device processing. Still, Apple’s capital spending remains just a fraction of its peers’.
More AI usage also gives Apple something to sell.
Siri AI is only beginning to reach customers. Apple launched the revamped assistant in beta for US English users in September and expanded it to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.
Apple plans to turn some of that usage into subscription revenue. Ternus said features relying on server-side models, including Siri AI and intelligent photo editing, will have usage limits. Customers who need more capacity “will be able to purchase expanded access in the future,” he said. “In the beginning, iCloud tiers were largely about storage, but we’ve been adding more capabilities and features to it.”
Apple also benefits when customers buy its hardware to run AI locally, including models developed by other companies. Mac, Ternus said, is “having an AI moment all its own.”
“We feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities.”
Apple offered specific examples of companies putting its computers to work on AI. Gap is running AI entirely on Mac Mini computers for loss prevention across hundreds of stores, avoiding cloud token costs for those tasks. Christie’s is running local models on Mac Studio computers to improve workflows including pricing estimates.
For those customers, buying Apple hardware provides a way to use AI without paying a cloud provider for every request.
Mac Mini and Mac Studio, Ternus said, “are pushing the boundaries of local, private AI, giving users the ability to do things once considered impossible.”
The Mac Mini’s emergence as an AI machine has given the small, screenless desktop a new constituency among developers and hobbyists looking for a relatively affordable way to run models locally. Earlier this year, then-CEO Tim Cook said customer recognition of the Mac Mini and Mac Studio’s capabilities for AI and agentic tools was happening faster than Apple had predicted, leading to higher-than-expected demand.
Apple also makes money when customers subscribe to someone else’s AI. Earlier this year, The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple was on pace to bring in more than $1 billion in App Store fees from generative AI apps in 2026, according to analytics firm AppMagic.
That revenue, of course, depends on customers paying through Apple’s system. OpenAI has begun directing potential subscribers to pay through its website instead of the App Store, bypassing Apple’s commissions, The Wall Street Journal reported. Apple’s position gives it a way to profit from competitors’ AI, but those competitors have an incentive to find a route around its fees.
Still, Apple already has multiple ways to benefit from people using AI. It can sell the computer, collect a subscription commission, and eventually charge for more of its own services. It doesn’t have to build every model — or fund infrastructure on its competitors’ scale — to get paid.

articles.title: How to write comparison content that doesn't age like milk
articles.body:
How to write comparison content that doesn't age like milk
Contents
Every marketing lead I talk with sees potential of comparison content, but also see it as a double-edged sword they're not comfortable investing in.
The hesitation usually comes from some mix of (1) it feels unnatural to give your competitors their flowers on your own website, and (2) comparison pages come with maintenance overhead nobody wants to deal with.
Competitors ship things, change their pricing, get acquired (or acquire others), and all of a sudden the article you wrote in March is outdated in June.
So how do you walk the line between being fair (complimentary, even) to your competitors while still capturing demand & showing off your product's strengths? And how do you keep the content accurate once it's out in the world to avoid spreading misinformation?
Both are worth figuring out if you want to write comparison content that doesn't get dunked on. And both are things I'm here to give some answers to based on our experience writing comparison content at PostHog.
Why bother with comparison content?
Because it works.
Since 2021, over 25k people have signed up for PostHog after reading a comparison. Almost 50% did it within 24 hours of reading; ~75% within 30 days.
It makes sense why they overperform. Someone searching for this style of content has already decided they need something, the only question left is which one. Comparison content sits at the sweet spot in the funnel where that decision gets made, and your job is to help make it (ideally in your favour, but not always and that's okay. More on that later).
Our credentials
Technically, our first comparison was a roundup. The best open source analytics tools went live in October 2021 and is still our single most-read piece of comparison content, at 150k+ pageviews and counting.
It set the template for the early days: "best open source X" for session replay, A/B testing, and feature flags. Open source was one of our wedges, so that's what we compared on.
The first head-to-head, PostHog vs Amplitude, followed in May 2022. It still gets a few hundred readers a month, which is more than I can say for most things we published back in 2022. Matomo and Mixpanel came next.
2023 was the year it became a thing. Every new PostHog product came with a new set of competitors. Session Replay brought Hotjar, FullStory, and LogRocket. Feature Flags brought LaunchDarkly, GrowthBook, and Statsig. Web Analytics brought GA4.
We went from three to fourteen in a year, and the maintenance problem flared up. Three pages you can keep accurate by hand; fourteen, each with a feature table and pricing that changes every quarter, not so much. It's, to this day, a workflow we're constantly working on solving for and improving.
2024 was the alternatives year. A lot of our competitors got a "best X alternatives" piece: Hotjar, Statsig, Plausible, Matomo, and about fifteen more. We also launched error tracking, wrote PostHog vs Sentry in August, and watched it become our most-read head-to-head of all time within two years.
2025 and 2026 followed the products; Best Sentry alternatives and best error tracking tools for error tracking, best open source LLM observability tools for AI observability, and best Datadog alternatives as the first hint of what was coming next. Most recently we started doubling down on our observability stack: PostHog vs Langfuse and a full set of AI observability roundups (best AI observability tools, plus Langfuse, LangSmith, and Braintrust alternatives). Then logs: best log monitoring tools, Grafana Loki and Splunk alternatives, and PostHog vs Datadog.
This isn't an AEO fad for us; we were writing comparison content BeFoRe iT wAs cOoL, back when the answer engine was a guy named Greg on Stack Overflow.
And while they have shapeshifted plenty since then, we've stayed true to two principles:
- Do no harm. We don't trash-talk competitors, we don't straw-man them, and we admit when and where they're better than us. No sneaky shit, as our handbook puts it.
- Respect the reader's intelligence, and meet them where they are. A developer comparing tools is smart, busy, and already halfway towards a decision. Give them the answer as accurately and as directly as possible, and let them make the right call for their product and use case. Also, they can tell if you're generating AI slop comparisons, it's a bad look.
Be the comparison page you'd want to read
PostHog doesn't have every feature every competitor has (yet), and we're fine admitting it. Our credibility with the reader is worth more than whatever we'd "win" by fudging the truth.
We're not the solution for everyone. We are the best solution for someone (a lot of someones, actually), and the job is capturing their attention. Which means you will, occasionally, lose a deal on your own website: someone reads PostHog vs Competitor, concludes Competitor is the better fit, and goes and buys Competitor. We wish them godspeed and focus on our ICP anyway.
In practice, this means picking up a few uncomfortable habits:
Acknowledge your gaps and credit their wins.
"If you need X, they do it better than we do today" is a sentence you'll find on our pages. Softening it with what's coming is fine (a roadmap link, a "we're working on it"), as long as you're clear about where you are right now for the readers deciding today.
For example, earlier this year our articles admitted we were weaker on APM because we hadn't shipped distributed tracing or metrics yet. True at the time. We've since shipped a full APM suite, and the articles now say that instead. Our content matches our shipping, not just our ambitions.
Readers don't think less of you for crediting a competitor; they think more. It's the cheapest trust signal in content marketing, and almost nobody uses it. And as AI eats everything else about content, trust is one of the few things left you can't generate. Say the nice thing.
There's another reader to keep in mind, too: LLMs. When someone asks Claude "PostHog vs Sentry for a Next.js app," we assume the model pulls from sources it judges to be balanced. So be balanced. You want to read as a source, not an ad.
Being honest used to be a brand decision (one we've proudly stood behind), but now it might be a distribution decision too.
Write a "who should pick them" section.
If you can't write a fair paragraph about where your competitor wins and who they might work better for, you don't understand them well enough to compare. Go read their docs.
It's also the place to be honest about who you are and aren't building for: plenty of our competitors are openly built for marketers for example, and while lots of marketers run all their reporting on PostHog (yours truly included), we're still building for AI-pilled engineers first, and we say so.
The reader who isn't a fit should leave feeling helped, not hustled. Honest pages also don't make enemies: the fastest way to go viral for the wrong reasons is a dodgy comparison, and if you'd rather not be bashed on Hacker News or Twitter for being slimy, be fair.
Take corrections from competitors.
We've shipped edits because someone at a competitor emailed us, DMed us, or better yet, opened a PR directly against our blog. We welcome it and encourage it. (Yes, if you're a competitor reading this, this is an invitation.)
Here's an example from today:
Lucas Harras, a Senior Customer Success Architect at Amplitude, read our PostHog vs Amplitude page, found four features we'd marked as missing that Amplitude actually has, and opened a PR.
We merged it the same day, and because every comparison table renders from that file (more on that below), every page that mentions any of these features was corrected by the next deploy.
Sometimes you'll be offered a slice of humble pie, and it's important to eat it gracefully.
My litmus test for every comparison: if a competitor wrote this exact page about PostHog, how would I feel reading it? Would it feel like they'd done their homework, or would I feel misrepresented and annoyed? If it's the latter, it's probably worth trying again.
We haven't always gotten this right. Part of it is that not everyone uses the same words for the same features, and some of our competitors have several hundred of them. A "sort of" column doesn't exist, so every row is ultimately a judgment call, and we've made some wrong ones.
But we're committed to doing better every time.
How to maintain comparison pages
Staying accurate across ~90 comparison and roundup pages for years is an engineering problem, and we started treating it like one.
1. Every competitor is a centralized data file.
In the posthog.com repo there's a folder with one file per competitor: sentry.tsx, amplitude.tsx, hotjar.tsx, and so on. Each file holds everything we claim about that company, in one place; here's a simplified version of what that looks like:
Feature keys come from a shared dictionary, so "session replay with network payloads" means the same thing on the Hotjar page as the LogRocket page.
Most of our comparison tables render from these files through one component. When a competitor ships a feature, someone changes one line in one file and every page that mentions them updates on the next deploy. The repo is public, so competitors can see exactly what we say about them and open a pull request if we're wrong.
2. Scouts checks our homework
Data files solve "update once, publish everywhere", but they don't solve for "notice that something changed" – that's what we've used Scouts for.
We run two. The first watches our competitors: it reads the competitor files I mentioned above, visits each competitor's pricing and docs pages, and reports back when what they say and what we say have drifted apart.
The second watches us. It turns out a very embarrassing way to get a comparison wrong isn't overstating a competitor, but understating yourself. (I learned this the hard way… occupational hazard of shipping as fast as we do. *wink*)
So the second scout reads our comparison pages against our own changelog, docs, open PRs, and Slack threads, and flags anywhere we might be underselling ourselves.
A few things make both of them better than a script that pings you every time a page changes:
- It has memory between runs, so it doesn't re-flag the same thing every week, and it learns what "normal" looks like for each site.
- It's selective by design. Most runs end with nothing to report, and that's it working. It ignores changes that don't affect the overall comparison.
- It shows its evidence: what their page says now, what our file says, and a suggested edit, with sources.
- A human ships the fix. The scout posts a digest to Slack with a link to open a PR. A person decides whether the change is necessary, opens the PR, and merges it.
Here's an example of what this looks like in practice. First, the Slack digest:
Then the full report in our self-driving inbox:
And finally, a pull request ready to merge:
The scout does the noticing, a human does the deciding, and nobody needs to add a recurring "re-read every competitor's pricing page" task to their calendar. Amen to that.
Where we go from here
We haven't reached our final form yet (will we ever?). One of my goals this quarter is going back through all of this content and making it better, and I'm sure there's plenty we're still getting wrong.
But the point is we started. Five years, 90-ish pages, and tens of thousands of signups later, "write honestly about the people trying to eat our lunch" has turned out to be one of the best decisions we've made for our organic content strategy; not the most intuitive one, but still one of the best.
So if you've been circling the plunge, take it. Be fair, be accurate, and let a robot handle the maintenance so you don't have to. (May I suggest ours?)
And if you're a peer who's nailed this (or who has failed at it and has war stories and words of caution to share), my DMs are always open.
PostHog is your product's context layer. With a full suite of developer tools – AI observability, product analytics, session replay, feature flags, experiments, error tracking, logs, and more – PostHog ingests and stores all the data agents need to diagnose problems, uncover opportunities, and ship fixes. A data warehouse and CDP tie it all together, unifying that context into one source agents can read across. You can steer it all from Slack, the web app, the desktop (PostHog Desktop), or your own editor via the MCP.

articles.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
articles.body:
Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
3rd November 2026
Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!
Weight-Space Programming
Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:
Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.
Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.
All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.
The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.
spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.
I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.
The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up, it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question:
The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response.
The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games:
I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others.
Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models
The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this:
llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \
  -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro
This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro, which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens.
But how about Qwen 3.8 27B? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use this version) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025.
I fired up LM Studio, ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command:
LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \
  llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \
  -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b
(I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue.)
After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here’s the reasoning trace):
Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets.
Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards.
Confidence: 72%
This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong (reasoning) in 1h 4m 54s:
Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object.
Description:
The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized.
Confidence:
75%
And Breakout (reasoning) in 52m 25s:
Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game.
Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty.
Confidence: 88%
Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn’t surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here’s that transcript—Qwen thought it was “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally”.
The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here’s a sample:
What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let’s list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right?
That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort.
It’s a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I’ve seen around it does not feel justified. I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.
The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.
spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.
I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.
The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up, it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question:
The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response.
The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games:
I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others.
Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models
The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this:
llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \
  -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro
This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro, which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens.
But how about Qwen 3.8 27B? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use this version) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025.
I fired up LM Studio, ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command:
LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \
  llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \
  -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b
(I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue.)
After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here’s the reasoning trace):
Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets.
Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards.
Confidence: 72%
This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong (reasoning) in 1h 4m 54s:
Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object.
Description:
The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized.
Confidence:
75%
And Breakout (reasoning) in 52m 25s:
Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game.
Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty.
Confidence: 88%
Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn’t surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here’s that transcript—Qwen thought it was “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally”.
The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here’s a sample:
What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let’s list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right?
That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort.
It’s a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I’ve seen around it does not feel justified. I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways.

articles.title: Gitbook Breached
articles.body:
We opened a ticket with support about Gitbook availability issues and got this in reply. We have yet to see any official customer communication or breach notification. Apologies for the formatting, did the best I could as it's a mobile paste.
Update:
GitBook security incident update
 Hey <$name>,
 The GitBook app, the GitBook API, and published docs are available again. A few services may still be degraded as we finish restoring everything to full performance.
*What happened*
 GitBook has been the target of a sophisticated, highly targeted attack using AI agents. 
 At 19:00 CET, November 2, the attacker gained unauthorized access to some of our infrastructure credentials. We detected the attack immediately and acted swiftly to block further impact. 
 To make sure our infrastructure was fully secure, we then took the GitBook app and authenticated docs sites offline. We kept publicly published content live for as long as possible, using cached data.
*What we did immediately*
* Blocked the attacker and closed the vulnerabilities involved
* Replaced every credential and secret across our infrastructure
* Brought services back only once we were confident they were secure
* Invalidated every customer’s API tokens on our platform
*Your data*
 Our investigation shows that the attacker may have accessed the following:
* Git Sync secrets.
* GitBook API tokens.
* Third-party API tokens used to connect external tools to GitBook.
* Questions asked to GitBook Assistant by your site visitors.
At this stage, we have found no evidence that any of your content in GitBook was modified.
*What you need to do now*
* Rotate any existing GitBook API tokens. We revoked all personal API tokens during the incident.
* Rotate any third-party API tokens or secrets you use to connect other tools to GitBook.
* If you have published integrations that use secrets, rotate those secrets.
* If you use the GitBook MCP server, re-authenticate it.
 Please contact your GitBook organization’s admin to assist with this process.
*What we are doing next*
* Monitoring the situation in case of further attacks.
* Introducing further security measures to our platform.
* Writing a full post mortem that will be published soon with more detailed information about the incident.
* If you have any further questions, please reach out to your account manager or our support team. You can also check status.gitbook.com for updates
Thank you for your patience, and we apologize again for the disruption
 The GitBook team

articles.title: Indie games are missing launch dates because Steam is backed up
articles.body:
Many indie game developers have recently posted on social media about unexpectedly long approval wait times for their game submissions on Steam, with some of the approvals causing developers to miss their planned launch dates.
Indie games are missing launch dates because Steam is backed up
One developer has been waiting for weeks on approval for a game it planned to release today.
For example, Studio Daimon, the team behind an upcoming title called Food Devils, had planned to launch the game in early access today after submitting its build on October 12th. But the game is “still awaiting approval,” according to a post from game director Alfred Kamon. “Even now, we don’t know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game. We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored.”
In October, publisher 2 Left Thumbs said it missed its planned launch of Wheel Make It “by nearly two weeks” due to the long wait for build reviews. You can read some details about the studio’s setbacks, including failing a review for a “one single option in the menu” not being accessible with a controller, in a Steam post. There are lots of other recent posts about review build waits as well.
Valve says on a Steam developer website that a review of a game’s store presence “typically takes 3-5 business days to complete,” though the company suggests submitting a page for review “at least 7 business days before you want it live to account for potential changes you’ll need to make.”
However, as of late, Steam has seemingly been grappling with a sharp increase in games; October’s Steam Next Fest had 7,240 games, a 65.2 percent increase over June’s Steam Next Fest, according to How to Market a Game. A Reddit user also found that 49.9 percent of all games released since Valve started asking developers in 2024 to label games that use AI now have an AI disclosure.
Kamon and 2 Left Thumbs suspect the longer waits are due to “slop” slowing down the process. “We can only assume it’s because Steam’s review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers,” said Kamon.
In a new post from Valve published after we first ran this story, the company acknowledged that following a “a significant increase in submissions for store and page review in recent months,” it’s “running a little behind right now” and taking “up to 12 business days” for reviews, saying that much of the delay is “having to re-review games.” It has updated its release checklist for developers, including requiring them to run a game through Steam for at least five minutes. Valve also says that further improvements are on the way for the build review process.
Itch.io has also been dealing with a rise in games, with the platform saying last weekend that “The number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past 2 months.” Last night, the platform said it “Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop 😌”
Update, November 3rd: Added new post from Valve.

articles.title: The Xbox Nano has a hidden cloud secret
articles.body:
Microsoft is about to launch its new Xbox Nano controller tomorrow, and the tiny device has a little secret. The Nano can connect directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming over Wi-Fi to improve latency. It’s a feature Microsoft hasn’t officially announced yet, but one I’ve been anticipating since the Xbox Nano leaked earlier this year.
The Xbox Nano has a hidden cloud secret
Microsoft’s miniature Xbox controller can connect directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming over Wi-Fi.
The Nano will be able to connect directly to Microsoft’s cloud servers to reduce latency, much like how Google’s Stadia controllers used to work. This new cloud connect feature for the Nano is being privately tested on the new Xbox Cloud Gaming website, and it will require you to pair the controller over Wi-Fi to Microsoft’s Xbox Cloud Gaming servers using the Xbox mobile app.
I’m expecting Microsoft to announce this as a preview for the new Xbox Nano controller soon, before it’s fully supported across Xbox Cloud Gaming on the web and on smart TVs. I first started reporting that Microsoft was planning a new controller with Wi-Fi connectivity to reduce Xbox Cloud Gaming latency earlier this year. I’d expect the upcoming Xbox Elite 3 controller will also have the same functionality.
Microsoft had also planned to introduce a direct-to-cloud feature on a new Xbox controller, codenamed Sebile, as part of an Xbox Series X refresh console in 2024. The refresh console was canceled, and it’s not clear when we’ll eventually see a new Xbox wireless controller with direct cloud functionality.

articles.title: Monsters of Ohio is OUT!!!
articles.body:
Monsters of Ohio is OUT!!!
Posted on November 3, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 25 Comments
It’s time! Monsters of Ohio is out in the world, available at your favorite bookseller in print and ebook, and also in audio through Audible. In the UK, it will be available on the 5th, because that’s just when books get put out over there. Here are links for Amazon, Barnes & Noble, Bookshop and of course it’s available just about everywhere else as well, including your own local bookstore.
MOO (as it rather delightfully initializes down to) has gotten great reviews, including starred reviews in Bookpage, Kirkus and Library Journal, which makes me happy. It’s also a Library Reads Hall of Fame pick, which also delights me.
Also, I’m on a book tour — starting today! — through (mostly) the American Midwest, because it seemed the right place to tour this particular book. Please come see me and support the booksellers hosting me this time around.
Not on my tour schedule but still want a signed copy? You can order a copy from any one of the bookstores hosting me on my tour and I will be happy to sign the book while I am in their shop so they can ship it to you. I will also be signing copies for my own local bookstore, Jay & Mary’s Book Center, today, so they will have signed copies available as well. All of those are likely to ship only to the US, sorry.
(Also we’ll be announcing our annual holiday signing thing tomorrow, so stay tuned for that!)
Monsters of Ohio takes place, as the title suggests, in Ohio — but more than that, it takes place where I live, in the fictional town of Richland, located in the very real Darke County. Lots of elements of the book are taken from or inspired by my immediate surroundings, and in many ways this is the most personal novel I’ve written, and certainly the novel closest to me in a geographical sense. Now, it also has monsters and exploding things, so there’s that too. There’s a lot going on here.
The point is, I’m really proud of this one. I hope you all like it.
Also, in the US it’s election day. If you’ve not done so already, vote! And then get this book as a reward. If every voter in the United States rewarded themselves with this book, then, well. It would be a very good day for me.
— JS

articles.title: Here’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch
articles.body:
It’s impossible to paint a full picture of what Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 will be right now. The watchOS 27.3 developer beta just dropped earlier this afternoon, and these features are meant to be lived with in day-to-day life. We’re definitely going to do that over the next few weeks at The Verge. That said, here are some initial impressions.
Here’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch
The watchOS 27.3 beta adds Live Rewind and Siri Recap to the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.
What’s newly available today is Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds, while the latter provides high-level summaries of your conversations. (The other two Audio Intelligence features have been available for the last few weeks. I wrote about those in my Series 12 review.) And as always, this is the developer beta. These features could still change quite a bit before a final version arrives for the public.
The first thing I noticed is that these features are not turned on by default. I wasn’t expecting anything different, but it’s worth remembering that these features don’t automatically turn every Apple Watch into a surveillance device. Audio Intelligence requires the latest Apple Watch hardware, a compatible version of iOS (so in this case, the iOS 27.3 developer beta), and someone has to actively choose to enable these features. You can download the beta and double-press the crown to initiate a Live Rewind. It won’t do anything. You must opt in via your iPhone’s Watch app. Same goes for Siri Recap. Enabling Live Rewind also requires an initial microphone calibration with your phone.
Privacy-wise, Apple has publicly available support documentation about its approach to these features. I’m not weighing in on how well it executes them in this hands-on. But Apple has pretty clear messaging in the onboarding process. There are quite a few customization options for when Siri Recap is active. You can get pretty granular. For example, you can have Siri Recap on only at the office during weekdays from 1PM to 4PM if that’s when you have meetings. This is hard to convey to bystanders, and I think ethical use should come with an in-person heads-up to the people you frequently interact with. (Hello, fellow Verge writers and editors.)
Live Rewind, so far, has worked as described — with the heavy caveat that I’ve only tested it in my quiet home office with my spouse. Even so, it takes a hot second to learn the timing of a double press. My spouse noticed the audible chime signaling the feature is in use, though they didn’t notice the animation. I’ll have to see how this fares in louder environments. Siri accurately captured our attempts to get my cat to roll over, though in subsequent tests, it misheard a word or two.
I’m more hesitant to comment on Siri Recap. It’s not just because I haven’t had many organic, lengthy spoken conversations yet since downloading the beta. (Siri did not deem my brief conversation with my spouse as worthy enough for recapping.) But I won’t really get a sense for how this feature feels until I’ve tested it in a wide variety of scenarios. Will it work if I talk to myself aloud? How well does it filter out gossip? How will this change how people speak to me? That’ll be the true test of this feature and Apple’s bystander privacy claims.
My first Siri Recap was for an editorial planning meeting for a story I’m working on. It was decent at identifying different topics discussed, and I was impressed that it stripped out some sensitive information. Any outsider looking at these notes would be terribly confused. Ironically, it meant that this summary wasn’t the most useful for my job.
What I will say is that I’ve been testing the Amazon Bee Frontier for the past few weeks. In the little time I’ve spent with the watchOS 27.3 beta, the differences between Audio Intelligence and the Bee are very clear. The latter has more of what I’d call an AI-forward presence. Bee, for example, offers insights about the emotional tone of a conversation. I’ve also found that the AI can be a bit judgy about insights and takeaways. Live Rewind is just a straight transcript. Apple’s said publicly that Siri Recap is meant to be highly factual notes to jog a person’s memory. That rings true based on my first one. And, as far as I can tell, there is no commerce angle for Siri Recaps, whereas Bee has an Amazon integration that surfaces buying suggestions based on conversations.
In any case, I’ll be diving deep into these features in the days to come. Let us know in the comments what you’re most curious about.

articles.title: Just a little AI resistance, as a treat
articles.body:
At the recent EMFCamp, I bumped in to Professor Kate Devlin who was talking a little about the AI Resist List. I think one of the useful things we can do is loudly complain about shitty uses of AI. Here's an example.
As mentioned in a previous post, I'm contacting companies which send malformed calendar invites. One of the organisation I contacted was the British online supermarket Ocado. They don't have an easy way to contact their technical team, and no obvious paths to raise a bug report, so I filled in their usual customer service feedback form. I included a clear statement of the problem and a detailed technical analysis of why I thought it was a problem with their service.
After sending in my message, I received this back from "Lulu" at Ocado:
						
Thanks for getting in touch and sharing this feedback about our calendar files.
You're entirely right—having a technical glitch pop up when you're trying to organise your delivery is a real pain, so I've made sure to pass your feedback on to our technical and webshop team.
We really appreciate you taking the time to help us improve our service. I hope you have a wonderful rest of your day
I mean, that's AI right? It starts with the classic tell of a sycophantic agreement.
Next up is the em-dash. Beloved by chatbots but almost unheard of in British English style guides.
Finally (and this is hard to quantify) it just doesn't feel like a customer service response. They're usually poorly spelled, have dodgy grammar, and ask a bunch of irrelevant questions. The message gave me no confidence that anyone had looked at the problem and I doubted it had been passed on to a technically competent human.
I immediately got a customer satisfaction survey. Usually I give top marks to humans because, even though Net Promoter Score is bullshit, I don't want customer service agents to suffer the indignity of a bad review. But in this survey I vented my spleen - giving crappy 1 ⭐ scores on every metric and complaining vociferously about how rude it is to use an AI to deal with a genuine complaint.
I was both surprised and delighted to receive this back a few days after my invective was sent:
						
I saw your survey comment about getting a robotic, AI-generated response previously, and I wanted to reach out personally to apologise. There is nothing more frustrating than pointing out a legitimate bug only to feel like you're talking to a brick wall. I promise you there is a real person typing this out!
Second, I wanted to send a massive thank you for the incredibly detailed diagnostic. It is rare to get feedback that tells us exactly what is broken and how to fix it.
I can assure you that this has been passed to our team to look into. Your feedback is going to make things much smoother for a lot of people, and we really appreciate you taking the extra time to help us get it right.
Thank you again, I do hope that this issue is resolved quickly. If there is anything else I can help with in the meantime, please don't hesitate to get in touch.
Perhaps I'm being touchingly naïve, but that feels a lot more human, right? The grammar isn't perfect, the sentences are a bit more rambly, and it appears to have actually engaged with the contents of my message.
I get that having a million irate customer service messages is a hassle. Using AI to triage them probably makes business sense, summarising the verbose ones could be useful for customer service agents, and totting up general themes is almost certainly a sensible way to gather metrics without overloading the workforce.
But using an AI to reply to a human is just disrespectful. It says the organisation values their customer's time at less than their own.
It's OK to call out shitty AI responses and insist that a human engages with you.

articles.title: Microsoft fixes a Windows 11 annoyance as PC revenue declines
articles.body:
Microsoft is beginning the rollout of a Windows 11 preview update that finally addresses a persistent power user complaint with the operating system: the right-click menu that obliterated years of muscle memory on command locations and hid others behind an additional click. The timing is notable, as the announcement comes alongside Microsoft’s quarterly financial report, which showed a continued decline in the business of selling Windows licenses for new PCs.
The preview update, KB5127936, is cumulative for Windows 11 versions 26H2 and 25H2. The update will be a gradual rollout before eventually moving on to a normal rollout for all Windows 11 devices once it reaches general availability. The highlight of the new update should calm annoyed users who have spent years with custom scripts and services in an attempt to shape Windows the way they would prefer it. Users will get a “customize menu” button that controls what commands appear when they right-click their mouse. Users can toggle built-in commands such as Send To or Create Shortcut on or off, rearrange what appears on the main menu, and control which third-party extensions show up in either the main or submenus. The gripe with the right-click menu had been that Microsoft hid familiar command locations behind a top row of icons while moving other familiar commands under the “Show more options” submenu. Now, Windows users can customize the whole thing around their habits.
The new preview also highlights a new Windows feature called Cloud Rebuild, a recovery option that can reinstall Windows 11 directly from the cloud, even when an existing Windows 11 fails to boot. Cloud Rebuild will pull the Windows 11 image and needed system drivers directly from Windows Update. Users will not need a custom recovery image or external media to reinstall Windows. There is an important distinction to note, however. Microsoft classifies Cloud Rebuild as a recovery option, but it behaves more like a fresh Windows install than a repair, as existing applications and files will not be included. Those worried about data security can sanitize entire system drives prior to reinstalling. For a full list of improvements coming to Windows 11, including changes to Xbox mode and settings, you can view the official Microsoft release announcement.

articles.title: This Election Day, remember which party ran against EVs and tethered us all to the gas pump
articles.body:
It’s the midterms! Here’s a fun fact for you as you head to the polls: Gas prices today are the highest ever recorded for a US Election Day.
This Election Day, remember which party ran against EVs and tethered us all to the gas pump
Donald Trump and congressional Republicans spent years waging a culture war against EVs. Now, record gas prices and a foreign war are leaving voters stuck footing the bill at the pump.
The national average for a gallon of gasoline is $4.12 and $6.28 for a gallon of diesel, according to GasBuddy. Meanwhile, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which is maintained by the US Department of Energy as a safeguard during energy crises, is down to 282.2 million barrels of crude, the lowest level in 44 years.
Gas prices, along with other essential cost-of-living items, are certainly top of mind for many voters this election cycle. And perhaps many will also remember which political party ran on a campaign message of ending the fictional “EV mandate” and “drill, baby, drill.”
For the past two years, Donald Trump and congressional Republicans have made gutting EV incentives, freezing charging infrastructure funding, and rolling back fuel economy standards a hallmark of their tenure in power. As a result, EV sales plummeted in the US, ensuring that Americans would stay indefinitely shackled to fossil fuels for years to come. For Trump, it was fulfilling a promise he made during the 2024 campaign. And for his donors from the oil and gas industry, it was money well spent.
Most voters might not have cared that much. After all, skepticism toward EVs was already high, driven by premium prices and lingering charging anxiety. But when Trump went to war with Iran, the resulting surge in gas prices sent Americans scrambling for cheaper ways to get around. Many turned to hybrid and electric vehicles as a solution — only to find vehicle prices were still higher than average, with no federal incentive to help defray the costs. Dealerships saw a surge of foot traffic from drivers who were skeptical of battery-powered cars, now desperate for anything that ran on a plug or a hybrid motor.
While automakers had made strides toward cheaper EVs, the average transaction price still hovered well over $50,000. But the incentive that once helped close that gap — the $7,500 federal clean vehicle tax credit, applied instantly at the point of sale — was gone. The subsidies had been systematically dismantled or left to lapse under the banner of fiscal discipline and anti-green populism.
Here is the real irony of this election. Republicans spent years painting electric cars as an out-of-touch, liberal fad, doing everything they could to kill tax credits and charging programs. They rolled back fuel economy standards that would have forced automakers to build more fuel-efficient powertrains, claiming they were saving everyday drivers from expensive technology they didn’t want.
Instead, they took away an important tool that could have protected family budgets from a global energy crisis. Electricity is made right here at home; its price doesn’t spike every time conflict breaks out in the Middle East. But because Republicans treated EVs like a partisan culture war, millions of Americans are stuck standing at the pump, watching the price roll higher.
Even if Democrats win back Congress, don’t expect them to bring back the Biden-era EV tax credits. The political fight over what kind of car people drive is probably stuck. At the same time, major car companies are backing Trump’s push in court to roll back strict fuel-economy rules. Electric cars aren’t disappearing, but they now have to stand on their own two feet. Companies like General Motors and Ford do have plans to make them more affordable, as long as the government keeps blocking cheap Chinese models from entering the market.
In the end, Trump won his culture war against the electric car. Automakers retreated, subsidies vanished, and the traditional combustion engine was saved from the bureaucrats. But victories have price tags. And as voters step into the booth with a $4 gallon of gas on their minds, they might finally realize what was traded away: the simple freedom to drive past the pump and never look back.
