articles.title: MIT Researchers Used GPT-6 Astra To Edit Qwen's Open Weights Directly, Boosting Math Scores
articles.body:
MIT Researchers Used GPT-6 Astra To Edit Qwen's Open Weights Directly, Boosting Math Scores 38
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from VentureBeat: Researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) reported today that they used OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra language model to raise a small, open source Qwen model's math score roughly sixfold by directly editing its weights -- the numerical parameters that govern its behavior. Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab described their work in a research blog post published November 2. They call the approach "weight-space programming" and tested Astra's ability to interpret and alter networks without using conventional training procedures to generate the edits.
In the strongest language-model example, Astra's intervention raised Qwen3.5-0.8B's MATH-500 score from 7.9% to 48.1% while touching approximately 0.016% of its weights. The improvement came primarily from correcting repetitive reasoning—a distinction that shaped both the technical findings and the debate over their implications. Their experiments explored a broader possibility: AI systems that inspect, repair and construct other neural networks by working directly on their internal machinery. "This is cool as heck!" wrote Yuchen Jin, a technical staffer at Databricks and former co-founder and CTO of Hyperbolic Labs who was unaffiliated with the research, on X. "Imagine using a large LLM to directly edit a smaller model's weights and dramatically improve its capabilities. It's like gene editing for neural networks. Even cooler than distillation!"
Voyage AI staff researcher Chandan Singh, formerly of Microsoft AI, also reacted to the findings: "For anyone questioning whether this post is overhyped, I think they are actually *underselling* the approach."

articles.title: Google takes Dreambeans to India in bid to bring AI-generated personal stories to the masses
articles.body:
Google has launched its experimental AI app Dreambeans in India, its first market outside the U.S., as the company looks to tap the world’s second-largest internet market to bring personalized visual stories drawn from users’ digital activity to a broader audience.
On Monday, Google expanded Dreambeans, available on Android and iOS, to India with support for 13 local languages, including Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Bengali, alongside English. The launch comes less than two months after Google made the app available to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older.
Introduced in June, Google’s Dreambeans uses information from connected Google services, including Calendar, Gemini, Gmail, Photos, Search, and YouTube, to proactively generate personalized, illustrated stories about users’ interests and everyday lives, without requiring them to enter a prompt. The app initially featured static, AI-generated illustrations, but Google recently added a feature that uses its Veo video-generation model to even animate images in select stories.
Google said it chose India as Dreambeans’ first international market because of strong interest from Indian users seeking access to the app and the widespread use of its services in the country. India stood out for its high overlap of users across Gemini, Gmail, and Google Photos, Google product manager Gozde Oznur said during a press briefing.
Dreambeans has recorded nearly 55,000 downloads in the U.S. since its June debut, according to estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower shared with TechCrunch. About 63% of those downloads came in September, when Google opened the app to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older. However, downloads dropped 84% month over month to about 5,500 in October.
In the first 30 days after Google opened Dreambeans to all eligible U.S. users, the app recorded an estimated 29,000 downloads, compared with 7.4 million for Meta’s Muse, 2.8 million for ChatGPT, 362,000 for Grok Bot, and 155,000 for Claude during their respective first 30 days after launch, Sensor Tower estimates show. However, unlike those general-purpose AI apps, Dreambeans focuses on generating personalized stories instead of responding to a broad range of user queries.
Even though Dreambeans supports many widely spoken Indian languages, users can select only one language at a time for their generated stories. The app can draw on information across Google services in multiple languages, but it cannot currently generate stories that mix languages, Oznur said during the briefing.
That could limit Dreambeans’ appeal in India, where many people regularly switch between languages, including Hindi and English, often mixing the two in what is commonly known as Hinglish.
Dreambeans’ dependence on information from users’ Google accounts also raises questions about privacy and data access. The app uses Google’s Personal Intelligence technology to draw on connected services and personalize its AI-generated stories. Those services can contain sensitive personal information that some users may not want to share with an AI app just to receive personalized content.
Users can choose which Google services to connect to Dreambeans and disconnect them at any time, Oznur said. They can also delete their Dreambeans data from within the app. Moreover, Oznur asserted that information deleted from the underlying connected services is also removed from Dreambeans’ personalization system.
Users, Oznur said, can tell Dreambeans to avoid certain subjects, including business-related information, and the app will try to adjust its stories accordingly. She added that Dreambeans is available only to personal Gmail account holders, not enterprise users, and that generated stories are visible only to the account holder.
Dreambeans’ proactive approach also carries the risk of surfacing memories that users may find upsetting. Oznur acknowledged that Dreambeans could generate stories involving people who have died, for instance. She said users can tell the app to stop showing certain subjects, comparing the feature to controls in Google Photos that let users limit which memories appear.
Oznur told reporters that Google is exploring ways to make Dreambeans more actionable, moving beyond personalized stories and recommendations to help users act on the app’s suggestions.

articles.title: New York City’s Mamdani criticizes Madison Square Garden owner over surveillance tech
articles.body:
Mayor of New York City Zohran Mamdani has criticized the owner of Madison Square Garden, one of the city’s largest entertainment venues, arguing that the company’s surveillance technology should not be allowed.
Mamdani told Wired in an interview on Tuesday that surveillance technologies are “indicative of much that is wrong in our country today.” He added that City Council member Shahana Hanif introduced two pieces of local legislation aimed at banning the collection of biometric data, such as using facial recognition, in public places across the city. Mamdani said that the draft legislation is “an important response to this kind of an issue.”
The comments come after a stream of reporting from Wired detailing how Madison Square Garden’s owner James Dolan relies on surveillance cameras and face-scanning technology to track people across and outside of its venues.
In one report, Wired revealed that Dolan’s company keeps a database that, among other things, marks some visitors, including celebrity performers, as “LGBTQIA,” for reasons that are unclear. Dolan subsequently sued Wired over its reporting.
In 2021, MSG made headlines after a woman was banned from Radio City, another Dolan-owned venue, after being recognized by facial recognition systems as an attorney at a law firm who was suing Dolan’s company but was not involved in the litigation.
When reached by TechCrunch, Madison Square Garden spokesperson Mikyl Cordova said: “Wired’s reporting is inaccurate and false. MSG is pursuing legal remedies,” without providing evidence for its claim.
Since 2021, New York City has required businesses to disclose when they are collecting biometric data from visitors.
Updated with comment from MSG.

articles.title: Bethesda Confirms The Elder Scrolls 6 Is Called 'Sentinel'
articles.body:
Bethesda Confirms The Elder Scrolls 6 Is Called 'Sentinel' 13
			
		 	
				During a video celebrating Bethesda's 40th anniversary, the studio officially confirmed that The Elder Scrolls VI will be titled The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. "Thank you for 40 years of shared memories," wrote Bethesda in a separate tweet. "We can't wait to make even more together with The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. Development continues, and while it'll be some time before we're ready to share more, it feels great to finally reveal the name and location with you." Video Games Chronicle reports:  "You know, as we're here in the 40th anniversary, we think about all of the games we've made," Bethesda's executive producer Todd Howard said in the video, walking past a display case. "And you know, every day when I walk by this case, obviously I look at the games and think about them, but more so I think about the teams that made them, and the time and the passion that everybody put into the games. And then what they meant to all of you, and hearing from you, and the time that you spent in them, how meaningful that was to you, and to let you know when we hear that, how meaningful that is to us.
And so even though yes, we're looking back, we're also looking forward to all we're doing, particularly with the Fallout franchise and obviously The Elder Scrolls. You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6. And we thought, hey, given the the moment, what a perfect time to tell you what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called." The video then showed the logo for the game.

articles.title: Firefox's New Mini Window Is Every Multitasker's Dream
articles.body:
Firefox's New Mini Window Is Every Multitasker's Dream (zdnet.com) 28
			
		 	
				Mozilla is testing a new Firefox Nightly feature called Mini Window that lets users pop an entire webpage into a small, always-on-top window stripped of most browser controls. "The idea behind the Firefox Mini Window feature is simple: allow users to move a currently open tab (or a section of a tab) into a separate mini window," writes ZDNet's Jack Wallen. "Think of it as moving a tab from one window to what appears like a web app." From the report:  At first blush, there's no address bar, controls, scroll bar, or anything else that would normally be associated with Firefox. The Mini Window appears to be a web app, without having to actually create it. However, when I hover my cursor inside the Mini Window, I do see the address bar, the back/forward/reload buttons, and the window close button -- and that's it. The browser gets out of your way, so the only thing I see is the content.
On top of that (pun intended), the Mini Window stays on top of other Firefox windows, so I can have that popped-out content always in focus while I work on other things. This feature comes in handy when I'm working with limited display space (say, on a laptop) and need to reference a page while working on another. For multitasking, it comes in very handy. [...] Let's say I'm writing a paper on Linux and need to read a particular article for background information. I could have my document open in the main window, and then open the article in question in a Mini Window. I could then reference the article without having to click back and forth between them -- even when working on a smaller display.
Here's another use case I've found: When using MacOS's Stage Manager feature, I only have one window available at a time. The Mini Window bypasses that limitation, so I can have my main browser window focused as well as the page open in the Mini Window. Another handy way I like to use Mini Window is to open a favorite search engine, move it to a Mini Window, and then I have an always-ready search tool at my fingertips. I could also open my favorite AI service and use it in the same way.

articles.title: The Elder Scrolls VI officially has a name: Sentinel
articles.body:
Bethesda is officially confirming today that the next Elder Scrolls game will be called The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. The confirmation came in a less than 10-minute video celebrating 40 years of Bethesda game studios.
The Elder Scrolls VI officially has a name: Sentinel
Bethesda celebrates 40 years with a fresh Elder Scrolls VI teaser.
It’s been more than eight years since Bethesda officially announced the existence of the sixth game in its Elder Scrolls series, and studio chief Todd Howard made the announcement today and called it the “perfect time” to fully name the game.
Bethesda isn’t sharing any more details on The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel today, though. The Xbox Wire press release on the name is literally just a picture of the logo.
I reported in Notepad last week that Bethesda was planning to name the game in November, during a period that will mark 15 years since The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim was released. Sentinel will be set in Hammerfell, a province in the Elder Scrolls universe that’s appeared in The Elder Scrolls Adventures: Redguard and The Elder Scrolls Online. Sentinel will be the first game about the history of the Elder Scrolls, and help uncover the secrets of these mysterious ancient artifacts.

articles.title: Adobe’s Premiere mobile app is adding licensed music from ‘leading artists’
articles.body:
Adobe is teaming up with Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group to add a library of licensed music clips to the Premiere mobile video editing app. No specific musicians have been announced with this partnership, but Adobe said it will include “popular songs” from “leading artists,” and enable Premiere mobile users to quickly jump on “the latest trend.”
Adobe’s Premiere mobile app is adding licensed music from ‘leading artists’
Universal and Warner music groups are working with Adobe to provide a browsable library of fully licensed song clips.
“By bringing licensed music from UMG artists into Adobe Premiere mobile, we’re giving creators new ways to build their stories around the songs they love for the first time, while helping our artists and songwriters reach new audiences,” Universal Music Group’s Bryan Stone said in the announcement.
Adobe says this feature is “coming soon,” and will allow Premiere mobile users to:
- Add up to 60 seconds of a popular track directly to the video.
- Browse, search and preview trending music by artist or track, filter by genre and duration, bookmark favorites, and explore popular music through label-featured collections.
- Access customizable templates that are already paired with music to speed up editing.
- Export finished videos in Premiere mobile and post to licensed social platforms.
The Premiere Pro desktop app and Premiere mobile both already include a built-in library of royalty-free music that editors can work into their videos, but licensed audio needs to be manually imported. This update aims to make it easier to incorporate recognizable music into video edits, and help Adobe’s mobile video editor compete against popular rivals like CapCut. We have asked Adobe if these updates will also be coming to Premiere Pro, and will update if we hear back.

articles.title: All the news about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake
articles.body:
Ahead of the release of Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto VI, Nintendo is launching its own fall juggernaut: a Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.
The remake, which is releasing 28 years after the launch of the original version on Nintendo 64, has a much more realistic visual style and some modern improvements like a jump button, a way to sprint, full voice acting, and a “Threads of Time” feature that helps you keep track of your progress. But while the game has a new coat of paint, it appears many elements will still remain faithful to the classic N64 release. Nintendo has also launched a special version of the Switch 2 and Switch 2 Pro Controller with Triforce imagery to celebrate the game.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is scheduled to release on November 5th. You can follow along with all of our coverage of the game right here.
- Keep on rolling. For the Ocarina of Time remake, Nintendo developers said in a new interview that they wanted to “preserve the experience of spamming the Roll Attack to forward roll your way across Hyrule Field.” I have very fond memories of rolling around the world in the original. In the remake, you can still spam Roll Attack, but you can also dash.
- A link to the past. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches later this week, and in the lead-up Nintendo has put out the first half of a lengthy developer Q&A, covering everything from what changed gameplay-wise, to the new visual style, which was inspired by puppet shows. As art director Aya Shida explains: Neither puppet shows nor practical effects films reproduce reality exactly as it is. Even so, both create a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds. We also felt that there was some overlap between these forms of expression and the distinctive nostalgia evoked by the original game.
- There’s one week left to preorder the Ocarina of Time remake for $10 off The long-awaited remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2 launches next Thursday, November 5th. In other words, you have a week remaining to secure your physical edition with a $10 discount at Amazon and Walmart. Once the game launches, the physical version will almost certainly go from $59.99 to $69.99 while the digital version will stay at $59.99. Nintendo had the unenviable task of reimagining its Nintendo 64-era masterpiece for the Switch 2, and based on our hands-on time with some sections of the game, it’s a lot of fun to play. The graphics and art style are fantastic, and the controls have been modernized to be simpler to pick up for those who are already experienced with third-person action games, including other modern Zelda titles. Read Article >
- Here’s Nintendo’s overview trailer for the Ocarina of Time remake. I’ve really warmed up to the game’s art style, especially in this new trailer. And after reading my colleague Cameron Faulkner’s hands-on preview, I’m looking forward to returning to Hyrule even more. The game launches on Switch 2 on November 5th.
- The Ocarina of Time remake feels remarkably modern — and surprisingly terrifying With its upcoming remake for the Switch 2, Nintendo might have nailed the best thing about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time: its timelessness. The 1998 3D action adventure game for the Nintendo 64 that pioneered so much — 3D graphics, movement, exploration, openness — has been reengineered with changes that make it feel more modern, and surprisingly terrifying at times. Based on my early hands-on time with the game, it’s shaping up to be the best-looking, best-playing version of the game that addresses the most frustrating aspects of playing the original. More than just sanding off its roughest edges, Nintendo also fitted Ocarina of Time with modern trappings to make it more welcoming to those who were introduced to Zelda through more modern releases, like Breath of the Wild. The remake has a new progression marker, called Threads of Time, that’s viewable when you pause. It also has Zelda Notes integration within the Nintendo Switch app to let you view game maps and other info on your phone. Oh, it also has a dedicated jump button. Read Article >
- Hori’s electronic Ocarina of Time requires no musical talent. It was briefly shown during Nintendo’s The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct today, but Hori’s website now has a listing for its $49.99 electronic ocarina. You can play your own songs by pushing buttons, play one of 12 pre-programmed songs from the games, use it with the Ocarina of Time remake’s sound recognition feature, or connect headphones for a private jam session.
- Nintendo’s Ocarina of Time remake launches in November Link’s next adventure now has a release date. The release date makes Ocarina of Time one of just a few big-budget titles launching in the same month as Grand Theft Auto VI. Nintendo first teased the remake in June, though it didn’t reveal much aside from a brief trailer. Today’s event provided a clearer glimpse at how the company is approaching remaking one of its most influential games and the first 3D Zelda adventure. The updated version of Ocarina of Time will be the first Zelda release that’s exclusive to the Switch 2, and longtime Zelda producer Eiji Aonuma described the remake as “a faithful interpretation using modern technologies.” Read Article >

articles.title: Bambu’s nine-nozzle H3C foretells the future of 3D printing
articles.body:
Three years ago, I told you how home 3D printers had evolved for speed, producing parts in minutes that used to take hours or days. Now, the next evolution is here: printers that can swap between materials on the fly, mix different colors to produce nearly the full rainbow, mix soft and hard materials, and even mix different sizes of nozzle and different diameters of filament so you can switch between high speed and fine detail in a single print.
Bambu’s nine-nozzle H3C foretells the future of 3D printing
The Bambu H3C is a tool-changing, color-mixing, nine-nozzle printer that keeps your filament dry too.
Today, Bambu Lab is announcing its most advanced 3D printer yet, the $2,499 H3C, which can do all of that mixing goodness — by loading nine different rolls of filament into nine different print heads.
Even if you’d never buy a printer this pricey, even if you’ve sworn off Bambu printers for good, the H3C is the perfect vehicle for me to explain where the state of the art in home printing tech is headed.
While the H3C still only prints in one material at any given moment, Bambu’s new “Swaptek” system lets the printer swap in any of the eight other nozzles in six seconds flat. All nine tools are stored in a rack at the front of the printer, where they can independently preheat to the correct temperature right before they’re needed.
With Bambu’s new “PLA Palette” cyan, magenta, yellow, and white filament, I printed a beautiful rainbow bird feather that emulated most of the other colors between those inks. With a mix of flexible TPU and rigid PLA filaments, I was able to print a hard wristwatch housing with an integrated flexible watchband. With an ultra-soft “75A” TPU filament plus a harder 90A variety, I printed a breathable, wearable shoe that… didn’t quite fit, unfortunately. (I’ll measure and try again.)
To be clear, Bambu didn’t invent toolchanger printers or color mixing. You could even argue Bambu’s slightly behind the curve, particularly after the $700-$900 Snapmaker U1 and its four-color, five-second swaps pleasantly surprised the community earlier this year. (Prusa also sells its hotly anticipated 8-tool INDX system for $2,249, though I’ve heard it has some issues.)
But I would have never bought previous toolchangers for myself, because they don’t have a place to keep your filament dry when you’re not printing. (Wet filament is one of the biggest remaining causes of print failures.) The H3C theoretically changes that by storing its nine rolls in an ostensibly airtight auto-loading container called the AMS 3H. Two of those nine slots even have built-in dryers that can hit 85 degrees Celsius and keep on drying your filament while you print, a big step up from Bambu’s previous AMS systems.
I haven’t tried the H3C for long enough to tell you if it’s ready to buy, and I’ve definitely run into some quirks in my first couple weeks of testing. I’ve had to start every single print twice because the printer complains that its “toolhead camera” isn’t initializing properly, I once lost half a day of printing to a false-positive print failure detection, and the beta build of Bambu Studio provided to reviewers initially got confused when I tried to mix colors. (I’m told that last one will be fixed by launch, and Bambu eventually provided some troubleshooting steps for the toolhead camera close to embargo time.)
You also have to load flexible TPU filaments into the H3C manually, and I learned the hard way that not all of the printer’s nine slots can actually accept a roll of TPU without causing trouble. Slot #6 can load standard filaments, but if you load the flexible stuff, another printhead can snag it and cause a nasty jam:
This also isn’t a printer where you can quickly repair a nozzle without tools, or use previous-gen toolless H, P, and A series swappable nozzles. It’s an all-new system that involves some minor disassembly, and I’m not sure about Bambu’s decision to leave filament in the toolheads between prints where it might attract moisture.
But so far, this seems like an easier, more reliable printer than the two-nozzle Bambu H2D was at launch. Other than the Slot #6 TPU jam, which Bambu actually warns reviewers about in a section of the reviewer’s guide that I missed reading, everything I’ve tried to print has come out great so far — and without creating a mountain of little “printer poop” waste when I switch between colors! Dramatically reduced waste is one of the benefits of having extra nozzles.
With any luck, the future of 3D printing won’t just be for hobbyists willing to figure out which colors of filament they need to order before each and every project, or obsessives who store dozens of colors in vacuum-sealed bags. Instead, it should be more like today’s inkjet printers — an entire rainbow of color, ready to go at a moment’s notice. And hopefully without all the inkjet printer shenanigans, of course.
If you like Bambu’s toolchanger system, you probably won’t have to pay $2,499 for long. Certification filing leaks show that the company’s already prepping a smaller “P3C” with seven tools and seven rolls of filament storage instead of nine.
Bambu Lab H3C
The H3C is a very large, very tall printer with a large build volume. Compare it to my normal size P1P.
Additionally, Bambu will let all three of its existing dual-nozzle printers print with two different sizes of nozzle by next spring, including the H2D, the H2C, and the X2D.

articles.title: The Internals of PostgreSQL
articles.body:
After a temporary stay in Japan to focus on my health and personal responsibilities, I am fully recovered, ready, and excited to work abroad again.
I am highly interested in returning to Europe, as well as opportunities in the Southern Hemisphere and Southeast Asia.
Looking for:
- Challenging tasks in PostgreSQL.
- Roles offering international visa sponsorship OR Remote work that supports a digital nomad lifestyle.
If your team is hiring, let’s connect! Please feel free to reach out via e-Mail(hironobu @ interdb.jp or interdb.mx @ gmail.com) or DM.
What’s New
- 26 Sep 2026: 11th Anniversary! This content was launched on 26 September 2015.
- 28 Jun 2026: Section 8.5, “Asynchronous I/O in PostgreSQL” Published.
- 1 May 2026: Chapter 12, “Logical Replication” (Beta Version) Published.
- 14 Dec 2024: Added Conflicts in Section 11.2.4.
The Internals of PostgreSQL
PostgreSQL is a well-designed, open-source multi-purpose relational database system which is widely used throughout the world.
It is one huge system with the integrated subsystems, each of which has a particular complex feature and works cooperatively with each other. Although understanding of the internal mechanism is crucial for both administration and integration using PostgreSQL, its hugeness and complexity make it difficult.
The main purposes of this documentation are to explain how each subsystem works, and to provide the whole picture of PostgreSQL.
This documentation covers versions 19-beta (excluding the new buffer page lock mechanism) and earlier.
Some academic papers have referred to this documentation. The Chinese version of this documentation was published in June 2019.
This documentation was first published on 26 September 2015.
- Chapter 1. Database Cluster, Databases and Tables
- Chapter 2. Process and Memory Architecture
- Chapter 3. Query Processing
- Chapter 4. Foreign Data Wrappers (FDW)
- Chapter 5. Concurrency Control
- Chapter 6. VACUUM Processing
- Chapter 7. Heap Only Tuple (HOT) and Index-Only Scans
- Chapter 8. Buffer Manager
- Chapter 9. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
- Chapter 10. Online Backup and Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR)
- Chapter 11. Streaming Replication
- Chapter 12. Logical Replication (Beta Version)
Author
Hironobu SUZUKI
I am a software programmer/engineer, the author of:
I graduated from graduate school in information engineering (M.S. in Information Engineering), have worked for several companies as a software developer and technical manager/director. I published seven books in the fields of database and system integration (4 PostgreSQL books and 3 MySQL books). In June 2019, the Chinese book of this documentation was published.
As a director of the Japan PostgreSQL Users Group (2010-2016), I organized the largest (non-commercial) technical seminar/lecture on PostgreSQL in Japan for more than six years, and also served as the program committee chair of the Japan PostgreSQL Conference in 2013 and as a member in 2008 and 2009.
In June 2022, my interview article was published in “PostgreSQL person of the week”.
Cuando era joven, vivió en Sudamérica por unos años. Recientemente, a veces vuelve a allí.
I am seeking a remote position focused on the application of ML and AI technologies to DBMS. For personal reasons, I will be living in Japan for several years.
Contact
Please read the following FAQ before sending messages.
After reading, send a message to my twitter in public.
If you use email, please provide at least two SNS addresses (e.g. LinkedIn, Twitter) for verification purposes. Due to the XZ backdoor incident, I no longer accept contact from anonymous individuals.

Exception Educational institutions can use this documentation freely.

articles.title: macOS 27 does not support CoreStorage volumes
articles.body:
macOS 15 Sequoia had a hard time with CoreStorage – and thus encrypted HFS+ volumes – since it deprecated both technologies and callously crippled some important tools for working with them, but nonetheless it mostly still worked. While I’d often – but not always – have to manually unlock one of my HFS+ volumes – but not the others – at boot, and it also refused to convert some – but not all – volumes from HFS+ to APFS1, keeping me trapped in the situation – it ultimately still worked. I could get at my data and use the volumes more or less normally.
Unfortunately, in macOS 27 that’s no longer the case. Not only does Golden Gate just not support CoreStorage / encrypted HFS+ volumes, out of the box you can’t do anything with them – can’t mount them, can’t convert them to APFS, can’t even erase them. It renders your expensive storage hardware completely useless.
Worse, macOS 27 puts up a misleading dialog, upon boot, saying that macOS 28 (the next version) won’t support these volumes. I have no idea what Apple’s doing or thinking. Maybe it’s all just an embarrassing misunderstanding – the file system team told the notifications team that CoreStorage & encrypted HFS+ support is going away, and typoed the version number as 28 rather than 27?
Details
macOS 27 cannot mount CoreStorage volumes automatically or through any normal means. Worse, Disk Utility can’t mount them even when manually told to – it just fails with the cryptic error:
com.apple.DiskManagement.disenter error 49,153
diskutil mount also fails, this time with an error message that is a blatant lie:
disk27 is a CoreStorage Logical Volume which is locked; use "diskutil coreStorage unlockVolume"
$ diskutil cs unlockVolume BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D
BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D is already unlocked and is attached as disk27
$ diskutil cs list
CoreStorage logical volume groups (1 found)
|
+-- Logical Volume Group 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
=========================================================
Name: Smash
Status: Online
Size: 2000054960128 B (2.0 TB)
Free Space: 0 B (0 B)
|
+-< Physical Volume 1B5A1754-184B-4F17-A797-BF69B4BB627F
| ----------------------------------------------------
| Index: 0
| Disk: disk10s2
| Status: Online
| Size: 2000054960128 B (2.0 TB)
|
+-> Logical Volume Family 376204CD-8048-4962-B05C-72F4FC16B77B
----------------------------------------------------------
Encryption Type: AES-XTS
Encryption Status: Unlocked
Conversion Status: Complete
High Level Queries: Fully Secure
| Passphrase Required
| Accepts New Users
| Has Visible Users
| Has Volume Key
|
+-> Logical Volume BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D
---------------------------------------------------
Disk: disk27
Status: Online
Size (Total): 1999702634496 B (2.0 TB)
Revertible: No
LV Name: Smash
Volume Name: Smash
Content Hint: Apple_HFS
But what’s even worse about this dumpster fire is that macOS 27 can mount these volumes just fine – it’s just that all the normal ways to do it are completely broken.  If you go down to a lower level and run mount_hfs directly, it does work:
$ sudo mkdir -p /Volumes/Smash
$ sudo mount_hfs -o rdonly /dev/disk27 /Volumes/Smash
$ ls /Volumes/Smash
Documents Pictures Scratch space
That said… that -o rdonly parameter… in principle it shouldn’t be required, but I could not get macOS 27 to let me mount any HFS-on-CoreStorage volume as read-write – no matter what I did, it always fails with error “Resource busy” (EBUSY). I spent a lot of time trying to debug this, and could find no evidence of anything having the volume in question open (nothing in lsof etc).
But wait, it gets worse.
macOS 27 can’t even erase the volume.  All the normal tools – diskutil, Disk Utility, etc – fail with that same “Resource busy” error.
Workaround
Thankfully, with the help of Gemini 4 Argon, I did find a workaround. It’s convoluted, but takes only a few steps, thankfully.
First, while if you try to delete the logical volume group it ostensibly fails, it doesn’t completely fail – it does actually delete the logical volume(s) within:
$ diskutil cs delete 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
Started CoreStorage operation
Unmounting Logical Volumes
Destroying Logical Volume Group
Erasing disk10s2
newfs_hfs: cannot create filesystem on /dev/rdisk10s2: Resource busy
Mounting disk
Could not mount disk10s2 after erase
Error: -69832: File system formatter failed
1 💣 $ diskutil cs list
CoreStorage logical volume groups (1 found)
|
+-- Logical Volume Group 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
=========================================================
Name: Smash
Status: Offline
Size: 2000054960128 B (2.0 TB)
Free Space: -none-
|
+-< Physical Volume 1B5A1754-184B-4F17-A797-BF69B4BB627F
----------------------------------------------------
(No properties)
$ diskutil cs delete 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
Started CoreStorage operation
Destroying Logical Volume Group
Error: -69783: Unable to delete the CoreStorage Logical Volume Group
You still can’t destroy it completely, nor can you erase the physical volume yet – the “Resource busy” errors persist. But, the trick is to restart – after that, you can then erase the volume.
So it seems that whatever broken thing is holding the physical volume (or logical volume group) in a ‘busy’ state is tied to the existence of the logical volume(s) therein, and once they’re deleted (and the machine rebooted) the bug stops being triggered.
Call for better workarounds
I’ve glossed over a lot of debugging and attempts I made to save the volume in-place, by either making it work as-is (even if only with e.g. hfsutils) or by converting it to APFS, but neither I nor Gemini 4 Argon could find anything that worked. It’s too late for me – I was forced to just delete all my HFS+ & CoreStorage volumes and rebuild them painstakingly from backups – but if anyone finds a way, I’d love to amend this post, for the benefit of future readers.
- The problem remains the same in macOS 27 – so three major macOS versions, at a minimum, where essential system update functionality has not worked.  Sigh.
$ diskutil apfs convert disk27
Converting the volume on disk27 to an APFS Volume on an APFS Container
Started APFS operation on disk27 (Smash)
Converting HFS Volume to an APFS Container which will export one APFS Volume
The target is the Journaled HFS+ volume "Smash" on disk27 backed via CoreStorage on disk10s2
Checking booter partition disk10s3
The target is a data disk; it is not a macOS system disk

The target is encrypted
Unmounting disk27

articles.title: Stringman, an $800 open-source room scale gripper robot
articles.body:
Secure the cleats to wall studs near the ceiling with wood screws, or to columns with ratchet straps.
In robotics, price is basically actuator count. Stringman reaches an entire room with four motors, hanging its gripper from lines anchored in the ceiling corners. Working from above, it reaches floors too cluttered for any wheeled or legged robot. And since the lifting force is shared by all motors, payload capacity scales with their combined torque instead of a single actuator's, peaking near the center of the room where the lines share the load most evenly.
*0.75 m serial arm using the same DM-H6215 1 N·m direct drive actuators at rated torque, ignoring the weight of its own links. Stringman figure is for a 7 × 7 × 3 m room at the 28 N line tension limit, net of its 638 g gripper and marker.
Stringman is open source and OSHWA certified. The mechanical CAD, the PCBs, and the control software are all published.
We believe owners should be in control of their own robots. That's why Stringman can run air gapped on your local Wi-Fi network: the UI is served locally, AI models run on your own hardware, and no data ever leaves your network.
Give your home lab the capability of carrying parts from one workcell to another anywhere in the room, so you can get more out of your other robots. The Python API and MCP server is made for agents so you can get your workflow running right away.
2022 Porsche 911 GT3 RSR model by No Limits, CC BY 4.0, simplified. SO-101 arm from TheRobotStudio/SO-ARM100, Apache 2.0.
Unlike desktop arms limited to a fixed radius, Stringman leverages a cable-driven architecture to access the full volume of a room. The work area volume per dollar of this type of robot is completely unmatched, all with fewer actuators than even the simplest mobile robots. Anchors and eylets are mounted in the corners of the room near the ceiling and define a four-sided work area within which any object can be moved from point to point.
That's roughly 500× the work area volume per dollar, at comparable 2 kg payload.
Step-by-step: picture guide or video guide
The original prototype was built in a room with a ceiling fan, and it still runs there today. Mount the anchors at or below the level of the blades and the lines can't physically reach it.
Several methods are available for control with default models for automatic grasping, target, and destination selection to make it easy to quickly build new behaviors.
Stringman is fully capable of LeRobot control using including Pi.05, JEPA, Multitask DiT, and others.
Collecting training data for new behaviors can be done from the UI, and as few as 50 episodes can be enough for certain models like DiT to learn a behavior.
As long as it remains installed, yes. However, when parked, they are up near the ceiling and out of the way. Clutter on the ceiling is preferable to clutter on the floor in our opinion. If you need to remove the anchors, they can be detached from their mounts without tools, leaving a relatively small white cleat on the wall.
Yes, it's just a matter of mounting the anchors at or below the level of the fan, making it physically impossible for the lines or marker tag to touch it. Similarly, the work area can be shrunk to exclude low hanging light fixtures if they are off to the side, but if the center of the room does contain low hanging objects, Stringman cannot be installed in that room.
When reaching a tension limit of 28 newtons (about the weight of a backpack), all motors relax and the lines can be pulled loose. Since they are overhead most of the time, it's uncommon for people to collide with them.
Not by default, but if you bind it with neufangled.com/playroom then you or anyone you share access with can operate it from anywhere, and access can be revoked at any time. Neufangled Robotics does not store any of the information from your robot that is forwarded through its servers.
For those who prefer to make the trade-off by binding their robot to an account, our web-based console allows you to monitor and control Stringman from anywhere. Think of it as a security camera with a hand.
If you do decide that you would like to make use of our cloud telemetry relay, You can use it, and still go back to a completely lan only mode whenever you want. Your data is never collected.
Organizing your home is a physical process, not a coding task. Use our clip-on fiducial tags to designate your laundry bin, toy box, and trash can. Stringman maps these locations visually. You don't need to tag individual pieces of clutter—just the destination. If there's something you never want it to pick up, you can mark that item as off-limits.
Networks trained to control stringman have learned that the word "toybox" refers to that tag, so you can use it to mark anything even if it doesn't look like the toyboxes from our training set.
You can also use the tags as arbitrary source and destination markers for ferry jobs, such as carrying items from one robot arm to another. or carrying laundry from the ground to a robotic folding station
A classroom with a Stringman robot gives your students a chance to become familiar with robotics fundamentals such as inverse kinematics, telemetry, and imitation learning while controlling an exotic and capable flying gripper. If you have walls and a MacBook, you're more than halfway there.
Cross embodiment is one of the biggest challenges in robotics, and showing that a model can operate a vastly different body type is a stronger result than moving it from one bimanual robot to another. Our datasets are public on Hugging Face, there's a controller-in-the-loop MuJoCo sim, and Stringman works with LeRobot, making it one of the most inexpensive robots to test on and a natural capstone project.
Mobile robots spend a significant portion of their time charging. Because Stringman is a powered from the wall, it's always ready for work. Furthermore, by removing the heavy battery pack, we've increased the payload capacity per dollar compared to mobile platforms that must waste energy carrying their own power supply.
The gripper's power is delivered via one of the support cables. A two-conductor FEP jacketed twisted pair cable with a tensile strength of 50N.
What's that pole for? Stringman's gripper hangs below the pivot point so it can reach the floor next to beds and tables. This additional linkage could allow unconstrained motion so Stringman employs active swing cancellation algorithms to counteract momentum, without adding the cost of any additional motors. This ensures the gripper remains steady and predictable even during rapid cross-room traversals.
There's a whole video about swing cancellation if you're curious about how it works!
Often, a simple solution that gets the job done has more value than a complex one. Stringman uses a two fingered gripper with a wrist. This is enough dexterity for the clutter it is designed to pick up, keeping weight and cost low and reliability high. In our household tests we have determined that more layers of grip tape is simply a better return on investment than more articulated fingers.
The gripper can rotate it's wrist to better place the fingers around flat sided or long objects.
For a easy preview of how it looks in your room, print the anchor mockup in white PLA and hold it up in a corner. Get the files.
TThe Stringman faceplate is easily swappable. Grab the STL or bambu 3MF files to print your faceplate in any color.

articles.title: Are the Fridges Ok?
articles.body:
Latest wave: 2 November 2026
Based on incident dates in news reports ↗
Are the fridges ok?
Supermarket refrigeration systems are still being hacked. Internet-exposed Danfoss controllers are part of the problem.
How we got here
Our baseline counts each IP once, even when it exposes several StoreView services. Shodan-tagged honeypot records are excluded, but an IP with both tagged and untagged records can remain. IP addresses are a proxy for systems, not a count of physical fridges.
Indexed StoreView IPs · tagged service records excluded
Loading measurement…
Loading total including tagged honeypots…
One IP.
Many fridges.
One public IP can front several controllers, and each controller can manage many fridges. Exposure alone does not prove compromise.
What we're measuring ↗
Still out in the open.
Historical service totals before IP deduplication and honeypot filtering. These use a different unit from the distinct-IP baseline above; they do not count compromised fridges.
These totals include tagged honeypots. Historical sources did not provide a honeypot breakdown. Published observations may use different search details and collection times. Gaps are unmeasured; points are not interpolated.
View observations & sources
Is the exposed fleet getting newer?
Daily inferred firmware mix across indexed Danfoss StoreView services worldwide. This chart is weighted by services, so one IP can contribute multiple ports; the headline baseline counts distinct IPs. These daily versions come from cached headers.
A rising share of newer versions can reflect upgrades, older systems going offline, new arrivals, or changes in Shodan's index. This chart does not follow individual devices or prove upgrades. Multiple ports can still inflate counts, and untagged honeypots may remain.
Latest version breakdown & methodology
Exact cached Last-Modified fingerprints are matched to the firmware-build timestamps published by Censys. Shared fingerprints remain ambiguous; unmatched banners remain unknown. The chart uses the same StoreView query as the headline count, with an optional honeypot exclusion. Newer StoreView Web titles were present in this query during our baseline census; this is still not a complete inventory of all Danfoss products.
Counts are collected from Shodan's existing index, not from a live vulnerability test. The queries run sequentially and are not a single atomic snapshot. The headline uses a separate distinct-IP snapshot; this chart counts services. Exposure and firmware totals may differ because Shodan answers those API requests separately. The collector rejects changing population totals or inconsistent sums and preserves the last valid observation. “4.3.1 or 5.x” is a version grouping, not an assurance that equipment is secure. Download full measurement history ↗
A pattern, not a one-off.
From suspected attacks at military bases to repeated disruption in European supermarkets.
The problem predates 2026. Danfoss also documented attacks on supermarket refrigeration in Russia and Israel in 2022. Danfoss newsletter, page 9 ↗
Cold facts.
Clear limitations.
A quiet news cycle is not an all-clear.
What does “No” mean?
This is an editorial assessment of the reported attacks and continuing exposure, not a live test of every fridge. It does not automatically turn to “Yes” after a quiet stretch.
What resets the counter?
A reviewed, substantial attack wave that disrupts refrigeration at multiple sites. We use the incident date, not the date of a later article. Suspected incidents are labeled; a new headline about an old incident does not reset the clock. Days use UTC calendar dates.
What does the Shodan number measure?
The prominent baseline counts distinct IP addresses with at least one matching service not tagged by Shodan as a honeypot; the small-print totals include tagged service records. An IP with both tagged and untagged records remains eligible. The exposure history retains unfiltered historical totals, while the firmware chart excludes tagged honeypots by default. All counts are matching internet service banners, worldwide, for http.title:"Danfoss StoreView". It is a narrow fingerprint, not all Danfoss products. Multiple ports can inflate the total; one controller can serve many fridges. Shodan's index also lags real-world changes. Download distinct-IP history ↗ · API methodology ↗
What did the one-off landing-page measurement find?
On 3 November 2026, a separately authorized active measurement made one ordinary unauthenticated request to / at one cached endpoint for each of 2,050 eligible IPs. It recognized 212 StoreView landing pages; 1,409 requests timed out and 332 had TLS failures. The remaining 97 produced other pages, responses or errors. Another 51 IPs had no eligible cached endpoint. There were no retries, redirect following, logins, scripts or controller changes.
This is a conservative observation, not a complete live-device count: timeouts and TLS failures do not establish that equipment is offline. Among recognized pages, 205 retained the cached firmware inference and seven differed or became unknown; this does not establish seven upgrades. Visible UI versions are not controller firmware. A later code audit reproduced an undercount risk: the original reader could receive a valid title, then time out waiting for more body data. The number of affected timeouts cannot be recovered, so 212 is only the number recognized by that checker. The checker has since been corrected and tested locally; this measurement has not been rerun.
A later cached Shodan query found 106 IPs with honeypot-tagged StoreView records. The original filter excluded tagged records, rather than every IP with any tagged record. The overlap between those IPs and the 212 recognized pages is unknown because no IP-to-outcome linkage was retained. Download the cached honeypot audit ↗. Only aggregate results are retained. Daily updates continue to use cached Shodan data; this active measurement is not scheduled. Download the aggregate report ↗
How does this stay up to date?
GitHub Actions requests aggregate Shodan IP, service and firmware counts daily at 11:17 UTC and saves their dated history. News is reviewed separately each day by a scheduled Codex task; its last completed review is shown above. Failed collections preserve prior data and show its age. Historical published snapshots remain separate from our own samples.
How can operators reduce exposure?
Follow the manufacturer's and your national CERT's guidance: restrict access to management interfaces, use protected remote access, and apply supported updates. Internet exposure does not by itself identify an exploited vulnerability. Read CERT-FR's advisory ↗

articles.title: Bear turns 10, and it still feels like day one
articles.body:
Back in 2013, three friends who loved Apple and design couldn’t find a notes app they liked, so they built their own. That side project became Bear. It arrived on the App Store in November 2016, and within a year it had been named Mac App of the Year and won an Apple Design Award. This November, the little Bear turns 10. Today it helps millions of people around the world capture their ideas and organize their lives every day, and we’ve felt so much love and support from all of you along the way.
The idea
We couldn’t find a notes app that fit how we write, so we started building our own.
More
We built it in our spare time. Our day job back then was building apps and websites for clients.
First prototype
Our friends loved it. Would everyone else?
Launch day!
Bear arrives on the App Store and hits #1 on Product Hunt.
Mac App of the Year
Apple names Bear its Mac App of the Year.
Apple Design Award
Bear wins a 2017 Apple Design Award.
More
…and we got a selfie with Tim Cook!
Project Panda
We start rewriting Bear’s editor from scratch, code name “Panda”.
More
Your feedback showed us where the original Bear was hitting its limits. Six months in, we realized we needed our own Markdown parser too, so we started over. Again.
Bear 2 is here!
Bear 2 launches with an all-new editor and 20+ new features.
Bear Web beta
Bear comes to your browser in public beta.
Bear Web
The full release of Bear Web is almost here, and we have more features brewing in house…
Over the years, one thing we hear again and again is that Bear just feels good to use. So for this special occasion, we want to share the principles behind every design decision we make. Along the way you’ll find some tiny details we’ve hidden all over the app (you may be using a few right now without knowing it), a peek at an idea that never shipped, and some brand new Bear swag. Grab a slice of cake and come on in!
Bear Principles
Every change in Bear goes through a long journey from first idea to final release. Big or small, visible or under the hood, they all follow the same two principles: Bear should be delightful to use, and safe to trust.
A feeling-good experience by design
We want you to feel delighted every time you open Bear. In practice, that comes down to three things.
Simple. No sign up, no tutorial. Just open a note and write. Bear has grown much more powerful over the years, but all of that power waits quietly underneath and never gets in your way.
💡 Did you know?
To make sure Bear stays easy to use, we always ask our parents to test it first!
Natural. We believe the best tools disappear while you use them. So we put a lot of effort into making things work exactly the way you expect, and you’ll find these quality of life touches all over the app.
Take moving lines around. Press ⌘⌥ with the up or down arrow to move the current line, which is perfect for rearranging your writing. Bear understands what you’re moving and where it’s going, so it won’t break apart a list or a table along the way. It’s one of those things that feels so obvious you’d never guess someone had to design it.
Rewarding to explore. Bear has a lot of depth, but we don’t believe in pushing everything to your face to promote it because we don’t know when or if you will need them. Many of our favorite user stories start with a happy little accident. Resize an image from its corner, and it snaps to line up with the images around it; swipe left on a note on iOS, and the Info Panel slides into view. We love those “Oh wow, I didn’t expect that to work!” moments. They’re a big part of why we sign off every post with “Happy writing!”
💡 Did you know?
Some of our favorite details are so small that you may be using them without ever noticing. Here are a few to try:
✍️ Typing in bold or italic? Press Return or the same shortcut again to step right out of the style.
⌨️ Press ⌘A inside a code block to select just the code. Press it again to select the whole note.
🖱️ Select some text and type (, [, " or`. Bear wraps your selection instead of replacing it.
🔗 Select some text and paste a URL. The text becomes a link.
Built to be safe
You can’t feel truly comfortable in a space you don’t trust. Your notes hold your ideas, your plans, and sometimes things you’d never share with anyone. That’s why safety has shaped Bear’s most fundamental choices from the very start.
Private. We have no servers holding your notes, and we never see what you write. We also don’t build Bear on top of third party APIs, plugins, or outside services we can’t control. If one of them changed its rules, shut down, or simply stopped working, you would be the one paying the price. So we build what matters ourselves, and Bear keeps working the way you expect.
💡 Did you know?
We collaborated with Cossack Labs for note encryption to ensure a reliable and smooth experience. Even if your iCloud account were ever hacked, you can rest assured your encrypted notes stay unreadable.
Keeping a note taking app private and standard wasn’t a revolutionary idea in 2016 when we first launched Bear, but today, it kind of is. And we are glad we stick to what we believe since day 1. The world is changing and we don’t know where it leads us to, but we know your notes are safe with us and you have full control of them anytime, anywhere.
How features get made
Every design in Bear starts with a problem: a feature people need, something that’s broken, or simply something we don’t like. From there, we are on a journey of problem solving.
That usually means a designer and a developer pairing up for a week or two, then bringing something working to the whole team. Then the real fun begins. Matteo, one of our cofounders, describes fun as “clashing heads with wonderful people to make great things.” Everyone in the team gets to express their opinions no matter what title they have. As a matter of fact, job titles mean nothing to us as you can see on our website.
The feedback discussion can be brutal. “No” is a very welcome answer here, with one house rule: you have to give a reason. Wall of text and hour long slack huddles come and go, then the paring up buddies return to the improvement part and provide a second round, a third round, until we are all happy with it. There are lucky days that some ideas get a big yes on the first try. Others spark weeks and months of debate and never ship at all. We’d rather be a little stubborn about what feels like Bear than chase every trend.
💡 Did you know?
Back in 2022, we had the idea to create a fourth column for the info panel, TOC, and Backlinks in Bear 2 update. The concept was discussed internally and also shared with on our forum, but at the end we were not convinced by the design at practical level, and thus the feature was never born in Bear 2.
A milestone, and more to come
Over the years, Bear has grown up much bigger than we expected with millions of users enjoying Bear everyday. We’ve seen so many different ways of using Bear: prepare teaching materials in school, work as their second brain, or just write grocery lists (yes, that’s our parents!). 10 years is a huge milestone for us and we want to say a huge thank you to everyone no matter if you have been here since day 1 with us, or just downloaded Bear two minutes ago.
We won’t hand you a flashy roadmap, but here’s what we can say for sure. Bear Web is almost ready for its full release, and we’re also working on note versioning and some other top secret things. Beyond that, we’ll keep doing what we’ve done for ten years: working our best to provide you a comfortable, private space to create beautiful notes.
🎁 Present time!
Kumagotchi: a writing pal for your Home Screen
Meet Kumagotchi1, a cute pixel bear who lives in a widget on your Home Screen and keeps you company while you write. Its status quietly follows how you use Bear: it strolls around the meadow when you’ve opened Bear recently, scribbles in its own little notebook while you write, watches the clouds while you read, and takes a nap in the grass when you’ve been away for a while. It’s as old as your very first note, and its weight grows with every note you write.
Six new app icons
What’s a birthday without a little dress up? We’ve crafted six new app icons2 for the occasion: a special 10th anniversary icon, Bear with Birdie, a golden Bear, a peeking Bear, and two classic pixel Bears. We hope they bring a bit of fun to your Home Screen, and a gentle reminder to enjoy the little things in life.
Did somebody say Bear swag?
Yes, they are finally here! Many of you have been asking for Bear merch and we have been secretly working on them! Our 10th anniversary merch features pixel art of a classic Macintosh with the Bear logo glowing on its screen and our little Birdie perched on top, a nod to where it all began. Check our merch page below to grab your Bear swag!
See you in the next decade
Thank you for being part of the story, whether you’ve been here since day one or found Bear last week. We’d love to hear about your favorite hidden detail, or one you just discovered in this post. Come say happy birthday to us on our Community Forum, Reddit, X (Twitter), Bluesky, or directly at bear@shinyfrog.net.
Happy Writing!
🐻❤️📝
